guides.title: Atmospheric Circulation and Global Wind Belts
guides.summary: How the sun, the spin of the Earth and the arrangement of land and sea organize the atmosphere into trade winds, westerlies, jet streams and monsoons, and why those wind belts decide where deserts, rainforests and storm tracks sit.

sections.heading: Why the Atmosphere Circulates: Uneven Solar Heating
sections.body:
The whole global wind machine runs on one simple imbalance: the sun does not heat the Earth evenly. Averaged over the year, the top of the atmosphere receives about 340 watts per square meter of incoming sunlight, but that average hides an enormous difference between latitudes. Near the equator the sun climbs high in the sky every day of the year, so its rays strike the surface almost head on and are concentrated onto a small area. Near the poles the same beam of sunlight arrives at a shallow, glancing angle and is smeared across a much larger area, and for months at a time in winter it does not arrive at all. The tropics therefore absorb far more energy than they radiate back to space, while the polar regions radiate more than they absorb.

If nothing moved that energy around, the tropics would grow hotter year after year and the poles colder, yet measurements show both stay roughly in balance. The books are balanced by transport: the atmosphere and the oceans together carry surplus heat poleward, with the peak flow near latitude 35 degrees amounting to several petawatts, thousands of times the output of all human power plants combined. The atmosphere does the larger share of this work in most latitudes, moving warm air poleward and cold air equatorward, while ocean currents such as the Gulf Stream handle much of the rest.

The basic mechanism is convection, the same process that stirs a heated pot of water. Warm air near the tropical surface expands, becomes less dense than its surroundings, and rises. Cold dense air near the poles sinks and spreads out along the surface. Rising air in one place must be replaced by air flowing in along the surface, and sinking air must spread away, so a closed loop, or circulation cell, forms. In 1735 the English lawyer and amateur scientist George Hadley proposed exactly this picture: air rises at the equator, flows poleward aloft, sinks at high latitudes and returns along the surface.

Hadley imagined a single giant loop in each hemisphere stretching from equator to pole. The real Earth is more complicated, because the planet rotates and because a single cell that long turns out to be dynamically unstable. What actually forms in each hemisphere is a chain of three linked cells, the Hadley cell in the tropics, the Ferrel cell in the middle latitudes and a polar cell near each pole, with distinct wind belts at the surface beneath each one. Those belts, the trade winds, the westerlies and the polar easterlies, were known to sailors centuries before anyone could explain them.

Everything in the rest of this guide, from why the Sahara sits where it does to why storms cross the United States from west to east, follows from this one chain of causes: unequal heating creates pressure differences, pressure differences drive winds, and the rotation of the Earth bends those winds into the belts we observe. Keep that chain in mind and the global pattern stops looking arbitrary and starts looking inevitable.

sections.heading: The Hadley Cell and the Intertropical Convergence Zone
sections.body:
The Hadley cell is the largest and most reliable feature of the general circulation. Intense sunshine over the equatorial belt heats the surface, and the moist air above it rises in towering thunderstorm clouds whose tops reach the tropopause, the ceiling of the weather layer, at roughly 15 to 17 kilometers over the tropics. This rising branch is concentrated in a narrow band called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, usually shortened to ITCZ, where the surface winds of the two hemispheres flow together. From space the ITCZ appears as a broken chain of bright white cloud clusters circling the planet near the equator.

Air that rises in the ITCZ cools, sheds its moisture as heavy tropical rain, and spreads poleward at high altitude in both hemispheres. It cannot travel all the way to the poles; by about latitude 25 to 30 degrees it has cooled, converged and begun to sink. The descending branch of the Hadley cell produces the subtropical high pressure belts described in a later section. At the surface, air flows back from those highs toward the equator, completing the loop, and the rotation of the Earth bends that returning flow westward to create the trade winds. The whole cell was named for George Hadley, who described its essential physics in 1735, though he wrongly imagined it reaching the pole.

The rising branch is where much of the rain in the world falls. Places under the ITCZ for most of the year, such as the Amazon basin, the Congo basin and the islands of Indonesia, receive 2,000 to 4,000 millimeters of rain annually and host the great equatorial rainforests. Sailors called the zone the doldrums, because between the steady trade wind belts lies a strip of light, fitful winds and glassy calms punctuated by violent squalls, a notorious trap for sailing ships that could drift for weeks waiting for wind.

The ITCZ is not fixed. It migrates with the seasons, following the zone of strongest heating, moving north in the northern summer and south in the northern winter. Over the oceans it shifts only a few degrees, but over large landmasses, which heat and cool quickly, it can swing 20 degrees or more of latitude. This seasonal march is what gives much of the tropics a wet season and a dry season rather than year-round rain. The Sahel region on the southern edge of the Sahara, for example, gets nearly all its rain in the few months when the ITCZ reaches its northernmost position; a year when the zone stops short brings drought and failed harvests.

The Hadley circulation also sets the vertical structure of tropical weather. The sinking air on its poleward flanks creates a persistent temperature inversion, a lid of warm air aloft that caps convection, which is why fair-weather cumulus clouds over the trade wind oceans all seem to flatten at the same modest height. Understanding where the Hadley cell rises and sinks in a given season is the single most useful key to tropical climate.

sections.heading: Trade Winds: The Steady Easterlies of the Tropics
sections.body:
Between the subtropical highs near 30 degrees latitude and the ITCZ near the equator blow the most dependable winds on Earth, the trade winds. In the Northern Hemisphere they arrive from the northeast, in the Southern Hemisphere from the southeast, both bending toward the west as they approach the equator. The name comes from an old use of the word trade meaning a fixed track or course; the winds blow so steadily along the same path that the great sailing routes of the sixteenth through nineteenth centuries were built around them. Christopher Columbus rode the northeast trades west across the Atlantic in 1492, covering the crossing in about five weeks, and returned home on the westerlies farther north, a loop Spanish navigators later formalized as the volta do mar, the turn of the sea.

Over the open ocean the trades typically blow at 15 to 25 kilometers per hour, day after day, with a persistence unmatched by any other surface wind. They exist because air flows out of the subtropical high pressure belts toward the low pressure of the ITCZ, and the Coriolis effect, weak but not absent at low latitudes, deflects that equatorward flow toward the west. Because the pressure difference driving them is renewed constantly by the Hadley circulation, the trades rarely fail, though their strength breathes with the seasons and weakens dramatically during El Niño events in the Pacific.

A characteristic feature of the trade wind zone is the trade wind inversion, a layer of warm, dry, sinking air from the descending branch of the Hadley cell that sits a kilometer or two above the sea surface. Moist air rising from the warm ocean hits this lid and flattens, producing the endless fields of puffy, flat-topped cumulus clouds that fill the tropical oceans. The inversion keeps most trade wind weather fair, with brief showers rather than deep storms, which is one reason island groups like Hawaii have such famously pleasant climates on their windward coasts.

The trades are also a global conveyor of material. Every year they carry on the order of one hundred million tons of mineral dust from the Sahara westward across the Atlantic; some of it fertilizes the Amazon rainforest with phosphorus, some settles on Caribbean reefs, and a thick dust outbreak can turn skies milky as far away as Texas. The same winds steer tropical weather systems: Atlantic hurricanes are born in disturbances that roll off West Africa and are carried west toward the Caribbean by the trade flow, which is why forecasters watch the eastern tropical Atlantic so closely from August through October.

Where the trades blow across warm ocean toward a mountainous coast, they wring out heavy rain on windward slopes and leave rain shadows behind. Where they blow offshore or parallel to a coast, as along Peru and Namibia, they help drive cold upwelling water to the surface and create coastal deserts. A sailor, a farmer or a forecaster in the tropics who knows the local behavior of the trades knows most of what the sky is likely to do.

sections.heading: Subtropical Highs and the Horse Latitudes
sections.body:
Near 30 degrees of latitude in each hemisphere, the air that rose over the equator and traveled poleward aloft finally sinks back to the surface. Sinking air is compressed and warms as it descends, and warming air can hold more moisture, so clouds evaporate and rain becomes rare. The result is a belt of persistent high pressure, clear skies and light winds girdling each hemisphere, known as the subtropical high or subtropical ridge. Sailors of the square-rigger era called these becalmed belts the horse latitudes; one popular though unproven story says the name comes from ships bound for the Americas that, stalled for weeks without wind, ran short of water and threw dying horses overboard.

Over the oceans the belt organizes itself into enormous semi-permanent cells of high pressure that appear on every weather map. The Azores High, also called the Bermuda High when it noses westward, dominates the North Atlantic; the North Pacific High sits between Hawaii and California; the South Atlantic, South Pacific and Indian Oceans each carry a counterpart. These highs are strongest and shift poleward in summer, weaker and closer to the equator in winter. Air spirals outward from them clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern, feeding the trade winds on their equatorward side and the westerlies on their poleward side, which makes them the hinge of the entire surface circulation.

The sinking air of the subtropical ridge is the direct cause of the great warm deserts of the world. Run a finger along 25 to 30 degrees north on a globe and it crosses the Sahara, the deserts of Arabia and Iran, the Thar of India and the Sonoran and Chihuahuan deserts of North America; the matching line in the south crosses the Atacama, the Namib, the Kalahari and the vast arid interior of Australia. These are not accidents of geography but the fingerprints of the Hadley cell, deserts stamped onto whatever land happens to lie beneath its descending branch. The Sahara alone covers about nine million square kilometers, roughly the area of the United States.

The same ridges explain the prized Mediterranean pattern of dry summers and mild wet winters. In summer the Azores High expands and shields Spain, Italy, Greece, California and Chile from storms; in winter it contracts toward the equator and lets the westerlies and their rain-bearing lows sweep in. Regions on the eastern flanks of the ocean highs also sit over cold upwelled water, which stabilizes the air and produces the persistent marine stratus and fog of San Francisco, Lima and Walvis Bay.

For forecasting, the position and strength of the local subtropical high is a master variable. A strong summer Bermuda High pumps hot humid air into the eastern United States and steers hurricanes along its southern rim, sometimes into the Gulf of Mexico, sometimes harmlessly out to sea. A displaced South Pacific High is among the first signs of a developing El Niño. Watch the highs and much of the rest of the weather follows.

sections.heading: The Ferrel Cell and the Prevailing Westerlies
sections.body:
Between about 30 and 60 degrees of latitude lies the belt where most people in Europe, North America and East Asia live, and its prevailing surface winds blow from the west. These westerlies are the reason weather systems in the middle latitudes almost always arrive from the west, why a storm leaving the Rockies reaches the Atlantic seaboard a few days later, and why flying from New York to London is typically about an hour faster than flying back. The belt is named for the American schoolteacher and self-taught scientist William Ferrel, who in 1856 worked out how the rotation of the Earth shapes the winds and proposed the mid-latitude circulation cell that carries his name.

The Ferrel cell is different in kind from the Hadley cell. The Hadley cell is thermally direct, driven straight by heating, with warm air rising and cold air sinking. The Ferrel cell is indirect: on average, air in it rises near 60 degrees, where it is relatively cold, and sinks near 30 degrees, where it is relatively warm, the opposite of what heating alone would do. It is best thought of not as a sturdy conveyor belt but as the statistical residue of countless traveling storms and eddies, which do the real work of moving heat poleward in the middle latitudes. The surface westerlies are what those eddies add up to over a season.

Because the westerly belt is a battleground where warm subtropical air meets cold polar air, its weather is famously changeable. The boundary between the two air masses, the polar front, spawns the traveling low pressure systems, warm fronts and cold fronts described in a later section. Between the storms, migrating high pressure cells bring spells of settled weather. Day-to-day forecasting in the middle latitudes is largely the art of tracking this endless procession of highs and lows riding the westerly current.

The Southern Hemisphere shows the westerlies in their purest form. South of 40 degrees there is almost no land to slow the wind, only the unbroken ring of the Southern Ocean, and the belt howls around the planet with legendary force. Sailors named the bands the Roaring Forties, the Furious Fifties and the Screaming Sixties, and clipper ships bound from Europe to Australia deliberately dropped deep into them to ride winds that could drive a ship over 400 nautical miles in a day. Modern round-the-world racing yachts follow the same track, and the persistent gales build the largest average waves on Earth, routinely six meters and more.

In the Northern Hemisphere the westerlies are constantly interrupted by the Rockies, the Alps, the Himalaya and the alternation of warm oceans and cold continents, which is why northern mid-latitude weather is less regular but also less relentlessly violent. The westerlies strengthen in winter, when the temperature contrast between tropics and pole is greatest, and weaken in summer. Their long-term behavior matters enormously: a small poleward shift of the southern westerlies in recent decades has altered rainfall in Australia, Patagonia and South Africa and changed how the Southern Ocean absorbs carbon dioxide.

sections.heading: The Polar Cells and the Polar Easterlies
sections.body:
The third and weakest link in the three-cell chain sits over the highest latitudes. Air above the poles is intensely chilled, especially through the long polar night, and cold air is dense, so it sinks. The sinking air creates shallow domes of high pressure at the surface, the polar highs, from which air drains outward toward lower latitudes. As it flows away from the pole the Coriolis effect bends it toward the west, so the surface winds between roughly 60 degrees and the pole blow on average from the east. These are the polar easterlies, the least steady and least famous of the global wind belts, but a real and measurable feature, particularly around the edge of Antarctica and over the Arctic Ocean in winter.

Where the cold easterly flow from the pole meets the warmer westerly flow of the middle latitudes, near 60 degrees, the two air masses do not mix easily. The warmer, lighter air is forced to rise over the dense polar air along a boundary called the polar front. Rising air means low pressure, and indeed a belt of frequent low pressure rings each hemisphere near this latitude, expressed as the semi-permanent Icelandic Low and Aleutian Low in the north and an almost continuous trough around Antarctica in the south. The rising branch over 60 degrees and sinking branch over the pole complete the small polar cell, which, like the Hadley cell, is thermally direct.

The polar regions add a purely local wind of their own that can dwarf the gentle easterlies: the katabatic wind. The ice sheets of Antarctica and Greenland sit kilometers high, and the air in contact with the ice surface becomes brutally cold and dense. Gravity pulls this heavy air downslope toward the coast, accelerating it through valleys like water in a funnel. At Commonwealth Bay in Antarctica, where the explorer Douglas Mawson wintered in 1912 and 1913, katabatic gales average around 80 kilometers per hour over the year and gusts have exceeded 300 kilometers per hour, making it by many measures the windiest sea-level place on Earth.

The cold dome over each pole also anchors an upper-level feature that has entered everyday vocabulary, the polar vortex. This is a broad ring of strong westerly winds in the stratosphere, 15 to 50 kilometers up, that forms each winter and corrals the coldest air over the pole. When the vortex is strong and circular, polar air stays locked up and the middle latitudes have a mild winter. When it weakens or splits, an event meteorologists call a sudden stratospheric warming, lobes of frigid air can spill southward, and places like the central United States, Europe or East Asia experience the severe cold outbreaks that headlines attribute to the vortex.

The polar cells are also where climate change shows itself first and fastest. The Arctic has warmed roughly three to four times faster than the global average since 1979, shrinking the temperature contrast that drives the northern belts, and scientists actively debate how this is reshaping the jet stream and mid-latitude weather. The quietest wind belt, in other words, has become one of the most closely watched.

sections.heading: The Coriolis Effect: Why Winds Curve
sections.body:
If the Earth did not spin, winds would simply blow in straight lines from high pressure to low pressure and the global circulation would be a pair of simple loops from equator to pole. The reason it is not, the reason for trade winds that blow from the northeast rather than the north and storms that spin, is the Coriolis effect, named for the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis, who worked out the mathematics of motion in rotating systems in 1835. It is not a push or a pull but a consequence of observing motion from a platform that is itself turning.

The standard way to see it is with a merry-go-round. Roll a ball straight across a spinning carousel and, to someone standing on the carousel, the ball appears to curve, because the floor rotates beneath it while it travels. The Earth is such a carousel. A parcel of air at the equator is being carried eastward by the rotation of the planet at about 1,670 kilometers per hour; at 45 degrees latitude the ground moves eastward at only about 1,180 kilometers per hour, and at the poles not at all. Air that moves north or south carries its original eastward momentum with it, so relative to the ground it drifts ahead of or behind the surface it arrives over. The net rule is simple and worth memorizing: in the Northern Hemisphere moving air is deflected to the right of its direction of travel, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left, and the effect is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles.

The deflection is subtle. It is far too weak to influence water draining from a sink or bathtub, a persistent myth; drain direction is set by the basin shape and any leftover swirl in the water. The Coriolis effect matters only for motions that persist for hours and stretch over many kilometers, which is exactly the scale of winds, ocean currents and artillery shells. Long-range gunners genuinely must correct for it; a shell fired 40 kilometers can land tens of meters to the side of its aim point if the rotation of the Earth is ignored.

On the weather map the Coriolis effect produces a beautiful compromise called geostrophic balance. Air starts moving from high toward low pressure, the deflection bends it sideways, and it settles into a path running parallel to the isobars, with the pressure force pulling one way and the Coriolis deflection the other. This is why winds circulate around pressure centers instead of rushing into them: counterclockwise around lows and clockwise around highs in the Northern Hemisphere, the reverse in the Southern. The Dutch meteorologist Christophorus Buys Ballot summarized it in 1857 in a rule every sailor once learned: stand with your back to the wind in the Northern Hemisphere and low pressure lies on your left.

Applied to the global belts, the effect explains everything about their direction. Surface air flowing equatorward from the subtropical highs bends westward and becomes the easterly trades. Air flowing poleward from the same highs bends eastward and becomes the westerlies. Air draining off the polar highs bends westward into the polar easterlies. One planet-sized bookkeeping rule, three wind belts.

sections.heading: Jet Streams: Rivers of Air Aloft
sections.body:
High above the surface wind belts, near the top of the weather layer at 9 to 12 kilometers, flow narrow, fast currents of air called jet streams. A jet stream is typically a few hundred kilometers wide, only a few kilometers deep, and thousands of kilometers long, snaking around the hemisphere like a river seen from space. Core wind speeds commonly run 150 to 250 kilometers per hour in winter and have been measured above 400 kilometers per hour in the strongest segments over the northwest Pacific and East Asia. Each hemisphere has two main jets: the polar jet, near 50 to 60 degrees latitude, and the weaker subtropical jet near 30 degrees, sitting atop the descending edge of the Hadley cell.

Jet streams exist because of temperature contrast. Cold air is compact and warm air is expansive, so the pressure at a given altitude falls off much faster on the cold side of a boundary than on the warm side. Where tropical and polar air meet, this creates a strong horizontal pressure difference aloft, and the Coriolis effect turns the resulting flow into a fast current running parallel to the temperature boundary, from west to east in both hemispheres. The sharper the temperature contrast, the faster the jet, which is why the jets are strongest in winter and why the polar jet sits directly above the polar front at the surface.

The existence of these currents was suspected by the Japanese meteorologist Wasaburo Oishi, who tracked weather balloons above Mount Fuji in the 1920s and measured astonishing westerly speeds, but his reports, published in Esperanto, went largely unread. The jets forced themselves on the world during the Second World War, when American B-29 crews flying toward Japan at high altitude found themselves battling headwinds or riding tailwinds of 200 kilometers per hour and more, wrecking their bombing runs. Japan even used the current deliberately, launching some nine thousand paper balloon bombs into the jet stream toward North America in 1944 and 1945.

Aviation has been shaped by the jets ever since. Eastbound flights across the Atlantic and Pacific ride them, saving an hour or more and significant fuel; westbound flights route around their cores. Clear-air turbulence, the invisible bumpiness that injures more airline passengers than any other weather hazard, is concentrated along the sheared edges of jet streams, which is one reason pilots ask passengers to keep seat belts fastened even in cloudless skies.

For surface weather, the polar jet is the conductor of the mid-latitude orchestra. Storms form and intensify beneath particular segments of the jet where its structure favors rising air, and they are steered along its path. A jet flowing nearly straight west to east, called zonal flow, sends weather systems marching briskly and brings changeable but moderate conditions. A jet thrown into deep north-south meanders, called meridional flow, drags tropical warmth far poleward on one side and arctic cold far equatorward on the other, and can lock weather patterns in place for weeks. Every forecast of a cold outbreak, an atmospheric river or a heat dome begins with a map of where the jet stream is and where it is going.

sections.heading: The Polar Front, Rossby Waves and Mid-Latitude Storms
sections.body:
The changeable weather of the middle latitudes is organized by a single great boundary: the polar front, the zone where cold, dry polar air masses meet warm, moist subtropical ones. The contrast across it can be dramatic, ten or fifteen degrees Celsius in a few hundred kilometers. Just after the First World War, a group of meteorologists working in Bergen, Norway, led by Vilhelm Bjerknes and his son Jacob, built the modern picture of how storms grow on this boundary, and they deliberately borrowed the word front from the battlefields of the war they had just lived through.

In the Bergen model, a mid-latitude storm begins as a small ripple on the polar front. Warm air starts to bulge poleward and cold air to push equatorward behind it, and the ripple wraps up into a spinning low pressure center, a cyclone, typically a thousand to two thousand kilometers across. Ahead of the center, the advancing warm air glides up over the retreating cold air along a warm front, producing a broad shield of layered cloud and steady rain that can arrive a day before the center itself. Behind the center, dense cold air drives under the warm air along a cold front, a sharper boundary marked by a narrow line of showers and thunderstorms, a quick wind shift and a drop in temperature. Eventually the cold front overtakes the warm front, the warm air is lifted entirely off the surface in an occlusion, and the storm, cut off from its energy source, slowly spins down. The whole life cycle takes three to seven days, during which the storm may travel from the central Pacific to the Rockies or from Newfoundland to Norway.

These surface storms are the lower half of a deeper structure. The upper westerlies and the polar jet do not flow in a circle; they meander in enormous horizontal waves named for the Swedish-American meteorologist Carl-Gustaf Rossby, who explained them in 1939. A hemisphere typically carries three to seven of these Rossby waves at once. Their equatorward dips are called troughs and their poleward bulges ridges, and the geometry matters intensely: air rising ahead of an upper trough is exactly what a surface low needs to deepen. Forecasters therefore live on upper-air charts, hunting the troughs that will breed the next storm.

Sometimes the westerly flow buckles so deeply that a wave stops moving altogether, a situation called blocking. A blocking high can park over a region for one to three weeks, diverting the storm track around it. Blocks produce many of the most damaging weather events in the record: the Russian heat wave of 2010, which killed tens of thousands, the repeated cold spells of European winters when a block over Scandinavia drags in Siberian air, and long wet sieges when storms are funneled again and again over the same valleys.

Seen from this altitude, mid-latitude weather stops being a sequence of random events. It is the polar front flexing, wrinkling into storms, and being folded by planetary waves, an endless negotiation between the cold half of the planet and the warm half, conducted in the language of wind.

sections.heading: Monsoons: Seasonal Wind Reversals
sections.body:
A monsoon is not simply a rainy season; it is a wholesale seasonal reversal of the wind, and it happens because land and ocean respond to the sun at different speeds. Rock and soil heat quickly and cool quickly; the ocean, which mixes heat through tens of meters of water, changes temperature slowly. In summer a great landmass becomes much warmer than the neighboring sea, the air over it rises, surface pressure falls, and moist ocean air pours inland, bringing months of rain. In winter the land becomes colder than the sea, pressure over the continent rises, and dry air drains back out toward the ocean. The word comes from the Arabic mausim, meaning season, coined by sailors of the Indian Ocean who scheduled entire trading voyages around the reversal, running east to India and beyond on the summer southwesterlies and home on the winter northeasterlies.

The most powerful example is the South Asian monsoon. Through spring the Indian subcontinent bakes, with pre-monsoon temperatures in the north routinely above 40 degrees Celsius, while the Tibetan Plateau acts as a raised hotplate warming the air at altitude. Around the first of June, with a punctuality that has been tracked for more than a century, the southwest monsoon bursts onto the coast of the state of Kerala, then advances northward over the following six weeks until the whole subcontinent is under its clouds. Between June and September India receives roughly three quarters of its annual rainfall. Where the moist flow is forced up mountain slopes the totals become almost unbelievable: Mawsynram and Cherrapunji, villages in the Khasi Hills of northeastern India, average close to 12,000 millimeters of rain a year, the highest on Earth.

The stakes could hardly be higher. Nearly half of humanity lives in regions watered by monsoons, and in India alone hundreds of millions of farmers depend on rain-fed fields. A monsoon season ten percent below normal is a national emergency; historic failures, as in 1876 to 1878 and 1899, contributed to famines that killed millions. Modern forecasting agencies therefore spend enormous effort predicting the onset date and seasonal total, and the Indian economy is still described, only half in jest, as a gamble on the rains.

Asia has the largest monsoon, but not the only one. The East Asian monsoon soaks China, Korea and Japan, with a distinctive early-summer stationary front called the meiyu or baiu rains. The West African monsoon draws Atlantic moisture into the Sahel between June and September and its year-to-year mood decides harvests from Senegal to Sudan. Northern Australia has a wet season driven by the same physics between December and March, and the southwestern United States and Mexico have a smaller North American monsoon that brings summer thunderstorms to Arizona and New Mexico, typically beginning in early July.

In the framework of this guide, a monsoon is what happens when continental heating becomes strong enough to drag the ITCZ and its rain belt deep over land, temporarily overwriting the ordinary wind belts. It is the loudest annual demonstration that the circulation is not fixed scenery but a live response to where the heat is.

sections.heading: Local Winds: Sea Breezes, Mountain Winds and Famous Named Winds
sections.body:
Beneath the planetary belts, geography brews its own winds on scales of a few kilometers to a few hundred. They matter because they are the winds people actually feel on a given afternoon, and because they follow the same physics as the global circulation in miniature: differential heating makes pressure differences, and air flows to even them out.

The classic example is the sea breeze. On a sunny day the land warms much faster than the sea, air rises over the coast, and by late morning a cool onshore breeze sets in, usually 15 to 30 kilometers per hour, penetrating tens of kilometers inland by afternoon. Its leading edge, the sea breeze front, behaves like a small cold front and often fires a line of afternoon thunderstorms; peninsular Florida owes its status as one of the most lightning-struck places in North America largely to sea breezes converging from both coasts. At night the circulation reverses into a gentler land breeze as the ground cools below the sea temperature. Mountain regions run a similar daily cycle: heated slopes draw valley winds upward during the day, and after sunset cold dense air drains downslope and pools in valley floors, which is why frost gathers in hollows and why vineyards and orchards are planted on slopes above the cold pool.

When wind crosses a mountain range, the descending air on the lee side is compressed and warms at about one degree Celsius per hundred meters. The result is the foehn family of warm, dry, gusty downslope winds, called the chinook on the eastern side of the Rockies, where it can raise winter temperatures by 20 degrees Celsius in an hour and strip snow cover in a day, and the foehn proper in the Alps. The Santa Ana winds of Southern California are a related drainage of dry desert air from the Great Basin that accelerates through coastal passes in autumn, drying vegetation and fanning the region's worst wildfires. Cold katabatic relatives include the mistral, which funnels down the Rhone valley of France and can blow over 90 kilometers per hour for days, and the bora of the Adriatic, dense polar air spilling over the Dinaric Alps.

Other famous names belong to seasonal or belt-driven flows. The harmattan is the dry, dusty northeasterly trade wind of West Africa in winter, hazing skies from November to March. The sirocco carries hot Saharan air, and often red dust, north across the Mediterranean into Italy and the Balkans. The levanter squeezes easterly wind through the Strait of Gibraltar, and the etesian or meltemi winds ventilate the Aegean every summer as air flows from the Balkan high toward the Asian monsoon low, a direct visible link between local sailing weather and the planetary monsoon system.

For practical purposes, local winds reward local knowledge. A coastal sailor plans an afternoon return trip around the sea breeze; a mountain pilot avoids lee slopes in strong cross-mountain flow because of violent rotor turbulence; a firefighter in California watches the autumn pressure pattern for Santa Ana setups. Learn the handful of winds your own landscape makes, and the daily forecast becomes far less mysterious.

sections.heading: El Niño, La Niña and the Walker Circulation
sections.body:
The wind belts described so far run roughly east to west or north to south, but the tropics also host giant circulation loops oriented along the equator, driven by differences in ocean temperature from one side of an ocean basin to the other. The most important is the Walker circulation over the Pacific, named for the British scientist Sir Gilbert Walker, who in the 1920s, while directing the observatories of India and hunting for monsoon predictors, discovered a mysterious seesaw in pressure between the eastern and western Pacific that he called the Southern Oscillation.

In a normal year the trade winds pile warm surface water into the far western Pacific, where sea temperatures around Indonesia exceed 29 degrees Celsius and the warm layer runs deep. Air rises over this warm pool in constant thunderstorms, flows eastward aloft, and sinks over the cooler eastern Pacific near South America, where the trades drag deep cold water to the surface along the equator and the Peruvian coast. That upwelled water is rich in nutrients and supports one of the greatest fisheries on Earth, the Peruvian anchoveta. The loop of rising air in the west and sinking air in the east, closed by the trades below and westerlies aloft, is the Walker circulation working as designed.

Every two to seven years the machine slips. The trade winds slacken, the warm pool sloshes eastward along the equator, and the upwelling of cold water off South America shuts down. Peruvian fishermen, who noticed the warm coastal water often arrived around Christmas, named the phenomenon El Niño, the Child, after the Christ child. With the warm water goes the rainfall: the thunderstorm zone follows the warmth into the central and eastern Pacific, drought grips Indonesia and eastern Australia, often with severe forest fires, while normally arid coastal Peru and Ecuador can suffer catastrophic floods. The opposite phase, La Niña, is an overachieving normal state, with harder trades, a colder eastern Pacific and rainfall crowded even farther west. The whole coupled cycle is called ENSO, for El Niño Southern Oscillation, and Jacob Bjerknes in 1969 supplied the key insight that the ocean pattern and the pressure seesaw Walker found are one phenomenon.

Because the tropical Pacific spans a third of the circumference of the Earth, rearranging its rainfall disturbs the whole atmosphere. These remote effects, called teleconnections, are statistical but strong. A significant El Niño typically brings a wet, stormy winter to California and the southern United States, a mild winter to the northern states and western Canada, drought to southern Africa and northeastern Brazil, a weakened Indian monsoon and a quiet Atlantic hurricane season, because its altered winds shear Atlantic storms apart. La Niña tends to flip most of those signs, and its cooler Pacific has historically coincided with active Atlantic hurricane years and drought in the American Southwest.

The strongest recorded events, in 1982 to 1983, 1997 to 1998 and 2015 to 2016, each reshuffled global weather for a year and temporarily lifted global average temperature. Forecasting agencies now watch the equatorial Pacific with moored buoys, satellites and models, and issue ENSO outlooks months ahead; for seasonal prediction, no other single number carries as much weight.

sections.heading: How Wind Belts Shape Deserts, Rainforests and Ocean Currents
sections.body:
Lay a vegetation map of the world beside a diagram of the three-cell circulation and the correspondence is unmistakable. The rising branch of the Hadley cell paints a green stripe of rainforest along the equator through Amazonia, the Congo and Southeast Asia. The sinking branches near 30 degrees stamp out the tawny belts of the Sahara, Arabia, Australia and the Atacama. The stormy westerlies water the temperate forests of Europe, the Pacific Northwest, Chile and New Zealand, and the cold dry interiors under continental winter highs grow steppe and taiga. Climate classification schemes, from the Koppen system of 1884 onward, are in large part maps of what the wind belts deliver.

The belts also drive the ocean. Wind dragging on the sea surface is the engine of the great surface currents, and the pattern of trades below 30 degrees and westerlies above it spins the water of each ocean basin into an enormous loop called a gyre, clockwise in the Northern Hemisphere and counterclockwise in the Southern. The North Atlantic gyre, for example, runs westward with the trades as the North Equatorial Current, pours poleward along North America as the Gulf Stream, crosses toward Europe under the westerlies as the North Atlantic Current, and drifts back south past the Canaries. Warm western boundary currents like the Gulf Stream and the Kuroshio carry tropical heat poleward and give northwestern Europe winters far milder than its latitude deserves; cool eastern boundary currents like the California, Humboldt, Canary and Benguela chill their coasts, suppress rain and help maintain the coastal deserts and fog belts.

Because of the Coriolis effect, wind-driven surface water does not move straight downwind; the net transport in the upper ocean is about 90 degrees to the wind, a result worked out by the Swedish oceanographer Vagn Walfrid Ekman in 1905. Where trade winds blow along the equator or alongshore winds blow toward the equator on the west coasts of continents, this Ekman transport pushes surface water away and cold, nutrient-rich water rises to replace it. These upwelling zones, off Peru, California, Northwest Africa and Namibia, cover a tiny fraction of the ocean yet yield a large share of the global fish catch, which is why an El Niño that shuts down Peruvian upwelling is an economic disaster as well as a curiosity of physics.

Humans have always ridden the belts. The Manila galleons of 1565 to 1815 ran west across the Pacific on the trades and home on the westerlies; the tea clippers dropped into the Roaring Forties; modern airline dispatchers file eastbound flight plans along the jet stream, and shipping companies still route to use following winds and currents.

The belts are not eternal. Observations since 1979 show the tropical Hadley circulation widening by roughly a quarter to half a degree of latitude per decade, pushing the dry subtropical zones poleward, and the southern westerlies have shifted south and strengthened, changes implicated in drying trends in southern Australia, central Chile and the Mediterranean. The wind map of the next century will not quite be the one in this guide, which is one more reason to understand the machinery behind it.

guides.title: The Stratosphere and the Ozone Layer
guides.summary: How the stratosphere is structured and why it is warm at the top, the chemistry that creates and destroys the ozone layer, how industrial chemicals thinned it and how the Antarctic ozone hole forms, the Montreal Protocol and the state of recovery, and what stratospheric behaviour means for weather and for ultraviolet exposure at the surface.

sections.heading: A Thin Shell That Makes the Land Habitable
sections.body:
Roughly ten to fifty kilometres above your head lies a layer of air that weighs about as much as a
sixth of the atmosphere and contains, spread very thinly through it, a gas that exists nowhere in
useful quantity at ground level. That gas is ozone, and it absorbs the band of solar ultraviolet
radiation that breaks the chemical bonds in DNA. Without it, the surface of the continents would be
sterilised by sunlight. Life would be confined to a few metres of water, roughly where it was before
the Great Oxidation Event some two and a half billion years ago. The ozone layer is not a comfort; it
is a precondition.

The layer is also startlingly insubstantial. Ozone makes up only about one molecule in a hundred
thousand of the air even at its peak concentration around twenty-five kilometres. If you could gather
all the ozone in a vertical column above one square metre and compress it to the pressure and
temperature at sea level, it would form a shell about three millimetres thick, roughly the height of
two stacked coins. That three millimetres does all the work. The realisation in the 1970s that
industrial chemicals could measurably thin it, and the discovery in the 1980s that a hole opened over
Antarctica each spring, is one of the few occasions in history when humanity identified a global
environmental threat, understood its chemistry, agreed a binding treaty and reversed the damage.

The stratosphere matters for a second reason, which is meteorological rather than biological. It is
the lid on the weather. Almost all cloud, rain, storms and wind that anyone experiences occur in the
troposphere below it, and they stop at the boundary because the stratosphere is stable in a way the
troposphere is not. That stability is a direct consequence of ozone: absorbing ultraviolet radiation
heats the upper stratosphere, so temperature increases with height there, which suppresses vertical
motion. The ozone layer therefore both shields the surface and structures the atmosphere. Change one
and you change the other, which is why ozone depletion has measurably altered Southern Hemisphere
wind patterns and rainfall.

Finally, the stratosphere is where the atmosphere keeps its long memory. Air that enters through the
tropical tropopause takes months to years to travel poleward and descend, so a volcanic aerosol cloud
or a nuclear test signature persists for a year or more where a tropospheric plume would rain out in a
week. That slow overturning connects the tropics to the poles, sets the lifetime of ozone-destroying
chemicals, and explains why a refrigerant released in Ohio in 1975 was still destroying ozone above
Antarctica in 2020. What follows works through this system from the ground up: the structure, the
physics of the temperature inversion, the chemistry that makes and unmakes ozone, the catalytic cycles
that industry accidentally amplified, the polar hole, the treaty that fixed it, and the couplings that
tie all of it back to the weather you actually experience.

sections.heading: The Vertical Structure of the Atmosphere
sections.body:
The atmosphere is conventionally divided into layers by how temperature changes with height, because
that quantity controls stability, mixing and almost everything else. Working upward, there are four
main layers, separated by boundaries whose names end in -pause.

The troposphere runs from the surface to between about eight kilometres at the poles and seventeen or
eighteen kilometres over the tropics, and holds roughly eighty per cent of the atmosphere's mass and
almost all of its water vapour. Temperature falls with height at an average of about six and a half
degrees Celsius per kilometre, the environmental lapse rate, from a global mean near fifteen degrees
Celsius at the surface to somewhere between minus fifty-five and minus eighty at the tropopause. The
name comes from the Greek tropos, meaning turning: it is the layer that overturns, driven by solar
heating of the ground.

The stratosphere sits above the tropopause and extends to the stratopause at about fifty kilometres,
where the pressure is around one hectopascal, a thousandth of surface pressure. Temperature is roughly
constant through its lower part and then rises with height, reaching close to zero degrees Celsius at
the stratopause. Ozone is concentrated in its lower and middle portions. Because temperature increases
upward, the layer is stratified, which gives it its name.

Above that the mesosphere runs to the mesopause near eighty-five kilometres, where temperature falls
again with height to the coldest temperatures in the whole atmosphere, around minus ninety degrees
Celsius, because there is little ozone to absorb sunlight but plenty of carbon dioxide emitting
infrared to space. Meteors burn up here, and the highest clouds on Earth, noctilucent clouds of ice on
meteoric dust, form at these temperatures. Above the mesopause, the thermosphere heats dramatically to
hundreds or thousands of degrees as extreme ultraviolet and X-ray photons are absorbed by atomic
oxygen and nitrogen, though the gas is so thin that this temperature carries almost no heat; the
International Space Station orbits within it.

Pressure, unlike temperature, falls monotonically and roughly exponentially with height. The scale
height, the distance over which pressure falls by a factor of e, is about seven to eight kilometres in
the lower atmosphere, so pressure halves roughly every five and a half kilometres. At the tropopause
it is about a quarter of surface pressure; at forty kilometres about three thousandths. Two further
classifications cut across these layers. The homosphere, below about one hundred kilometres, is well
enough mixed that the major gases keep constant proportions; above it, in the heterosphere, gases
separate by molecular weight. And the ionosphere, overlapping mesosphere and thermosphere, is the
electrically conducting region that reflects shortwave radio around the curve of the Earth, which is
why a transmitter in one hemisphere can be heard in the other.

sections.heading: Why Temperature Rises With Height in the Stratosphere
sections.body:
The single fact that defines the stratosphere is its temperature inversion, and understanding its
cause explains almost everything else about the layer. In the troposphere, sunlight passes largely
through the air and is absorbed at the ground, which then warms the air from below by conduction,
convection and infrared emission. Heat a fluid from below and it overturns; that is why the
troposphere convects and why temperature falls with height there. The stratosphere is heated from
within and from above instead, because ozone absorbs solar ultraviolet directly. The heating rate is
greatest where the product of ozone concentration and available ultraviolet flux is greatest, which is
in the upper stratosphere near forty to fifty kilometres, so that is where it is warmest.

The absorption happens in named spectral bands. The Hartley band, from about two hundred to three
hundred nanometres and peaking near two hundred and fifty-five nanometres, is the strongest and does
most of the heating. The weaker Huggins bands, roughly three hundred to three hundred and sixty
nanometres, mop up the tail. Molecular oxygen contributes too, through the Schumann-Runge continuum
below about one hundred and seventy-five nanometres and the Herzberg continuum out to about two
hundred and forty-two nanometres, though these act higher up. The energy absorbed does not stay as
chemical energy: an ozone molecule split by a photon produces fragments with excess kinetic energy
that is shared out by collisions, which is simply heat.

The numbers are worth fixing. Solar heating of the stratosphere by ozone amounts to a few degrees
Celsius per day in the upper stratosphere, balanced against infrared cooling to space by carbon
dioxide at fifteen micrometres, ozone at nine and six micrometres, and water vapour. The stratosphere
is close to radiative equilibrium, meaning its temperature is set mainly by this balance between
absorbed sunlight and emitted infrared, with dynamics playing a smaller role than in the troposphere.

This has a consequence that surprises people: adding carbon dioxide warms the troposphere but cools
the stratosphere. In the dense lower atmosphere, extra carbon dioxide traps outgoing infrared and
warms. In the thin stratosphere, where the air is already able to radiate to space efficiently, extra
carbon dioxide mainly adds emitters, so the layer sheds heat faster and cools by roughly one to two
degrees Celsius per decade in the upper stratosphere. This differential response, warming below and
cooling above, is one of the clearest fingerprints distinguishing greenhouse warming from an increase
in solar output, which would warm both. Observed stratospheric cooling since the 1980s is consistent
with the combined effect of rising carbon dioxide and ozone loss, which also cools by removing an
absorber.

sections.heading: Stability, the Tropopause and the Lid on Weather
sections.body:
Stability in the atmosphere is a question about what happens to a parcel of air that is nudged upward.
As it rises, ambient pressure drops and the parcel expands, doing work on its surroundings and cooling
without exchanging heat, a process called adiabatic expansion. For dry air the cooling rate is fixed by
thermodynamics at 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometre, the dry adiabatic lapse rate, equal to the
acceleration due to gravity divided by the specific heat capacity of air at constant pressure. If the
surrounding air cools faster than that with height, the displaced parcel ends up warmer and therefore
less dense than its surroundings and keeps rising: the atmosphere is unstable and convection occurs. If
the surroundings cool more slowly, the parcel ends up colder and denser and sinks back: stable.

The troposphere's average lapse rate of about 6.5 degrees per kilometre is less than the dry adiabatic
rate but often exceeds the moist adiabatic rate, which is around 4 to 7 degrees per kilometre because
condensing water vapour releases latent heat and slows the cooling. That is why moist air is so much
more prone to violent convection, and why thunderstorms are a summer and tropical phenomenon.

In the stratosphere temperature is constant or increasing with height, so a rising parcel is always
colder and denser than its surroundings and is always pushed back down. This is very strong stability,
and it is what makes the tropopause a lid. The quantitative measure is the Brunt-Väisälä frequency,
the frequency at which a displaced parcel oscillates about its equilibrium level. In the troposphere
that period is around ten minutes; in the stratosphere around four to five minutes, indicating far
stiffer resistance to vertical motion.

The practical consequences are everywhere. Thunderstorm anvils spread horizontally when the updraught
hits the tropopause, producing the classic flat-topped cumulonimbus; only the most violent storms punch
a small overshooting top a kilometre or two into the stratosphere before collapsing. Airliners cruise
at ten to twelve kilometres partly for fuel efficiency in thin air and partly because the lower
stratosphere and upper troposphere are smooth. Volcanic ash injected only into the troposphere washes
out in days, while ash and sulphur reaching the stratosphere persist for years.

The tropopause itself is not a smooth surface. It is highest and coldest over the tropics, around
seventeen kilometres and minus eighty degrees Celsius, because deep convection pushes it up, and
lowest over the poles at around eight kilometres. It breaks and folds at the jet streams, where a
tongue of stratospheric air can descend into the troposphere, bringing dry, ozone-rich air down; these
tropopause folds are detectable in surface ozone measurements and are one of the natural sources of
ozone at ground level. Because the tropical tropopause is the coldest point air encounters on its way
up, it acts as a cold trap that freeze-dries entering air to a few parts per million of water vapour,
which is why the stratosphere is one of the driest places in the Earth system.

sections.heading: The Chapman Cycle: How Ozone Is Made and Unmade
sections.body:
Ozone is O3, three oxygen atoms bound together, and it is unstable relative to ordinary molecular
oxygen. It exists in the stratosphere only because sunlight continuously manufactures it there, in a
scheme set out by the British geophysicist Sydney Chapman in 1930. The Chapman cycle has four
reactions and gets the basic picture right, though it overpredicts the amount of ozone.

The first step is photolysis of molecular oxygen. A photon of ultraviolet radiation shorter than about
242 nanometres has enough energy to break the O=O double bond, splitting O2 into two free oxygen
atoms. This wavelength requirement is the key to the whole architecture: such photons are absorbed
high up, so oxygen atoms are produced mainly above about thirty kilometres.

The second step forms ozone. A free oxygen atom collides with an O2 molecule and they combine, but the
new molecule carries excess energy and would immediately fly apart unless a third body, usually a
nitrogen molecule, collides simultaneously and carries the energy away. This is written O + O2 + M
gives O3 + M, where M is any third molecule. Because it needs a three-body collision, its rate depends
on the square of air density, so it is fast low down and slow high up.

The third step destroys ozone by photolysis. Ozone absorbs ultraviolet from about 200 to 320
nanometres and splits into O2 and a free O atom. This is the reaction that shields the biosphere, and
crucially it does not consume ozone permanently, because the freed oxygen atom quickly re-forms ozone
through step two. Ozone and atomic oxygen interconvert rapidly, thousands of times, absorbing
ultraviolet each cycle and turning it into heat. The pair together is called odd oxygen.

The fourth step is real loss: an oxygen atom collides with an ozone molecule and both become O2,
removing two units of odd oxygen. This is slow, because free oxygen atoms are scarce below thirty
kilometres, and it is the bottleneck of the whole scheme.

It is worth being clear that ozone at ground level is a different problem with the same molecule.
Tropospheric ozone is a pollutant formed when sunlight acts on nitrogen oxides and volatile organic
compounds from traffic and industry; it irritates airways, damages crops, and is a greenhouse gas.
Roughly ninety per cent of atmospheric ozone is stratospheric and beneficial, ten per cent tropospheric
and harmful. The old slogan good up high, bad nearby captures it.

The balance between production high up, where ultraviolet is plentiful but air is thin, and the
three-body formation low down, where air is dense but the short-wavelength ultraviolet has already been
absorbed, produces a peak in ozone concentration around twenty to twenty-five kilometres in the
tropics and lower toward the poles. That is the ozone layer. Chapman's scheme, however, predicts
roughly twice the observed amount, because the fourth reaction alone is too slow to balance
production. The missing loss is supplied by catalytic cycles involving trace species, which were not
recognised until the 1950s and 1960s and which turned out to be the mechanism by which human activity
could reach the layer at all.

sections.heading: Measuring Ozone: Dobson Units and the Vertical Profile
sections.body:
The standard measure of ozone is the total column: the amount in a vertical shaft of atmosphere from
the ground to space, expressed in Dobson Units. One Dobson Unit is defined as a layer of pure ozone
0.01 millimetres thick at standard temperature and pressure, which is 2.69 times ten to the sixteenth
molecules per square centimetre. Global average total column ozone is about 300 DU, corresponding to
that three-millimetre shell. Values range from around 230 DU in the tropics to 400 DU or more at high
northern latitudes in spring. Antarctic values inside the springtime hole have fallen below 100 DU,
and on 5 October 1993 the South Pole ozonesonde recorded a minimum of 73 DU with essentially total
destruction between fourteen and nineteen kilometres.

A counterintuitive but important fact is that ozone is produced mainly in the tropics, where sunlight
is strongest, yet the tropical column is the lowest on Earth. The reason is transport: ozone is made
in the tropical upper stratosphere and then carried poleward and downward, accumulating at middle and
high latitudes. Column ozone therefore reflects circulation as much as chemistry, and any explanation
of ozone amounts that ignores dynamics will be wrong.

Measurement techniques divide into ground-based, in situ and satellite. The Dobson spectrophotometer,
developed by Gordon Dobson at Oxford from 1924, compares the intensity of two ultraviolet wavelengths
in scattered skylight, one strongly absorbed by ozone and one weakly, and derives the column from the
ratio. Instruments of this design, plus the later Brewer, still form the calibration
backbone of the global network. Ozonesondes are balloon-borne electrochemical cells in which ozone
reacts with potassium iodide and produces a current; released weekly from around seventy stations,
they give the vertical profile to about thirty-five kilometres.

Satellites provide global coverage. The Total Ozone Mapping Spectrometer flew from 1978 on Nimbus-7
and produced the first complete maps; its successors include the Ozone Monitoring Instrument on Aura
from 2004 and the Tropomi instrument on Sentinel-5P from 2017. Backscatter ultraviolet instruments
measure sunlight scattered back from the atmosphere; limb sounders look sideways through the
atmosphere for finer vertical resolution; occultation instruments watch the Sun or a star set through
the atmosphere and measure absorption directly. Lidar, which fires ultraviolet laser pulses upward and
times the backscatter, gives high-resolution profiles from the ground. Cross-calibrating all of these
against the Dobson network is a permanent and unglamorous task, and drifts between instruments have
been a real source of confusion in trend detection.

Two quantities are routinely confused and should be kept distinct. Total column ozone, in Dobson
Units, is the whole shaft integrated from ground to space, and it is what controls ultraviolet at the
surface. Ozone concentration at a given height, expressed either as a number density in molecules per
cubic centimetre or as a mixing ratio in parts per million by volume, describes the profile. Number
density peaks near twenty-two kilometres because air density falls with height; mixing ratio peaks
much higher, near thirty-two to thirty-five kilometres, where the fraction of the air that is ozone is
greatest. Both statements are correct and they describe the same layer.

sections.heading: The Brewer-Dobson Circulation
sections.body:
Air does not simply sit in the stratosphere; it circulates in a slow, planet-wide overturning named
after Alan Brewer and Gordon Dobson, who inferred it in the late 1940s from two independent puzzles.
Brewer noticed that stratospheric air is extraordinarily dry, only a few parts per million of water
vapour, which could only happen if it had passed through the very cold tropical tropopause and been
freeze-dried. Dobson noticed that column ozone is highest at high latitudes in spring, far from where
sunlight makes it. Both observations point to the same answer: air rises into the stratosphere in the
tropics, drifts poleward, and descends at middle and high latitudes.

The circulation is not driven by heating in the way a convection cell is. It is driven mechanically,
by waves. Planetary-scale Rossby waves, generated in the troposphere by flow over mountain ranges and
by land-sea heating contrasts, propagate upward into the stratosphere and break there, depositing
westward momentum. That drag decelerates the westerly winds, and by the constraint of angular momentum
conservation on a rotating planet the response is a poleward drift, which must be fed by rising motion
in the tropics and balanced by sinking at high latitudes. This is often called the extratropical pump:
the wave breaking acts like a suction pump pulling air upward through the tropical tropopause. Smaller
gravity waves do a similar job higher up.

Because Rossby-wave generation depends on topography and land-sea contrast, and the Northern
Hemisphere has far more of both, the pump is much stronger in the north. The consequences are large
and asymmetric. Northern winters have a weaker, warmer, more disturbed polar vortex; southern winters
have a strong, cold, stable one. This asymmetry is the root cause of why the ozone hole forms over
Antarctica and not the Arctic.

The timescales are slow. The residence time of air in the stratosphere, often called the age of air, is
about one to two years in the tropical lower stratosphere and four to six years in the polar upper
stratosphere. Measurements using long-lived tracers such as sulphur hexafluoride and carbon dioxide
allow this age to be estimated directly. It is these timescales that set the response of the ozone
layer to emissions: a chlorofluorocarbon released today takes three to five years to reach the
stratosphere, and once there its chlorine remains for decades.

There is an important open question here. Climate models consistently predict that the
Brewer-Dobson circulation will accelerate as greenhouse gases increase, because a warmer troposphere
generates more wave activity, which would speed the transport of ozone from tropics to poles, lower
tropical column ozone and raise it at high latitudes. Observations of the age of air, particularly from
balloon-borne measurements in the northern midlatitudes, have not clearly confirmed this acceleration,
and reconciling the model expectation with the observational record remains an active and unresolved
research problem.

sections.heading: Ultraviolet Radiation and Why the Shield Matters
sections.body:
Solar ultraviolet is divided into three bands by wavelength, and the difference between them is the
whole point of the ozone layer. UVA runs from 315 to 400 nanometres, is barely absorbed by ozone, and
reaches the surface almost unattenuated. UVB runs from 280 to 315 nanometres and is strongly but
incompletely absorbed; roughly one to ten per cent gets through, and how much depends sensitively on
the ozone column. UVC, below 280 nanometres, is absorbed completely by ozone and oxygen and never
reaches the ground at all. Essentially all the biological risk that the ozone layer controls sits in
the UVB band, because that is the band where absorption is steeply sensitive to column amount.

The damage mechanism is direct and specific. DNA absorbs ultraviolet with a peak near 260 nanometres,
and absorption of a UVB photon by adjacent pyrimidine bases, typically two thymines, causes them to
bond to each other forming a cyclobutane pyrimidine dimer. That kink blocks replication and
transcription. Cells have repair enzymes, principally the nucleotide excision repair pathway, but
repair is imperfect and errors accumulate as mutations. People with the inherited disorder xeroderma
pigmentosum lack functional excision repair and develop skin cancers in childhood, which is the
clearest natural demonstration of the mechanism. UVA damages differently and more indirectly, by
generating reactive oxygen species that oxidise DNA, lipids and proteins, and it contributes strongly
to photoageing and to melanoma risk.

The dose-response relationship is quantified by the radiation amplification factor. For a one per cent
decrease in total column ozone, biologically weighted UVB at the surface rises by roughly one and a
quarter to two per cent depending on the action spectrum used, and the incidence of non-melanoma skin
cancer is estimated to rise by two to four per cent. Under the unrestrained emissions scenarios of the
1980s, models of a world without the Montreal Protocol project column ozone collapsing by two-thirds by
2065 and UV index values at midlatitudes exceeding 15, at which pale skin burns in about five minutes.

Effects extend beyond humans. UVB inhibits photosynthesis and damages phytoplankton, which sit at the
base of the marine food web and are unable to shield themselves in the top few metres of ocean where
light is adequate. Antarctic surveys during the 1990s measured productivity reductions of six to twelve
per cent under the hole. Amphibian eggs, laid in shallow water, are vulnerable, and UVB has been
implicated in some amphibian declines. Crop yields in sensitive cultivars of soybean and rice fall
measurably under elevated UVB. Materials degrade too: polymers embrittle, paints chalk, and outdoor
plastics and rubbers fail years earlier than their design life, which is why ultraviolet stabilisers
are added to almost every plastic intended to sit outside.

sections.heading: Catalytic Destruction: The Cycles That Thin the Layer
sections.body:
Chapman's chemistry predicts about twice as much ozone as exists, and the discrepancy is closed by
catalytic cycles. A catalyst is a substance that speeds a reaction and emerges unchanged, so a single
molecule can destroy ozone over and over. The general form is that a radical X reacts with ozone to
give XO and O2; then XO reacts with a free oxygen atom to give X back and another O2. The net effect
is that ozone plus an oxygen atom become two O2 molecules, exactly the slow Chapman loss reaction, but
enormously faster, and X is regenerated to do it again. A single chlorine atom can destroy on the order
of one hundred thousand ozone molecules before it is finally removed.

Four catalytic families matter. The HOx family, hydrogen and hydroxyl radicals, derives from water
vapour and methane oxidised in the stratosphere and dominates ozone loss in the upper stratosphere
above about forty-five kilometres and again in the lowest stratosphere. The NOx family, nitric oxide
and nitrogen dioxide, comes almost entirely from nitrous oxide, a gas produced by soil microbes and
greatly increased by nitrogen fertiliser, which is inert in the troposphere and only breaks down in
the stratosphere. Paul Crutzen identified this cycle in 1970 and showed it is the largest single loss
process through the middle stratosphere, around twenty-five to forty kilometres.

The ClOx family, chlorine and chlorine monoxide, was identified in the stratosphere by Richard Stolarski
and Ralph Cicerone in 1974, initially in the context of rocket exhaust. Natural chlorine comes mainly
from methyl chloride produced by oceans and biomass burning, giving a natural background around 0.6
parts per billion. The BrOx family, bromine and bromine monoxide, is present in far smaller amounts,
around twenty parts per trillion, but each bromine atom is roughly forty-five to sixty times more
destructive than a chlorine atom, because bromine forms weaker reservoir compounds and stays in its
active radical form more of the time. Bromine comes from methyl bromide, once a widespread soil
fumigant, and from halons used in fire extinguishers.

The reason these small quantities do not destroy the layer entirely is that the radicals spend most of
their time locked up in reservoir species: chlorine as hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate, nitrogen
as nitric acid and dinitrogen pentoxide, bromine as hydrogen bromide and bromine nitrate. These
reservoirs are unreactive toward ozone and eventually descend into the troposphere and rain out.
Chemistry that converts reservoirs back to active radicals therefore controls the whole system, and
under ordinary gas-phase conditions it is slow. The Antarctic ozone hole exists because a special set
of conditions makes it very fast indeed.

sections.heading: CFCs: The Perfect Chemical and Its Flaw
sections.body:
Chlorofluorocarbons were invented to solve a real and lethal problem. Early refrigerators used
ammonia, sulphur dioxide or methyl chloride as working fluids, all of which are toxic, and leaks
killed people; a Cleveland hospital fire in 1929 caused by methyl chloride killed more than a hundred.
In 1928 Thomas Midgley Junior, working for General Motors and Frigidaire, synthesised
dichlorodifluoromethane, marketed as Freon-12. He demonstrated its safety at a chemical society
meeting by inhaling a lungful and using it to blow out a candle, showing it was neither toxic nor
flammable. It was also non-corrosive, cheap, and had convenient boiling points. Midgley, who had
earlier developed tetraethyl lead as a petrol additive, has a fair claim to having had more adverse
impact on the atmosphere than any other single organism in history.

CFCs were so inert that they were used everywhere: refrigerants, air-conditioning fluids, aerosol
propellants for everything from hairspray to asthma inhalers, blowing agents for foam insulation and
packaging, and precision solvents for cleaning electronics. Global production reached around a million
tonnes a year by the mid-1970s. Their inertness was the selling point, and it was also the flaw. A
molecule that will not react with anything in the troposphere does not rain out and is not destroyed;
it simply accumulates and slowly mixes upward. CFC-11 has an atmospheric lifetime around fifty-two
years and CFC-12 around one hundred and two.

In 1970 the British chemist James Lovelock, having invented the electron capture detector, measured
CFC-11 in air over the Atlantic and found essentially all of it ever manufactured was still there. He
reported this as a curiosity and a useful tracer. In 1974 Mario Molina and F. Sherwood Rowland at the
University of California, Irvine, asked what eventually happens to these molecules, and worked out the
answer: nothing removes them until they drift above about twenty-five kilometres, where ultraviolet
shorter than 220 nanometres finally photolyses them and releases free chlorine atoms into precisely
the region where the ozone lives. Their paper in Nature in June 1974 estimated that continued
emissions would deplete the ozone layer by several per cent.

The reaction was fierce. The chemical industry, notably DuPont, dismissed the work as speculative, and
one industry figure called it science fiction. But the argument was chemically straightforward and
consumers moved first: US aerosol sales fell sharply, and the United States, Canada, Sweden and Norway
banned CFC propellants in 1978. Then the modelled depletion estimates were revised downward in the
early 1980s and urgency faded. Molina, Rowland and Crutzen shared the 1995 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
What restored urgency was not a model but a measurement that nobody, on either side of the argument,
had predicted or even thought possible.

sections.heading: The Antarctic Ozone Hole
sections.body:
In May 1985 Joseph Farman, Brian Gardiner and Jonathan Shanklin of the British Antarctic Survey
published in Nature a record from Halley Bay showing that October column ozone had fallen from around
320 Dobson Units in the 1960s to under 200 by 1984, a decline of more than a third. They had been
measuring with a Dobson spectrophotometer since 1957. The result was so far outside expectation that
they checked their instrument against a new one for a season before publishing. Satellite data from
TOMS had in fact been recording the same collapse, but the automated processing had been flagging the
low values as instrument error and discarding them; once reprocessed, the satellite record showed a
continent-sized hole.

No model had predicted it, because the responsible chemistry was not gas-phase chemistry. Susan
Solomon and colleagues proposed, and the 1986 and 1987 Antarctic airborne expeditions confirmed, that
the cause was heterogeneous chemistry on the surfaces of polar stratospheric clouds. The mechanism has
four stages and each requires the Antarctic winter's peculiar conditions.

First, isolation. In autumn the Antarctic stratosphere cools, a strong circumpolar westerly jet
develops, and the resulting polar vortex acts as a containment vessel, largely preventing exchange
with midlatitude air. Second, extreme cold. Inside the vortex, in total darkness, temperatures fall
below minus 78 degrees Celsius, cold enough for nitric acid trihydrate clouds to form, and below about
minus 85 for water-ice clouds. These are polar stratospheric clouds, visible at twilight as
iridescent nacreous clouds. Third, surface chemistry. On the cloud particles, reactions occur that are
negligibly slow in the gas phase: hydrogen chloride and chlorine nitrate react to give molecular
chlorine and nitric acid. The chlorine is released as a gas while the nitric acid stays in the
particle. As larger particles sediment out, they remove nitrogen from the region entirely, a process
called denitrification, which matters because nitrogen dioxide would otherwise mop the chlorine back
up into reservoir.

Fourth, sunrise. Through winter, molecular chlorine accumulates, but nothing happens because
photolysis needs light. When the Sun returns in late August and September, the accumulated chlorine
photolyses in days, and with nitrogen removed the chlorine monoxide concentrations become enormous,
hundreds of times normal. Loss then proceeds through the ClO dimer cycle discovered by Molina, in which
two ClO molecules combine and are photolysed, and through a ClO-BrO cycle. Neither requires free oxygen
atoms, which is essential because at twenty kilometres in early spring there are few. Ozone in the
fourteen to twenty-two kilometre layer is destroyed almost completely, at rates approaching two to
three per cent per day. The hole persists until the vortex breaks down in late November or December.

sections.heading: The Montreal Protocol and the Recovery
sections.body:
The policy response to the ozone hole is the most successful international environmental agreement
ever concluded, and it is worth understanding why it worked when others have not. The Vienna
Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer, agreed in March 1985 just before the Farman paper,
was a framework with no binding targets. The Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone
Layer, signed on 16 September 1987 and in force from 1 January 1989, added them: a freeze and then a
fifty per cent cut in the five main CFCs by 1999.

That original protocol was too weak, and its architects knew it might be. Its crucial feature was a
built-in mechanism for periodic scientific assessment and tightening. Successive amendments - London
1990, Copenhagen 1992, Montreal 1997, Beijing 1999 - accelerated the schedule to a complete developed-
country phase-out of CFCs, halons, carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform by 1996, brought in
methyl bromide, and set out the phase-out of the interim replacements, the HCFCs, by 2020 and 2030.
The Multilateral Fund, established in 1991, paid the incremental costs of compliance for developing
countries, which was the political price of universality. Montreal became the first treaty in United
Nations history to achieve ratification by every member state.

Several conditions made success possible. The number of producers was small and concentrated. Viable
substitutes existed or could be developed, and DuPont, having initially resisted, calculated that
being first to market with alternatives was better business than defending CFCs. The harm was vivid,
personal and easy to communicate: a hole, skin cancer, blindness in sheep. And the science, though
incomplete, converged rapidly on an unambiguous causal mechanism.

Recovery is real but slow, because chlorine already aloft must decay away. Total tropospheric chlorine
peaked around 1993 at about 3.7 parts per billion and stratospheric chlorine peaked around 1997 to
2000; both are now falling by roughly one per cent per year. The 2022 WMO/UNEP Scientific Assessment
concluded that the Antarctic ozone hole is expected to close around 2066, the Arctic around 2045, and
midlatitudes around 2040. Estimates suggest the treaty will prevent some two million skin cancer cases
per year by 2030. Because CFCs are also potent greenhouse gases, Montreal has delivered more climate
mitigation than any climate treaty; the 2016 Kigali Amendment, phasing down HFCs which harm no ozone
but are strong greenhouse gases, makes that explicit and is projected to avoid up to half a degree of
warming.

Compliance is not automatic. Between 2013 and 2018 atmospheric measurements detected unexpected CFC-11
emissions of about thirteen thousand tonnes a year, traced by monitoring stations to eastern China and
attributed to illegal use in foam blowing. Enforcement action followed and emissions dropped back by
2019, a demonstration that the global monitoring network functions as a verification system.

sections.heading: Sudden Stratospheric Warmings and the Polar Vortex
sections.body:
The stratosphere is not only acted upon by the troposphere; it acts back, and the clearest example is
the sudden stratospheric warming, discovered by Richard Scherhag in Berlin in 1952 when a routine
radiosonde ascent showed the stratosphere warming by tens of degrees in a couple of days.

The setup is the winter polar vortex, a band of strong westerly winds encircling the pole in the
stratosphere, formed because the polar night cools the pole and the resulting temperature gradient
drives a jet through thermal wind balance. This vortex is disturbed by upward-propagating planetary
Rossby waves generated in the troposphere by mountain ranges such as the Rockies and Himalaya and by
