land-sea heating contrasts. When a large pulse of wave activity propagates upward and breaks in the
stratosphere, it decelerates and can reverse the westerlies. Air converging over the pole descends,
compresses and warms adiabatically. In a major warming, defined by the World Meteorological
Organization as a reversal of the zonal mean zonal wind at 10 hectopascals and 60 degrees latitude,
polar stratospheric temperature can rise by 40 to 50 degrees Celsius in under a week and the vortex
either displaces off the pole or splits in two.

Major warmings occur roughly six times a decade in the Northern Hemisphere. In the Southern
Hemisphere they are rare: there have been only two on record, in September 2002 when the vortex split,
and a weaker one in September 2019. That rarity is the same asymmetry that produces the ozone hole.

The downstream effect on weather is the reason this matters to anyone outside the field. Following a
major warming, the anomaly of weakened westerlies descends through the stratosphere over one to three
weeks and couples into the troposphere, shifting the tropospheric jet stream equatorward and pushing
the North Atlantic Oscillation and Arctic Oscillation into negative phase. That typically means
blocking highs, a meandering jet, and outbreaks of cold Arctic air into northern Europe, eastern North
America and northern Asia. The European cold spell of February and March 2018, popularly called the
Beast from the East, followed a major warming on 12 February. The February 2021 Texas cold outbreak
followed a vortex disruption in early January. Because the stratospheric signal persists for four to
six weeks, monitoring the vortex gives genuine sub-seasonal forecast skill at lead times where
tropospheric forecasts have none, and operational centres now use it routinely.

A related coupling is the quasi-biennial oscillation, a reversal of the equatorial stratospheric winds
between easterly and westerly that descends at about one kilometre per month with a period averaging
28 months. It is driven by momentum deposition from upward-propagating equatorial waves, and it
modulates the frequency of sudden warmings, tropical cyclone activity and even the transport of ozone.
In 2016 the oscillation was disrupted for the first time in the sixty-year record, an event still not
fully explained.

sections.heading: Volcanoes, Aircraft and Deliberate Interference
sections.body:
Several things other than industrial halocarbons perturb the stratosphere, and each illuminates the
system's sensitivities.

Explosive volcanic eruptions inject sulphur dioxide, which converts over weeks to sulphuric acid
aerosol droplets. If the plume reaches the stratosphere, the aerosol persists for one to three years
because there is no rain to remove it, spreads globally, and does two things: it scatters sunlight back
to space, cooling the surface, and it provides particle surfaces for the same heterogeneous chemistry
that operates on polar stratospheric clouds. Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted on 15 June 1991,
injecting about twenty million tonnes of sulphur dioxide to twenty-five kilometres or more. Global mean
surface temperature fell by roughly 0.5 degrees Celsius over the following two years, the stratosphere
warmed by two to three degrees because the aerosol absorbs infrared and near-infrared, and global
column ozone dropped by about two per cent, with midlatitude losses of five to eight per cent, because
the aerosol converted nitrogen reservoirs to nitric acid and thereby liberated chlorine. Pinatubo was
an unplanned experiment that validated both climate models and ozone chemistry.

Aircraft matter in two ways. Subsonic airliners cruise near the tropopause and emit nitrogen oxides
which, at those altitudes, tend to produce ozone rather than destroy it, along with water vapour and
soot that seed contrails and cirrus. Supersonic transports flying at eighteen to twenty kilometres
would emit nitrogen oxides directly into the ozone layer, and it was this concern, raised by Harold
Johnston in 1971, that first drew serious attention to stratospheric chemistry and contributed to the
cancellation of the American SST programme. Rocket launches inject alumina and chlorine directly, and
the growth of launch rates plus the alumina produced by satellites burning up on re-entry is a small
but genuinely under-studied perturbation.

Deliberate interference is now openly discussed. Stratospheric aerosol injection, the proposal to
mimic a volcano by continuously injecting sulphate or another aerosol to reflect sunlight, is the most
studied form of solar geoengineering. The physics works, in the sense that Pinatubo demonstrated it.
The objections are serious: it would deplete ozone through the Pinatubo mechanism, particularly if
chlorine is still elevated; it does nothing about ocean acidification; it changes regional rainfall,
with monsoon disruption a recurring model result; termination shock means that stopping abruptly would
produce rapid warming; and governance of a technology any moderately capable state could deploy
unilaterally is unsolved. The 2021 US National Academies report recommended a modest, transparent,
governed research programme while explicitly not recommending deployment. This is a genuinely
contested area, and an honest account should present it as such rather than as either salvation or
taboo. The one point on which almost everyone agrees is that it is a treatment of a symptom and not of
the cause.

sections.heading: What Can Still Go Wrong, and What You Can Do
sections.body:
The ozone story is often told as finished, and it is not. Several loose ends deserve clear statement.

Recovery depends on continued compliance, and compliance can slip. The CFC-11 episode showed that
banned production can restart, and only the global monitoring network caught it. Banks of CFCs still
sitting in old refrigerators, chillers and foam insulation total on the order of a million tonnes; if
those are scrapped carelessly rather than recovered, they will vent. Very short-lived substances such
as dichloromethane, widely used as a solvent and not controlled by Montreal because it was assumed to
break down before reaching the stratosphere, have been rising and are now thought to contribute a small
but non-negligible amount of stratospheric chlorine, particularly where convection lofts them quickly
from tropical source regions.

Nitrous oxide is now the largest ozone-depleting emission not controlled by any ozone treaty. It comes
mainly from agricultural nitrogen and is projected to remain the dominant ozone-depleting substance
through the twenty-first century. Reducing it is a fertiliser-management problem, not a chemical
substitution problem, and is correspondingly harder.

Climate change complicates recovery in both directions. Stratospheric cooling driven by carbon dioxide
slows gas-phase ozone destruction, so upper-stratospheric ozone should over-recover to above 1980
values; but the same cooling makes polar stratospheric clouds more likely, prolonging polar loss, and
an accelerating Brewer-Dobson circulation would redistribute ozone away from the tropics. The 2020
Australian bushfires and the January 2022 Hunga Tonga eruption, which injected an unprecedented one
hundred and forty-six million tonnes of water vapour into the stratosphere, both produced measurable
ozone anomalies and demonstrated that the system can be perturbed in ways not previously modelled.
Expect further surprises.

There are also honest gaps in understanding rather than in policy. The predicted acceleration of the
Brewer-Dobson circulation has not been cleanly confirmed by observations of the age of stratospheric
air, and until that is reconciled, projections of tropical column ozone carry real uncertainty. Trends
in the lower stratosphere at midlatitudes, between roughly fifteen and twenty-four kilometres, have
continued to decline in several satellite records since 1998 even as the upper stratosphere recovers,
a discrepancy that is not fully explained and that matters because it is the lower stratosphere that
holds most of the column and therefore controls surface ultraviolet. Instrument drift, changes in
transport and unaccounted very short-lived chlorine sources are all candidates.

Finally, the institutional lesson is worth stating plainly, because it is the transferable part. What
made this problem tractable was not a single discovery but a system: a long, uninterrupted, carefully
calibrated measurement record maintained for decades before anyone knew what it would be needed for; a
treaty designed to be tightened as knowledge improved rather than fixed at the moment of signature;
and a monitoring network good enough to detect cheating from the composition of the air itself.
Nothing about the outcome was inevitable, and the ozone layer's recovery is currently on schedule only
because those three things are still being funded.

sections.heading: Protecting Yourself: Reading the UV Index and Acting On It
sections.body:
The practical consequence of all this chemistry, for an individual on the ground, is ultraviolet
exposure. The UV Index is a standardised scale in which each unit corresponds to 25 milliwatts per
square metre of erythemally weighted irradiance, meaning solar radiation weighted by how effectively
each wavelength reddens human skin. Below 3, protection is generally unnecessary. From 3 to 7, seek
shade around midday, wear a hat and use sunscreen. Above 8, unprotected pale skin can burn in fifteen
minutes or less, and above 11 in around five. Peak values reach 11 or 12 in the tropics at sea level
and exceed 15 on high tropical mountains.

Several properties of ultraviolet make intuition unreliable. It is not felt as warmth, because heat
is sensed from infrared, so a cool or hazy day can burn severely while feeling pleasant. Thin
or broken cloud transmits up to about eighty per cent, and scattered cloud can briefly push it above
the clear-sky value by reflecting off cloud edges. It rises roughly ten to twelve per cent per
thousand metres of altitude. Reflection compounds the dose: fresh snow returns up to eighty per cent,
dry sand about fifteen, open water about ten, so a day on a glacier or a boat can nearly double the
exposure and burns places a hat shades.

Time of day matters more than total time outdoors: roughly half of a day's ultraviolet arrives in the
four hours centred on solar noon, which under summer time is nearer one in the afternoon. Shadow
length is a serviceable gauge - if your shadow is shorter than you are, ultraviolet is near its peak.
Eyes deserve separate attention, because the cornea and lens absorb ultraviolet that never reaches the
retina, and decades of exposure is a risk factor for cataract. Acute overexposure causes
photokeratitis, sunburn of the cornea, appearing six to twelve hours later as pain and light
sensitivity; snow blindness is the classic form. Dark sunglasses that do not block ultraviolet are
worse than none, because they dilate the pupil.
steps: Check the UV index before extended time outdoors; it peaks within about two hours of solar noon, not at the hottest part of the afternoon.
Treat an index of 3 or above as requiring action; the published figure assumes clear sky at sea level, so add roughly 10 per cent per 1000 m of altitude and allow for reflection.
Apply broad-spectrum sunscreen of SPF 30 or higher 15 to 30 minutes before exposure, roughly 30 millilitres for a whole adult body, reapplied every two hours and after swimming or heavy sweating.
Prefer physical shade over sunscreen where possible: a hat with a brim of at least 7.5 cm, tightly woven long sleeves, and shade from about 10:00 to 16:00 solar time.
Wear sunglasses rated to block 99 to 100 per cent of radiation below 400 nanometres, and never look at the Sun through unfiltered optics.
Check your skin for moles that change in size, shape, colour or border, or that bleed or itch, and have anything changing assessed; early melanoma is highly treatable and late melanoma often is not.

guides.title: The Mesosphere and Thermosphere
guides.summary: A full account of Earth's two upper atmospheric layers: why the mesosphere cools with height and hosts the coldest temperatures on the planet, why the thermosphere is thousands of degrees hot yet would feel freezing, and how both shape meteors, noctilucent clouds, airglow, radio propagation, aurorae and satellite orbits.

sections.heading: Where the Middle and Upper Atmosphere Begin
sections.body:
Above about 50 kilometres, the air stops behaving like anything most people would recognise as weather. There is no rain, no thunderstorm, almost no water, and so little gas that the pressure has already fallen to less than one thousandth of what it is at sea level. Yet this region is not empty and it is not inert. It is where meteors burn, where the highest clouds on Earth form out of frost at temperatures colder than anywhere on the surface, where shortwave radio signals bounce back down to let a transmitter in one hemisphere be heard in another, where the aurora glows, and where every satellite in low orbit slowly grinds against the thin residual gas until it falls. The two layers in question are the mesosphere, roughly 50 to 85 kilometres up, and the thermosphere above it, extending from about 85 kilometres to somewhere between 500 and 1,000 kilometres depending on how active the Sun happens to be.

Together these layers hold a vanishingly small fraction of the atmosphere's mass. About 99.9 per cent of the air sits below 50 kilometres; everything discussed here is contained in the remaining tenth of a per cent. That makes the region easy to dismiss and easy to get wrong. The temptation is to treat it as a vacuum with decorations. In practice the physics is different rather than absent: with so few molecules, collisions become rare, sunlight can tear molecules apart faster than they can reassemble, electrically charged particles persist instead of immediately recombining, and waves launched by weather far below can grow to enormous amplitude as they climb into thinner and thinner air.

The mesosphere in particular has been nicknamed the ignorosphere, because it sits in an awkward observational gap. It is too high for balloons, which top out near 40 to 53 kilometres because the envelope can no longer displace enough air to lift itself. It is too low for satellites, which cannot maintain an orbit below roughly 150 kilometres for more than a few days before drag brings them down. For decades the only way to sample it directly was to fire a sounding rocket straight through it and take measurements during the few minutes of passage. That gap has narrowed since the 1990s with ground-based lidar and radar and with dedicated satellites looking sideways through the limb of the atmosphere, but it remains the least well measured part of the air column.

Why any of this matters to someone standing on the ground comes down to three practical threads. Radio communication over the horizon depends on the ionised gas in these layers. Satellite lifetimes, collision warnings and reentry predictions depend on the density of the thermosphere, which can double in a day. And the mesosphere responds to greenhouse gases in the opposite direction from the surface, cooling and contracting while the lower atmosphere warms, which makes it an unusually sensitive early indicator of change.

sections.heading: How the Layers Are Defined: Temperature as the Organizing Principle
sections.body:
Atmospheric layers are not defined by composition, by pressure, or by any physical boundary. They are defined by what temperature does as you climb. Every time the sign of the vertical temperature gradient flips, a new layer is declared and the flipping point is given a name ending in -pause. This convention dates to the early twentieth century, when Leon Teisserenc de Bort's balloon soundings from 1896 onward showed that temperature stopped falling above roughly 11 kilometres, revealing the tropopause and with it the stratosphere. The same logic, extended upward by rocket and radio measurements in the 1940s and 1950s, produced the four-layer scheme still in use.

In the troposphere, temperature falls with height at an average of about 6.5 kelvin per kilometre, because the air is heated from below by a sunlit surface and convection carries that heat upward while expanding and cooling it. At the tropopause, between about 8 kilometres over the poles and 18 kilometres over the equator, the fall stops. In the stratosphere temperature then rises with height, reaching roughly 270 kelvin, close to 0 degrees Celsius, at the stratopause near 50 kilometres. That inversion exists because ozone absorbs ultraviolet sunlight in the 200 to 310 nanometre band and converts it to heat, so the stratosphere is warmed from within rather than from below.

Above the stratopause the ozone runs out, and with it the heating. Temperature resumes falling, at roughly 2 to 3 kelvin per kilometre, and that falling branch is the mesosphere. It ends at the mesopause, the coldest level in the entire atmosphere, at about 85 to 100 kilometres depending on season and latitude. Above the mesopause temperature rises again, this time steeply and without limit until the gas becomes too thin to define a meaningful temperature at all: that is the thermosphere. Beyond roughly 500 to 1,000 kilometres lies the exosphere, where a particle's mean free path exceeds the scale height and individual atoms follow ballistic trajectories, some escaping to space entirely.

A practical consequence of this definition is that the boundaries move. The mesopause is near 100 kilometres in winter but drops to about 85 kilometres in summer, and the thermopause height depends on solar activity. Textbook numbers are averages, not walls. It is also worth separating this scheme from other ways of slicing the atmosphere that use different criteria entirely. The homosphere and heterosphere are defined by whether gases stay mixed. The ionosphere is defined by the presence of free electrons and overlaps the mesosphere, thermosphere and exosphere simultaneously. The magnetosphere is defined by magnetic control. These schemes coexist and are not alternatives to each other, which is a frequent source of confusion when different sources appear to put the same altitude in different layers.

sections.heading: Inside the Mesosphere: Pressure, Density, and Composition
sections.body:
Numbers make the mesosphere concrete in a way that descriptions cannot. At the stratopause near 50 kilometres, atmospheric pressure is about 80 pascals, or 0.8 hectopascals, compared with 1,013 hectopascals at sea level: roughly one thousandth of surface pressure. Climb to 70 kilometres and it is about 5 pascals. At 80 kilometres it is near 1 pascal, and at the top of the layer around 85 to 90 kilometres it is a few tenths of a pascal. Density falls in parallel, from 1.225 kilograms per cubic metre at sea level to about 1.8 by ten to the minus five kilograms per cubic metre at 80 kilometres, some seventy thousand times thinner. A cubic metre of mesospheric air at 80 kilometres weighs less than a fifth of a gram.

Despite that thinness, the gas is still a gas in the ordinary sense. Molecules collide often enough that pressure, temperature and sound all mean what they normally mean, and fluid dynamics still applies. The mean free path, the average distance a molecule travels between collisions, is around a centimetre at 80 kilometres, which is tiny compared with the scale of any atmospheric motion. This is the key difference from the thermosphere higher up, where the mean free path grows to hundreds of metres and then kilometres and the continuum description begins to break down.

Composition through the mesosphere remains almost exactly what it is at the ground, and this is one of the most important and least intuitive facts about the layer. Turbulent mixing is vigorous enough to keep the major gases in fixed proportion: about 78 per cent nitrogen, 21 per cent oxygen, 0.93 per cent argon, and a mean molecular mass of 28.96 grams per mole, the same as at sea level. What changes is the trace constituents. Water vapour, which is a few per cent by volume in the humid lower troposphere, is down to a handful of parts per million by the mesosphere, because the cold tropopause freeze-dries everything that passes through it. Ozone has a broad minimum through the middle mesosphere but recovers into a secondary night-time maximum near 90 kilometres, where atomic oxygen produced by daytime photolysis recombines after dark.

Carbon dioxide remains at roughly its surface mixing ratio, currently over 420 parts per million, well into the mesosphere, and this apparently boring fact turns out to control the layer's entire thermal structure. Atomic oxygen becomes increasingly important above about 80 kilometres, where ultraviolet photons split molecular oxygen faster than three-body collisions can put it back together. By 100 kilometres atomic oxygen is a major constituent rather than a trace one, and it dominates the chemistry, the airglow and the energy budget of everything above.

sections.heading: Why the Mesosphere Cools with Height
sections.body:
The mesosphere is the one substantial layer of the atmosphere that loses more energy than it gains, and the reason comes down to a competition between two molecules. The stratosphere below is warm because ozone absorbs ultraviolet light. Ozone forms where there is enough ultraviolet to split molecular oxygen and enough density for the resulting atoms to find a third body and stick together as O3, a balance first described by Sydney Chapman in 1930. That balance peaks near 25 kilometres and thins out rapidly above 50 kilometres, because the air becomes too rarefied for the three-body reaction to keep up. Remove the ozone and you remove the heater.

Meanwhile the cooling continues and even strengthens. Carbon dioxide radiates energy to space in a strong vibrational band centred at 15 micrometres in the thermal infrared. Deep in the troposphere this emission is reabsorbed almost immediately by neighbouring carbon dioxide molecules, which is precisely why carbon dioxide is a greenhouse gas down there: the atmosphere is optically thick and radiation cannot escape directly. In the mesosphere the same molecule has the opposite effect, because the air is optically thin. A 15-micrometre photon emitted at 70 kilometres has an excellent chance of flying straight out to space and never coming back. The gas loses that energy permanently.

There is a subtlety that makes this efficient. To radiate, a carbon dioxide molecule must first be vibrationally excited, and at these altitudes the main way that happens is collision with an atomic oxygen atom, which is unusually good at transferring energy into that particular vibration. So the atomic oxygen generated by ultraviolet photolysis at high altitude effectively pumps the carbon dioxide radiator. Increase the carbon dioxide and the mesosphere does not warm; it cools faster and contracts. This is the mirror image of surface greenhouse warming, and it is a robust prediction that observations broadly support, with estimated mesospheric cooling of roughly 1 to 3 kelvin per decade, though the precise rate is genuinely contested because long, stable measurement records at these altitudes are scarce and instrument changes can masquerade as trends.

The net result is a lapse rate of about 2 to 3 kelvin per kilometre from roughly 270 kelvin at the stratopause down toward 180 to 190 kelvin at the mesopause in the global average. It is worth noting what does not cause this cooling. It is not simply expansion, as in the troposphere, because there is no sustained convective overturning carrying air upward. It is not distance from the Sun, which changes by a negligible amount over 85 kilometres. It is a radiative imbalance, modified strongly by dynamics: the coldest temperatures of all are produced not by radiation but by air being forced to rise and expand where radiation alone would never take it.

sections.heading: The Mesopause and the Coldest Temperatures on Earth
sections.body:
The mesopause holds a record that surprises almost everyone who hears it. The coldest place in Earth's atmosphere is not Antarctica, where the surface record stands at about minus 89.2 degrees Celsius measured at Vostok Station in 1983. It is the mesopause above the summer polar cap, where temperatures routinely reach 130 kelvin, roughly minus 143 degrees Celsius, and occasionally dip below that. Colder still than the winter polar mesopause, which sits nearer 200 to 230 kelvin. The summer pole, bathed in twenty-four-hour sunlight, is the coldest; the winter pole, in permanent darkness, is comparatively warm. Any explanation resting purely on sunshine is therefore wrong.

The answer is dynamical. Waves generated in the lower atmosphere propagate upward, break in the mesosphere, and deposit their momentum, dragging the mesospheric wind and driving a slow pole-to-pole overturning circulation. This circulation, sometimes called the residual or Murgatroyd-Singleton circulation after the 1961 paper that first inferred it, flows from the summer pole to the winter pole across the mesosphere. To supply that flow, air must rise over the summer pole and sink over the winter pole. Rising air expands and cools adiabatically; sinking air compresses and warms. The vertical velocities are tiny, of order a few centimetres per second, but sustained over weeks that is enough to drive the summer mesopause tens of kelvin below its radiative equilibrium value and lift the winter mesopause far above it.

The mesopause also changes height with season, and this is a genuine two-level structure rather than a smooth shift. In summer at high latitudes it sits low, near 85 to 88 kilometres. In winter and at low latitudes it sits high, near 98 to 100 kilometres, and is much warmer. Instruments crossing from one regime to the other, for example during the spring transition, can record apparent jumps of 15 kilometres in a matter of days. Older textbooks quoting a single mesopause altitude of 85 kilometres are describing the summer polar case and quietly generalising it to the whole planet, which is why quoted values disagree so often.

These temperatures are cold enough for physics that happens nowhere else in the atmosphere. Water vapour present at only a few parts per million becomes supersaturated, because the saturation vapour pressure of ice at 130 kelvin is extraordinarily low, of order ten to the minus eight pascals. Ice can therefore nucleate and grow on whatever nuclei are available, which at that altitude are mainly the nanometre-scale smoke particles condensed from vaporised meteors. That is the origin of noctilucent clouds. It also means the mesopause functions as a second cold trap, freeze-drying air a second time and limiting how much water reaches the thermosphere, which in turn limits hydrogen escape to space over geological time.

sections.heading: Noctilucent Clouds and Polar Mesospheric Clouds
sections.body:
Noctilucent clouds are the highest clouds on Earth and among the most beautiful things the atmosphere produces. They form at 76 to 85 kilometres, most often near 83 kilometres, from water ice crystals typically 30 to 100 nanometres across, small enough that they scatter blue light preferentially and appear as electric-blue or silvery filaments and billows. Seen from the ground they are visible only in deep twilight, when the observer is in darkness but the clouds, eight times higher than a cirrus deck, are still catching sunlight. The geometry restricts sightings to roughly 50 to 70 degrees latitude with the Sun between about 6 and 16 degrees below the horizon, in the weeks around the summer solstice. From orbit the same phenomenon is observed looking down over the polar cap and is called polar mesospheric cloud, the same clouds under a different viewing geometry.

Their existence requires three things at once: temperature below about 150 kelvin, a supply of water vapour of a few parts per million, and condensation nuclei. Only the summer polar mesopause supplies the first, which is why the clouds are seasonal and hemispheric. The nuclei are believed to be meteoric smoke particles, nanometre-scale grains recondensed from metal vapour left by ablating meteoroids, though ion clusters may also play a role. The season opens abruptly, within a week or two of the mesopause reaching threshold temperature, and closes just as sharply.

The historical record is intriguing and unresolved. The first credible reports date to the summer of 1885, logged independently by Thomas William Backhouse in England and by Otto Jesse in Germany, two years after the eruption of Krakatoa. Jesse coined the term leuchtende Nachtwolken, luminous night clouds, and made the first photogrammetric height determinations of about 82 kilometres in 1887. Whether the clouds genuinely did not exist before 1885, or simply went unremarked, cannot be settled: sky-watching was widespread but the twilight window is narrow and the phenomenon is easy to mistake for cirrus if you are not expecting it.

What is clearer is that they have become brighter, more frequent and observed at lower latitudes over the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Two anthropogenic mechanisms are proposed and both are plausible. Atmospheric methane has more than doubled since pre-industrial times, and methane oxidised in the middle atmosphere is a direct source of water vapour up there. Separately, rising carbon dioxide cools the mesopause, pushing more of the summer season below the ice threshold. The NASA AIM satellite, launched in 2007 and carrying the CIPS imager and the SOFIE occultation instrument, was built specifically to measure these clouds and their environment, and its record confirms strong year-to-year variability driven partly by conditions propagating up from the winter stratosphere of the opposite hemisphere.

sections.heading: Gravity Waves and the Wave-Driven Circulation
sections.body:
Atmospheric gravity waves, which have nothing to do with the gravitational waves of general relativity, are oscillations in which buoyancy provides the restoring force. Displace a parcel of stably stratified air upward and it finds itself denser than its surroundings, so it falls back, overshoots, and oscillates at a characteristic frequency called the Brunt-Vaisala frequency, typically corresponding to a period of a few minutes in the middle atmosphere. Wind flowing over mountains, thunderstorm updraughts punching into the stratosphere, and imbalances in jet streams all launch these waves continuously from the lower atmosphere.

What makes them dominant in the mesosphere is a conservation argument. A wave carries a roughly constant flux of energy upward, and that flux scales as air density times the square of the wave's velocity amplitude. Since density falls by a factor of about e every 6 to 7 kilometres, a wave that starts with an amplitude of centimetres per second near the ground can reach tens of metres per second by 80 kilometres. Amplitudes grow exponentially until the wave becomes convectively or dynamically unstable and breaks, much as an ocean swell steepens and breaks in shallow water. Vertical displacements of 5 to 10 kilometres in a single wave are routine, and can be seen directly as the rippled, banded structure that noctilucent clouds and airglow layers show in photographs.

Breaking transfers the wave's momentum to the mean flow. Because the waves are filtered on the way up, being absorbed where the background wind matches their phase speed, the momentum that survives to the mesosphere systematically opposes the prevailing stratospheric jets. The consequence is dramatic: the mesospheric jets are not merely weakened but reversed, closing off near 80 to 90 kilometres, and the residual meridional circulation flowing from summer pole to winter pole is set up. That circulation is what drives the summer mesopause tens of kelvin colder than radiation alone would allow and the winter mesopause tens of kelvin warmer.

Gravity waves are joined by two other wave families. Atmospheric tides, forced primarily by daily solar heating of tropospheric water vapour and stratospheric ozone, propagate upward and also grow with height, reaching amplitudes of 30 to 50 metres per second in the lower thermosphere and dominating the day-to-day wind field there. Planetary waves, with wavelengths comparable to the circumference of the Earth, propagate up in winter and can trigger sudden stratospheric warmings, in which the polar stratosphere warms by 40 to 50 kelvin in a few days and the winter vortex reverses. Those events reach the mesosphere too, but with the sign flipped: a stratospheric warming is accompanied by a mesospheric cooling of comparable magnitude, because the induced circulation that compresses and warms one layer forces ascent and expansion in the other. This vertical coupling is the mechanism by which conditions near 30 kilometres can be predicted to alter conditions near 85 kilometres, and it works in the opposite direction as well.

sections.heading: Meteor Ablation and the Metal Layers
sections.body:
Earth sweeps up interplanetary dust continuously. Estimates of the daily input vary considerably, from about 5 to over 300 tonnes per day depending on the measurement technique, with values around 40 tonnes commonly quoted from radar and lidar constraints. Almost all of that mass is deposited in a narrow shell between roughly 80 and 120 kilometres, which is exactly the upper mesosphere and lowest thermosphere. The reason is a matter of physics rather than coincidence. A particle entering at 11 to 72 kilometres per second travels through essentially free space until the air becomes dense enough for collisions to heat it faster than it can radiate, which happens once the density reaches about ten to the minus seven kilograms per cubic metre. It then heats to over 2,000 kelvin in a fraction of a second and vaporises. The visible streak of a meteor is not the object burning; it is the glowing trail of excited air and vaporised metal atoms left behind.

That vapour has to go somewhere. The metals in ordinary chondritic material, principally iron, magnesium, sodium, potassium, calcium and silicon, are released as free atoms into a region where the air is cold and the chemistry is unusual. Sodium and iron in particular form persistent global layers between about 80 and 105 kilometres, peaking near 90 kilometres and only 8 to 10 kilometres thick. The sodium layer has a typical column abundance of a few times ten to the ninth atoms per square centimetre, which is minuscule in absolute terms but trivially detectable because sodium resonantly scatters yellow light at 589 nanometres with an enormous cross section.

This has one of the most elegant practical applications in modern astronomy. Large telescopes fire a 589 nanometre laser into the sky to excite that mesospheric sodium and create an artificial star at about 90 kilometres altitude, a laser guide star, whose apparent wobble reveals the atmospheric distortion the adaptive optics system must correct. The technique works only because a natural, stable, well-mixed layer of a single resonant metal happens to sit at exactly the right height, maintained by a steady meteoric supply.

Below the metal layers, the vapour recondenses. As metal atoms drift downward into colder, denser air they oxidise, cluster and form meteoric smoke particles, grains of a few nanometres composed largely of iron and magnesium silicates. Models suggest these are ubiquitous through the mesosphere at concentrations of thousands per cubic centimetre. They are believed to be the nuclei on which noctilucent cloud ice grows, they charge electrically and influence the electrical conductivity of the middle atmosphere, and after months to years of slow sedimentation they reach the stratosphere, where they can be measured in polar ice cores as an iridium and platinum signal. The chain runs from asteroid collisions in the solar system to a chemical trace in Antarctic ice.

sections.heading: Airglow, Sprites, and the Light of the Night Sky
sections.body:
A truly dark, moonless night sky is not black. Even with no city lights, no moon, no aurora and no zodiacal dust, the sky emits a faint glow of its own, and the majority of that light comes from the mesopause region. Airglow, sometimes called nightglow, contributes roughly as much light as all the stars combined, and from the International Space Station it is plainly visible as a thin green-brown band hugging the limb of the Earth in night-side photographs.

The mechanism is chemiluminescence: chemical reactions releasing energy directly as photons rather than as heat. During the day, ultraviolet sunlight dissociates molecular oxygen above 90 kilometres, producing atomic oxygen faster than it can recombine. At night that stored chemical energy is released. The single strongest emission comes from hydroxyl. Atomic hydrogen reacts with ozone to produce vibrationally excited OH, which then radiates in the near infrared Meinel bands from a layer centred near 87 kilometres and about 8 kilometres thick. Because that layer is thin and sits at a fixed height, imaging it from the ground is one of the standard ways to visualise gravity waves: the wave ripples appear as travelling bands of brightness. Other well-known emissions include the green line of atomic oxygen at 557.7 nanometres near 95 to 100 kilometres, the sodium D doublet at 589 nanometres from the meteoric metal layer, and the molecular oxygen atmospheric band at 762 nanometres.

A completely different and far more dramatic light source was confirmed only recently. On 6 July 1989, John R. Winckler and colleagues at the University of Minnesota were testing a low-light television camera and accidentally recorded a brief flash high above a distant thunderstorm. Pilots had reported such things for decades and been quietly disbelieved. The phenomenon, named sprites by Davis Sentman with deliberate whimsy because their nature was then unknown, is now understood as a large-scale electrical discharge in the mesosphere, spanning roughly 40 to 90 kilometres altitude, triggered by the sudden removal of charge in an unusually powerful positive cloud-to-ground lightning stroke. Sprites glow red from excited molecular nitrogen, last milliseconds, and can be tens of kilometres across.

Sprites belong to a family called transient luminous events. Elves are expanding rings of light up to 300 kilometres in diameter at about 90 kilometres altitude, produced when the electromagnetic pulse from a lightning stroke reaches the base of the ionosphere and heats electrons there. Blue jets shoot upward from thunderstorm tops to 40 or 50 kilometres. Gigantic jets bridge the gap entirely, connecting a cloud top directly to the ionosphere. Collectively they show that the electrical circuit of a thunderstorm does not stop at the anvil; it extends through the mesosphere to the conducting layer above, and the middle atmosphere is an active participant in the global atmospheric electrical circuit rather than a passive insulator.

sections.heading: The Turbopause: Where Mixing Ends and Diffusion Begins
sections.body:
One of the most consequential boundaries in the atmosphere is not a temperature boundary at all. Somewhere near 100 to 110 kilometres, the atmosphere stops being a well-stirred mixture and starts sorting itself by weight. That transition is the turbopause, also called the homopause, and it divides the homosphere below from the heterosphere above.

Below the turbopause, turbulent eddies mix air far faster than molecular diffusion can separate it. Every gas is dragged around together regardless of its molecular mass, so nitrogen, oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide maintain constant proportions all the way from a beach up to 100 kilometres, and the mean molecular mass of air stays at 28.96 grams per mole throughout. This is why a sample of mesospheric air at 80 kilometres has the same nitrogen-to-oxygen ratio as a sample from a living room. It is a striking fact that the composition of air is essentially uniform over a span of one hundred kilometres and a factor of ten thousand in density.

Above the turbopause, collisions become rare enough that molecular diffusion outpaces mixing. Each species then settles into its own hydrostatic equilibrium with its own scale height, given by the barometric relation in which scale height equals the gas constant times temperature divided by molecular mass times gravity. Because scale height is inversely proportional to molecular mass, heavy gases thin out with height much faster than light ones. Nitrogen and oxygen molecules fall away; atomic oxygen, produced by photodissociation and only sixteen mass units, becomes the dominant constituent between roughly 200 and 600 kilometres. Above that helium takes over, at about 600 to 1,500 kilometres, and above that atomic hydrogen dominates out into the geocorona. The atmosphere sorts into shells by weight, exactly as a very tall column of undisturbed gas mixture eventually must.

The turbopause has practical consequences that reach far beyond atmospheric science. Because atomic oxygen dominates the gas at 200 to 600 kilometres, the material environment of low Earth orbit is chemically hostile in an unexpected way. Atomic oxygen is an extremely aggressive oxidiser, and a spacecraft moving at 7.7 kilometres per second slams into it at an impact energy of about 5 electronvolts per atom, enough to break chemical bonds. Polymer films, Kapton thermal blankets, silver interconnects and paints erode measurably over months. The Long Duration Exposure Facility, retrieved by the Space Shuttle in 1990 after 69 months in orbit, showed erosion of tens of micrometres in exposed polymers. Materials selection for anything spending years below 600 kilometres must account for it. The turbopause also sets the top of the region where a single well-mixed tracer such as carbon dioxide can be used to infer transport, and it marks where the concept of a single air temperature begins to fray, since different species can hold different energies.

sections.heading: The Thermosphere: Why Hot Does Not Mean Warm
sections.body:
The thermosphere is routinely described as reaching temperatures of 500 to 2,000 kelvin, which sounds extraordinary and is the single most misunderstood number in atmospheric science. An unprotected object at 300 kilometres does not glow red or melt. It freezes. Reconciling those two statements requires being careful about what temperature actually measures.

Temperature in a gas is a measure of the average kinetic energy per particle, not of the total energy present. Thermospheric particles genuinely do move extraordinarily fast, and a thermometer probe placed there would find individual impacts to be energetic. But at 300 kilometres the number density is around ten to the fifteen particles per cubic metre, compared with roughly ten to the twenty-five at sea level, a factor of ten billion fewer. Heat transfer depends on how many particles strike a surface per second, so the actual heating rate from gas collisions is negligible. An object's temperature there is set almost entirely by the radiation balance between absorbed sunlight and emitted infrared, which is why spacecraft thermal design worries about sun angle and surface coatings rather than air temperature. On the night side of an orbit, radiating to a sky at 3 kelvin, surfaces plunge toward minus 100 degrees Celsius and below.

The heating that produces those high kinetic temperatures comes from the most energetic part of the solar spectrum, which never reaches the ground because the thermosphere absorbs it first. Extreme ultraviolet photons shorter than about 102.7 nanometres ionise atmospheric constituents; the Schumann-Runge continuum between roughly 130 and 175 nanometres dissociates molecular oxygen; X-rays penetrate deeper still. Each absorbed photon delivers several to hundreds of electronvolts to a single particle, and with so few particles to share it among, the energy per particle climbs enormously. Crucially, the thermosphere is also a poor radiator. There is little carbon dioxide activity relative to the heating rate, so the layer cannot easily shed the energy it absorbs, and heat is instead conducted downward. Molecular thermal conduction is efficient in a hot rarefied gas, which is why the temperature profile becomes nearly isothermal above about 300 to 400 kilometres, approaching an asymptotic value called the exospheric temperature.

That asymptotic temperature is the standard summary number for thermospheric state. Under quiet solar minimum conditions it may be only 500 to 700 kelvin. At solar maximum, or during a major geomagnetic storm, it can exceed 1,500 kelvin and occasionally approach 2,000. Because scale height is proportional to temperature, heating the thermosphere causes it to expand upward, pushing denser gas to higher altitudes. That expansion, not the temperature itself, is what matters operationally to everything in orbit. A useful way to hold the whole idea together is that the thermosphere has a very high temperature and a very low heat content, and those two quantities are only loosely related once a gas becomes thin enough.

sections.heading: Solar Control, the Solar Cycle, and Thermospheric Density
sections.body:
No other part of the atmosphere is as directly and violently controlled by the Sun as the thermosphere. The troposphere responds to total solar irradiance, which varies by only about 0.1 per cent over the eleven-year sunspot cycle, a change too small to dominate weather. The thermosphere responds to extreme ultraviolet radiation, which varies by a factor of two to ten over the same cycle. The result is that thermospheric density at a fixed altitude of 400 kilometres can differ by an order of magnitude between solar minimum and solar maximum. This is the single largest natural variation of any atmospheric quantity anywhere.

The workhorse proxy for that ultraviolet input is the F10.7 index, the solar radio flux at 10.7 centimetres wavelength, measured continuously since 1947 from Canada and expressed in solar flux units of ten to the minus twenty-two watts per square metre per hertz. It ranges from about 65 at deep solar minimum to over 250 at active maximum. Radio flux is not itself an important energy source, but it correlates well with the unmeasurable-from-the-ground extreme ultraviolet, so nearly every empirical thermosphere model, from the Jacchia models of the 1960s through the NRLMSIS family still in operational use, takes F10.7 and a geomagnetic index as its primary inputs.

Superimposed on the slow solar cycle are far faster changes. Geomagnetic storms, driven by coronal mass ejections striking the magnetosphere, dump energy into the high-latitude thermosphere through particle precipitation and through Joule heating, the resistive dissipation of ionospheric currents driven across the magnetic field. A severe storm can deposit hundreds of gigawatts, heating and expanding the thermosphere so fast that density at 400 kilometres doubles or triples within six to twelve hours. Large travelling atmospheric disturbances then propagate from the polar regions toward the equator at hundreds of metres per second, reaching the opposite hemisphere within hours. Density perturbations of this size are effectively unforecastable more than a day or two ahead, because they depend on the arrival time and magnetic orientation of a solar eruption.

Beneath both the cycle and the storms runs a long-term trend in the opposite direction. Rising carbon dioxide, which cools and contracts the upper atmosphere, has produced a measured secular decline in thermospheric density of roughly 2 to 5 per cent per decade at 400 kilometres, first robustly demonstrated by John Emmert and colleagues from decades of satellite orbital decay data. That may sound benign, and for satellite operators it extends mission lifetimes and reduces fuel needs. It also extends the orbital lifetime of debris by the same proportion, meaning defunct hardware and fragments linger years longer than they once would have, which worsens the collision environment in exactly the altitude band that is filling with constellations.

sections.heading: The Ionosphere and Radio Propagation
sections.body:
Ultraviolet and X-ray sunlight strips electrons from atoms and molecules in the mesosphere and thermosphere, creating a region of ionised gas called the ionosphere that spans roughly 60 to 1,000 kilometres. It is not a layer in the temperature sense; it overlaps the upper mesosphere, all of the thermosphere and part of the exosphere. Free electrons make the gas electrically conducting and refract radio waves, and that single property carried nearly all long-distance communication for the first half of the twentieth century. Guglielmo Marconi's transatlantic signal of December 1901 seemed impossible because radio should travel in straight lines; Kennelly and Heaviside independently proposed a conducting layer in 1902, and Edward Appleton measured its height in 1924, work for which he received the 1947 Nobel Prize.

The ionosphere is conventionally divided into regions. The D region, 60 to 90 kilometres, exists only in daylight; because the air there is comparatively dense, electrons collide frequently and absorb rather than reflect, which is why medium-wave broadcast stations are local by day and audible across a continent at night. The E region near 90 to 150 kilometres reflects reliably and produces sporadic E, dense patches of ionisation linked to metallic ions from meteor ablation that can open unexpected paths at 50 to 144 megahertz. The F region, splitting into F1 and F2 by day and merging at night, contains the peak electron density, typically ten to the eleven or ten to the twelve electrons per cubic metre near 250 to 350 kilometres.

A radio wave is reflected if its frequency is below the plasma frequency of the layer, which is proportional to the square root of electron density. The critical frequency foF2, the highest frequency reflected straight up, typically ranges from 3 to 12 megahertz. Oblique paths reflect much higher frequencies, and the maximum usable frequency for a given path is roughly foF2 divided by the cosine of the incidence angle, often three times foF2.
steps: Establish local solar time at both ends of the path, since ionisation follows the Sun. A path lit at both ends supports the highest frequencies; a path in darkness at both ends supports the lowest.

Start high and work down. In daylight over a 2,000 kilometre path, try 14 to 21 megahertz; after dark on the same path, drop to 7 or 3.5 megahertz, because the F layer weakens and will no longer reflect the higher bands.
Listen before transmitting. A band full of distant signals is open; one silent apart from local noise is closed, and no amount of power will change that.

Expect a skip zone. Ground wave reaches perhaps 50 to 150 kilometres, and the first sky-wave return may land 800 kilometres away, leaving a dead ring in between where nothing is heard on that frequency.
Use the lowest frequency that still gets through at night and the highest that still reflects by day, since daytime D-region absorption is severe below about 7 megahertz.

After a solar flare, expect a sudden ionospheric disturbance: the sunlit hemisphere's high-frequency bands may black out completely for ten minutes to an hour as D-region absorption spikes. Wait rather than retune.

sections.heading: The Aurora and Geomagnetic Storms
sections.body:
The aurora is the thermosphere made visible. Charged particles, mainly electrons with energies of about 1 to 15 kiloelectronvolts, are accelerated along magnetic field lines in the magnetosphere and precipitate into the upper atmosphere at high latitudes. They collide with atmospheric atoms and molecules, exciting them, and the excited species then radiate at characteristic wavelengths as they relax. The whole display is an atomic emission spectrum written across the sky at a height of 100 to 400 kilometres.

The colours identify both the species and the altitude, and understanding why is genuinely illuminating. The familiar green at 557.7 nanometres comes from atomic oxygen in the metastable O(1S) state, which has a radiative lifetime of about 0.7 seconds. Metastable means the transition is quantum-mechanically forbidden and therefore slow, so the atom can only emit if it survives that long without being knocked into a different state by a collision. That requires low density, which is why green emission is confined to roughly 100 to 250 kilometres and is absent lower down. The deep red at 630.0 nanometres comes from the O(1D) state with a lifetime near 110 seconds, so it can only radiate above about 200 kilometres where collisions are rarer still; high red aurora is a signature of soft, low-energy precipitation that never penetrates deep. Blue and violet at 391.4 and 427.8 nanometres come from ionised molecular nitrogen and appear at the lowest edges, below 100 kilometres, during energetic events.

Aurorae occur in two ovals centred on the geomagnetic poles, typically at 65 to 70 degrees magnetic latitude and offset toward the night side. During geomagnetic storms the oval expands equatorward, which is why mid-latitude sightings are newsworthy. The Carrington event of 1 to 2 September 1859, the most severe geomagnetic storm in the instrumental record, produced aurora visible from Cuba and Hawaii and induced currents that set telegraph paper alight. The March 1989 storm collapsed the Hydro-Quebec grid in ninety seconds, leaving six million people without power.

Storms are ranked by geomagnetic indices, principally Kp on a 0 to 9 scale updated every three hours, and Dst, which measures the depression of the equatorial magnetic field by the enhanced ring current in nanotesla. A Kp of 5 marks a minor storm; Kp 8 to 9 is severe and pushes the auroral oval toward 45 degrees magnetic latitude. Beyond the light show, these storms heat and expand the thermosphere, disturb the ionosphere enough to degrade satellite navigation accuracy from metres to tens of metres, and drive geomagnetically induced currents in long conductors such as power lines and pipelines. The aurora is the visible symptom of an energy input measured in hundreds of gigawatts.

sections.heading: Satellite Drag, Orbital Decay, and Reentry
sections.body:
Orbit is often described as being above the atmosphere, which is not true for anything below about 1,000 kilometres. Low Earth orbit is inside the thermosphere, and every spacecraft there is flying through gas, however thin. The drag force follows the same relation as for an aircraft: one half times density times velocity squared times drag coefficient times cross-sectional area. Velocity is about 7.7 kilometres per second, and because it is squared, even densities of ten to the minus twelve kilograms per cubic metre produce a measurable deceleration.

The effect on the orbit is counterintuitive and worth understanding properly. Drag removes energy, which lowers the orbit, and a lower orbit is a faster orbit. So a satellite experiencing drag speeds up rather than slowing down, a result sometimes called the drag paradox. The process is self-accelerating, because a lower orbit means denser air means more drag. Decay is therefore slow for years and then sudden: the final descent from 200 kilometres to reentry can take days, and from 150 kilometres a matter of hours.

Typical numbers give a feel for the timescales. Below about 200 kilometres, an uncontrolled object survives days to weeks. At 300 kilometres, months. At 400 kilometres, the altitude of the International Space Station, an object with typical mass-to-area ratio lasts perhaps one to several years, and the station itself loses roughly 50 to 100 metres of altitude per day at moderate solar activity, requiring periodic reboosts of a few kilometres. At 600 kilometres the lifetime is decades; at 800 kilometres, centuries. Because atmospheric density at a given altitude varies by an order of magnitude over the solar cycle, all of these figures can shift by factors of several depending on when the object is up there.

Two events illustrate the operational stakes. Skylab was expected to remain in orbit until the early 1980s, but solar cycle 21 was more active than forecast, the thermosphere expanded, drag exceeded predictions, and the station reentered over Western Australia on 11 July 1979. More recently, on 3 February 2022 SpaceX launched 49 Starlink satellites into an initial 210-kilometre parking orbit just as a modest geomagnetic storm raised thermospheric density there by roughly 50 per cent; 38 of the 49 could not climb out and were lost within days. Neither failure involved a broken spacecraft. Both were failures to predict the density of a gas so thin it is a better vacuum than any laboratory can easily produce.

This is also why reentry predictions carry such large error bars. Forecasting where an uncontrolled object will come down requires forecasting thermospheric density along its future path, which requires forecasting solar activity days ahead. Uncertainty of even 10 per cent in density translates to an along-track position error of thousands of kilometres by the final orbits, which is why official predictions for large reentries are usually quoted as a time window of several hours rather than a location.

sections.heading: Measuring the Region, and What Remains Uncertain
sections.body:
Because neither balloons nor sustained orbits can operate through the mesosphere, measuring it has always required indirect or brief methods, and the resulting patchwork explains why so much about the region remains genuinely unsettled. Sounding rockets remain the only routine way to take instruments physically into the layer. A rocket lofted from a range such as Andoya in Norway or Poker Flat in Alaska climbs through the mesosphere in about two minutes, releasing falling spheres, chaff clouds, or chemiluminescent trails of trimethyl aluminium whose drift reveals winds. The data are excellent but each flight samples one place at one moment, and each costs a great deal.

Ground-based remote sensing fills much of the gap. Rayleigh lidar retrieves density and temperature to about 90 kilometres from laser light backscattered by air molecules. Resonance lidar tuned to the sodium, iron or potassium lines measures winds and temperatures directly in the metal layers between 80 and 105 kilometres. Meteor radars track thousands of ionised meteor trails per day and infer winds from their drift. Incoherent scatter radars, of which only a handful exist worldwide, including Arecibo until its collapse in 2020, EISCAT in Scandinavia, Millstone Hill and Jicamarca, scatter powerful radio beams off thermal fluctuations in the ionospheric plasma and return profiles of electron density, ion temperature and drift up to a thousand kilometres.

From orbit, limb-viewing instruments look sideways through the atmosphere against the blackness of space, which gives good vertical resolution. The SABER instrument on NASA's TIMED satellite, operating since 2002, has produced the longest continuous temperature record of the mesosphere and lower thermosphere in existence. AIM monitored polar mesospheric clouds from 2007. Accelerometers on the CHAMP, GRACE and GOCE missions measured thermospheric density directly by sensing drag, and the archive of orbital element sets for tens of thousands of tracked objects has been mined to reconstruct density back to the 1960s.

Real uncertainties persist and should be stated plainly. The absolute meteoric mass input to the atmosphere is still uncertain by more than an order of magnitude, which propagates into uncertainty about metal layers, smoke particles and cloud nucleation. The magnitude of long-term cooling and contraction is agreed in sign but not in size, with published mesospheric trends spanning 1 to 3 kelvin per decade and thermospheric density trends spanning 2 to 5 per cent per decade, partly because separating a trend from an eleven-year solar cycle demands records longer than most instruments last. Gravity wave momentum fluxes cannot be measured globally and must be parameterised in every climate model, making them one of the largest sources of structural uncertainty in simulations of the middle atmosphere. And operational forecasting of thermospheric density beyond about two days remains poor, because it inherits the difficulty of forecasting the Sun. Anyone reading a confident single number for any of these quantities should treat it as a central estimate within a wide and honestly disputed range.

guides.title: The Composition of the Atmosphere
guides.summary: A thorough account of what Earth's atmosphere is made of, from the major and trace gases to water vapour and aerosols, how it is layered, how it formed, and how humans are changing it.

sections.heading: What the Atmosphere Is
sections.body: The atmosphere is the envelope of gases held to the Earth by gravity, a thin shell of air that surrounds the planet, sustains life, and drives weather and climate. Though it feels substantial when the wind blows, it is remarkably slight in relation to the planet it wraps. Its total mass is about five point one five times ten to the eighteenth kilograms, roughly a millionth of the mass of the Earth. Yet that mass presses down with real force: at sea level the weight of the air column above each square metre produces a standard pressure of about one hundred and one thousand three hundred and twenty-five pascals, or one atmosphere, equivalent to a ten-metre depth of water. The atmosphere has no sharp upper boundary. It simply thins with height until it fades into the near-vacuum of space, but by convention the Karman line at one hundred kilometres altitude marks the nominal edge, above which flight in the aeronautical sense gives way to spaceflight. Because air is compressible and gravity pulls it downward, density and pressure are greatest at the bottom and fall off rapidly with altitude; roughly half of the entire atmosphere's mass lies below about five and a half kilometres, and about ninety per cent lies below sixteen kilometres. A useful way to grasp the atmosphere's thinness is to note that if the Earth were the size of an apple, the layer of air that matters for weather would be no thicker than the apple's skin. What the atmosphere is made of can be considered in two ways. There is its chemical composition, the mix of gases, water vapour, and suspended particles that constitute air, which is the main subject of this guide. And there is its vertical structure, the way temperature, density, and certain properties change with height and divide the atmosphere into named layers. The two are linked: the mixing that keeps the major gases in nearly constant proportion up to about a hundred kilometres, and the chemistry that creates and destroys ozone and other compounds at particular altitudes, both depend on the physical layering. Dry air near the surface is dominated by just a few gases in strikingly stable proportions, but the atmosphere also carries a highly variable burden of water vapour and a shifting population of trace gases and aerosols whose small quantities belie their enormous importance for temperature, air quality, and life. Understanding the atmosphere's composition means understanding not only what the numbers are but why they hold so steady for some constituents and vary so wildly for others, how the mixture came to be over billions of years, and how human activity is now altering it measurably within a single lifetime.

sections.heading: The Major Permanent Gases
sections.body: When meteorologists speak of the composition of dry air, they mean air with its water vapour removed, because water is so variable that including it obscures the underlying regularity. Dry air is overwhelmingly a mixture of three gases. Nitrogen, in the form of the diatomic molecule N2, makes up about 78.08 per cent by volume, more than three-quarters of every breath. Oxygen, as O2, makes up about 20.95 per cent, roughly a fifth. Argon, a monatomic noble gas, accounts for about 0.93 per cent. Together these three constitute about 99.96 per cent of dry air; everything else is a trace. These proportions are so consistent that the major gases are called the permanent gases, and their constancy is one of the atmosphere's most important facts. It arises because turbulent mixing in the lower atmosphere stirs the air far faster than any process that would separate the gases by molecular weight, so the mixture stays uniform in composition, though not in density, up to about one hundred kilometres, a region accordingly called the homosphere. Nitrogen is abundant partly because the N2 molecule is held together by an exceptionally strong triple bond, making it chemically inert and slow to be removed from the air; it cycles only sluggishly through biological nitrogen fixation and its return by denitrification. Oxygen, by contrast, is highly reactive and would vanish from the atmosphere in a few million years through oxidation of rocks and organic matter were it not continuously replenished; its presence is a direct product of life, generated by photosynthesis in plants, algae, and cyanobacteria that split water and release O2 as a by-product. The atmosphere's oxygen is therefore a biosignature, a sign of a living planet, and its accumulation was one of the great turning points of Earth's history. Argon is essentially all argon-40, produced over geological time by the radioactive decay of potassium-40 in the crust and mantle and outgassed into the air, where, being a chemically unreactive noble gas, it simply accumulates. Beyond these three, the next most abundant permanent constituents are the noble gases neon, helium, krypton, and xenon, all present at parts-per-million levels or below, and hydrogen in tiny amounts. Because the major gases are so well mixed and so nearly constant, they form the stable backdrop against which the interesting variability of the atmosphere plays out. Curiously, the two gases that dominate air, nitrogen and oxygen, are nearly transparent to both incoming sunlight and outgoing heat radiation and so contribute almost nothing to the greenhouse warming that keeps the planet habitable; that role falls entirely to the trace gases and to water vapour, whose molecular structures let them absorb infrared radiation. Abundance and climatic importance, in the atmosphere, are very different things.

sections.heading: Water Vapour: The Great Variable
sections.body: Water vapour is the joker in the atmospheric deck, the one major constituent that refuses to hold still. Whereas nitrogen, oxygen, and argon keep nearly fixed proportions everywhere, the concentration of water vapour ranges from almost nothing, a few thousandths of a per cent by volume over cold polar deserts and in the frigid upper atmosphere, to as much as three or four per cent by volume in warm, humid tropical air, making it locally more abundant than argon and occasionally rivalling the trace of carbon dioxide many times over. This variability is why water vapour is excluded from the standard figures for dry air; averaged globally it makes up something on the order of a quarter of one per cent of the atmosphere's mass, but that average conceals enormous swings in space and time. The amount of water vapour air can hold is governed by temperature through a relationship captured by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, which states that the saturation vapour pressure rises steeply, roughly exponentially, with temperature; warm air can hold far more moisture than cold air, increasing its capacity by about seven per cent for each degree Celsius of warming. This single fact underlies much of meteorology. When moist air is cooled, by rising and expanding, by contact with a cold surface, or by mixing, it reaches saturation, its relative humidity reaches one hundred per cent, and further cooling forces the excess vapour to condense into the tiny droplets and ice crystals that form clouds, fog, dew, and frost, and ultimately rain and snow. Water is unique among atmospheric constituents in existing abundantly in all three phases, gas, liquid, and solid, under ordinary Earth conditions, and it is constantly changing between them. These phase changes make water vapour the atmosphere's great engine of energy transport. Evaporation absorbs a large amount of latent heat, about 2.26 million joules per kilogram, drawing energy from a surface and storing it in the vapour; when the vapour later condenses in a cloud, that latent heat is released, warming the surrounding air and powering thunderstorms, hurricanes, and the general circulation. Water vapour is also by a wide margin the most important greenhouse gas, responsible for roughly half of Earth's natural greenhouse effect and, with clouds, a large further share. Crucially, though, it acts not as an independent driver but as a feedback: because its concentration is set by temperature, a warming caused by some other agent increases evaporation and atmospheric moisture, which traps more heat and amplifies the original warming, while a cooling does the reverse. This water-vapour feedback roughly doubles the sensitivity of climate to other influences and is one of the reasons the atmosphere responds so strongly to changes in the long-lived greenhouse gases. Water vapour thus sits at the crossroads of composition, weather, and climate, a minor and variable ingredient by mass yet central to nearly everything the atmosphere does.

sections.heading: Carbon Dioxide and the Carbon Cycle
sections.body: Carbon dioxide, CO2, is present in the atmosphere in only trace amounts, yet it exerts an influence out of all proportion to its scarcity. As of the mid-2020s its concentration is about 420 parts per million by volume, or 0.042 per cent, meaning that fewer than one molecule in two thousand of dry air is carbon dioxide. Before the Industrial Revolution the figure was about 280 parts per million, and across the ice ages of the past several hundred thousand years it oscillated between roughly 180 parts per million in glacial periods and 280 in warm interglacials, a range documented with great precision by the analysis of ancient air bubbles trapped in Antarctic and Greenland ice cores. That such a minute constituent matters so much follows from its molecular structure: unlike the symmetric N2 and O2, the CO2 molecule can bend and stretch in ways that absorb and re-emit infrared radiation, making it a potent greenhouse gas that traps outgoing heat and warms the surface. Carbon dioxide is continually exchanged between the atmosphere and other reservoirs through the carbon cycle, a set of flows that under natural conditions keep it in rough balance. Photosynthesis by land plants and marine organisms draws CO2 out of the air and fixes its carbon into living tissue; respiration, decay, and combustion return it. The oceans hold about fifty times as much carbon as the atmosphere, dissolved as CO2 and as bicarbonate and carbonate ions, and they exchange it across the sea surface, absorbing more where waters are cold and releasing it where they are warm. These biological and oceanic exchanges produce a visible annual rhythm in the atmospheric record: the famous Keeling Curve, the continuous measurement of CO2 begun by Charles David Keeling at Mauna Loa in Hawaii in 1958, shows a saw-tooth seasonal cycle superimposed on a relentless upward trend. The seasonal wiggle reflects the breathing of the Northern Hemisphere's vast forests, which draw down CO2 in spring and summer and release it in autumn and winter. The upward trend reflects human activity, principally the burning of fossil fuels, coal, oil, and natural gas, which transfers carbon locked underground for hundreds of millions of years into the air far faster than natural sinks can remove it, together with deforestation and cement manufacture. Only about half of the carbon dioxide humans emit remains in the atmosphere; the rest is taken up by the oceans and the land biosphere, which has slowed the atmospheric rise but at a cost, since dissolving CO2 in seawater forms carbonic acid and drives ocean acidification, lowering the ocean's pH and threatening organisms that build shells and skeletons of calcium carbonate. Carbon dioxide is described as a long-lived and well-mixed greenhouse gas: a pulse of it added to the air persists in effect for centuries to millennia as it slowly redistributes among the reservoirs, and it spreads to nearly uniform concentration around the globe. This longevity is precisely why it is the central agent of long-term human-caused climate change.

sections.heading: Trace Greenhouse Gases and Ozone
sections.body: Beyond carbon dioxide, the atmosphere carries several other trace gases whose small concentrations conceal a large climatic and chemical importance. Methane, CH4, is present at about 1.9 parts per million, more than double its pre-industrial level of around 0.7 parts per million. Molecule for molecule it is a far more powerful absorber of infrared radiation than carbon dioxide, though it is much scarcer and shorter-lived, persisting only about a decade before oxidising in the atmosphere, largely to CO2 and water. Its sources are both natural and human: wetlands, where microbes produce it in waterlogged soils, along with livestock digestion, rice paddies, landfills, and leaks from fossil-fuel extraction. Nitrous oxide, N2O, laughing gas, sits at about 0.33 parts per million, is very long-lived, and comes chiefly from soils and from the use of nitrogen fertilisers, as well as from combustion. Ozone, O3, is a special and double-edged constituent that must be understood by altitude. In the stratosphere it forms the protective ozone layer discussed elsewhere in this guide, shielding the surface from ultraviolet radiation. In the lower atmosphere, near the ground, ozone is instead a pollutant and a greenhouse gas, formed by chemical reactions among sunlight, oxides of nitrogen, and volatile organic compounds emitted by vehicles and industry; there it damages lungs and vegetation and is a chief ingredient of photochemical smog. A further class of trace gases is entirely artificial. The chlorofluorocarbons, or CFCs, and related halocarbons, invented in the twentieth century for refrigeration, aerosols, and foam-blowing, are extraordinarily potent greenhouse gases and, as later sections describe, the agents that destroyed stratospheric ozone. Because they were purely industrial products with no natural source, their control under the Montreal Protocol became possible, and their atmospheric concentrations, having peaked, are now slowly declining. The strength of a greenhouse gas is compared using its global warming potential, an index of how much heat a given mass traps over a specified period, usually a hundred years, relative to the same mass of carbon dioxide; methane's is several tens of times that of CO2 over a century, nitrous oxide's is around three hundred, and some halocarbons exceed ten thousand. Yet global warming potential must be weighed against abundance and lifetime to judge a gas's actual contribution. Carbon dioxide, though individually the weakest of these absorbers, dominates the human-caused greenhouse effect because it is emitted in such vast quantities and lingers so long. The trace gases illustrate a recurring theme of atmospheric composition: chemical influence bears little relation to sheer abundance. A gas measured in parts per million or even parts per billion can steer the planet's radiation balance, its protective shielding, and the quality of the air people breathe, and small human perturbations to these trace constituents have produced some of the largest environmental changes of the modern era.

sections.heading: Aerosols and Particulates
sections.body: Not everything suspended in the atmosphere is a gas. The air also carries aerosols, tiny solid and liquid particles ranging from a few nanometres to tens of micrometres across, small enough to remain suspended for anywhere from hours to weeks. Though their total mass is minute, aerosols profoundly affect visibility, human health, cloud formation, and climate. Their sources are diverse. Natural aerosols include sea salt flung up as ocean spray dries, mineral dust lifted from deserts by the wind, volcanic ash and the sulphate droplets formed from volcanic sulphur dioxide, smoke from wildfires, pollen and other biological particles, and secondary particles that condense from natural gases such as the sulphur compounds emitted by marine plankton. Human activity adds a large burden of anthropogenic aerosols: soot, or black carbon, and sulphate particles from the burning of coal, oil, and biomass, along with nitrates, organic particles, and industrial dust. Aerosols are classified by size because size governs both how long they stay aloft and how deeply they penetrate the lungs; the fine fraction known as PM2.5, particles under two and a half micrometres, is especially dangerous to health because it can reach the deep airways and even enter the bloodstream, and air pollution of this kind is among the leading environmental causes of premature death worldwide. Climatically, aerosols act in two broad ways. Directly, they scatter and absorb sunlight: most, such as sulphates and sea salt, are bright and scatter incoming light back to space, exerting a cooling influence, while dark soot absorbs sunlight and warms the air while darkening snow and ice it settles upon. Indirectly, aerosols are essential to clouds, because water vapour does not readily condense in perfectly clean air; it needs a surface, and aerosol particles serve as the cloud condensation nuclei on which droplets form. More numerous aerosols tend to produce clouds made of more but smaller droplets, which are brighter and reflect more sunlight and may rain less readily and last longer, a set of effects that on balance also cools the surface but remains one of the largest uncertainties in climate science. The overall aerosol influence on climate is a net cooling that has masked part of the warming from greenhouse gases, which means that efforts to clean up air pollution, desirable for health, can unmask additional warming. Aerosols also produce some of the atmosphere's most dramatic transient effects. A large volcanic eruption that injects sulphur into the stratosphere, such as Mount Pinatubo in 1991, can spread a veil of reflective sulphate droplets around the globe and cool the surface by several tenths of a degree for a year or two before the particles settle out. Unlike the long-lived greenhouse gases, aerosols are removed quickly, chiefly by rain, so their concentrations vary greatly from place to place and their effects are regional and short-lived, though continually renewed by ongoing emissions.

sections.heading: The Vertical Structure of the Atmosphere
sections.body: The atmosphere is not uniform from bottom to top; it is layered, and the layers are defined chiefly by how temperature changes with height. Because temperature does not simply fall steadily upward but reverses direction several times, atmospheric scientists divide the atmosphere into four principal layers separated by boundaries whose names end in the suffix pause.
