The lowest layer is the troposphere, from a Greek root meaning turning or mixing, extending from the surface to an average of about twelve kilometres, higher over the tropics at some sixteen or seventeen kilometres and lower over the poles at around eight. Here temperature falls with height at an average environmental lapse rate of about six and a half degrees Celsius per kilometre, because the air is warmed from below by the sun-heated surface rather than directly by sunlight. The troposphere contains about three-quarters of the atmosphere's mass and nearly all its water vapour, and it is the layer of weather, of clouds, storms, and the vertical convection that its temperature profile encourages. Its top, the tropopause, marks where temperature stops falling. Above lies the stratosphere, reaching to about fifty kilometres, in which temperature rises with height, an inversion caused by the absorption of solar ultraviolet radiation by the ozone layer within it. This warm-over-cold structure makes the stratosphere very stable and resistant to vertical mixing, so it is calm and layered, which is why jet aircraft cruise in its lower reaches; material injected into it, such as volcanic sulphate, can remain for years. Its top is the stratopause. Next is the mesosphere, extending to about eighty-five kilometres, where temperature again falls with height, reaching the coldest temperatures found anywhere in the atmosphere, below minus ninety degrees Celsius near its top, the mesopause. It is in the mesosphere that most meteors burn up, heated by friction with the thin air. Above the mesopause is the thermosphere, a very deep layer extending to several hundred kilometres, in which temperature rises dramatically, to hundreds or even thousands of degrees, as the sparse gas absorbs the most energetic solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation. The air here is so tenuous, however, that this high temperature carries little heat; a thermometer would not feel hot because too few molecules strike it. The thermosphere hosts the aurora and, in its lower part, the orbits of the International Space Station. Finally the exosphere, from about five hundred kilometres outward, is the atmosphere's uppermost fringe, where molecules are so widely spaced that they follow long ballistic trajectories and the fastest, lightest ones, chiefly hydrogen and helium, can escape Earth's gravity into space. This thermal layering governs where different chemical processes occur, traps pollutants and weather within the troposphere, and shapes the paths of everything from thunderstorms to spacecraft.

sections.heading: The Ozone Layer
sections.body: Within the stratosphere, roughly between fifteen and thirty-five kilometres altitude, lies a region of relatively enhanced ozone concentration known as the ozone layer, one of the atmosphere's most important features for life. Even here ozone is a trace gas, never exceeding about ten parts per million, and if all the atmosphere's ozone were brought to the surface at standard pressure it would form a shell only about three millimetres thick, a quantity expressed as roughly three hundred Dobson units. Yet this thin veneer absorbs the great majority of the sun's biologically damaging ultraviolet radiation in the UV-B and UV-C bands, shielding the surface from wavelengths that would otherwise damage DNA, cause skin cancers and cataracts, and harm phytoplankton and crops. Stratospheric ozone is continuously created and destroyed in a natural cycle first described by the British scientist Sydney Chapman in 1930. High-energy ultraviolet light splits an oxygen molecule, O2, into two free oxygen atoms; each atom then combines with another O2 to form ozone, O3; and ozone in turn absorbs ultraviolet light and breaks apart, releasing the energy as heat, which is what warms the stratosphere. This creation and destruction stay in a balance that maintains the layer while constantly converting harmful ultraviolet into heat. In the 1970s scientists recognised that this balance could be upset by human-made chemicals. Mario Molina and Frank Sherwood Rowland showed in 1974 that chlorofluorocarbons, chemically inert at the surface, drift intact into the stratosphere, where intense ultraviolet finally breaks them apart and liberates chlorine atoms. A single chlorine atom can catalytically destroy many thousands of ozone molecules before it is removed, because the reaction regenerates the chlorine to attack again. The consequences became starkly visible in 1985 when British researchers reported a dramatic springtime thinning of ozone over Antarctica, the ozone hole, driven by chlorine chemistry made especially efficient on the surfaces of polar stratospheric clouds during the cold, dark, isolated Antarctic winter and its returning spring sunlight. The discovery galvanised an unusually swift international response. The Montreal Protocol of 1987, later strengthened, phased out the production of CFCs and related ozone-depleting substances worldwide, and it is often cited as the most successful international environmental agreement ever concluded. Because these chemicals are long-lived, recovery is slow, but atmospheric concentrations of the controlled substances have been falling since the late 1990s, the ozone layer is showing measurable signs of healing, and it is projected to return to its 1980 state around the middle of the twenty-first century over most of the globe and somewhat later over Antarctica. The ozone story is a defining example of how a trace constituent can be indispensable to life, how human chemistry can inadvertently threaten it, and how scientific understanding coupled with international action can pull an atmospheric system back from serious harm.

sections.heading: The Homosphere, Heterosphere, and Ionosphere
sections.body: Alongside the familiar division of the atmosphere by temperature, scientists use other classifications that capture different physical realities, and three of the most useful concern how the atmosphere is mixed, how its composition changes at great height, and how it becomes electrically charged. The first distinction is between the homosphere and the heterosphere, drawn on the basis of composition. Up to about one hundred kilometres, turbulent mixing dominates and stirs the gases so thoroughly that their relative proportions stay constant regardless of their differing molecular weights; this well-mixed region is the homosphere, and it is why the ratios of nitrogen, oxygen, and argon hold steady from the surface to the mesopause. Above about one hundred kilometres, in the heterosphere, the air is so thin that mixing becomes ineffective and molecular diffusion takes over, allowing gravity to sort the constituents by mass. The heavier gases settle out at lower levels and the lighter ones dominate progressively higher up, so that the composition changes with altitude: molecular nitrogen and oxygen give way to atomic oxygen, then to helium, and finally, in the outermost reaches, to hydrogen, the lightest gas of all, which forms the tenuous outer corona of the atmosphere. The boundary between these regions, near one hundred kilometres, is called the turbopause or homopause. A second important classification concerns electrical charge. Overlapping the upper mesosphere and the thermosphere, from roughly sixty kilometres to a thousand kilometres, lies the ionosphere, a region where solar ultraviolet and X-ray radiation are energetic enough to knock electrons off atoms and molecules, producing a partially ionised plasma of free electrons and positive ions. The ionosphere is not a distinct layer in the temperature sense but a property superimposed on the mesosphere and thermosphere, and it is itself subdivided into regions labelled D, E, and F by altitude and ionisation. Its degree of ionisation rises and falls with the sun, strengthening by day and during periods of high solar activity and weakening at night as the ions and electrons recombine. The ionosphere has great practical significance because it reflects and refracts radio waves. Certain radio frequencies bounce off the ionosphere and are thereby returned to Earth, enabling long-distance shortwave communication that follows the curve of the planet far beyond the horizon, a technique that shaped twentieth-century broadcasting and remains important for aviation, maritime, and amateur radio. Disturbances in the ionosphere caused by solar flares and geomagnetic storms can disrupt these communications and degrade satellite navigation signals that pass through it. Beyond the ionosphere and merging with it lies the magnetosphere, the region where the Earth's magnetic field dominates the behaviour of charged particles, deflecting the solar wind and channelling energetic particles toward the poles, where they collide with atmospheric gases and excite the shimmering light of the aurora. These overlapping classifications remind the reader that the single word atmosphere names a system that can be sliced many ways, by temperature, by mixing, by chemistry, and by electrical state, each division illuminating a different aspect of the whole.

sections.heading: How the Atmosphere Formed and Evolved
sections.body: The atmosphere that surrounds the Earth today is not the one the planet was born with; its composition is the outcome of more than four and a half billion years of geological and biological history, and it has been transformed almost beyond recognition. The Earth's earliest, or primary, atmosphere is thought to have consisted of light gases captured from the solar nebula, chiefly hydrogen and helium, but this was quickly lost. The young Earth was too warm and its gravity too weak to retain such light molecules, and any remnant was stripped away by the intense radiation and particle wind of the young Sun. A second, or secondary, atmosphere then accumulated from within the planet, released by volcanic outgassing as molten rock degassed and by the impact of comets and volatile-rich asteroids. This atmosphere was rich in water vapour, carbon dioxide, and nitrogen, with sulphur compounds and other volcanic gases, but it contained essentially no free oxygen. As the planet cooled, the water vapour condensed and rained out over long ages to form the oceans, and much of the carbon dioxide dissolved in that water and was eventually locked into carbonate rocks, drawing down what had been a massive greenhouse and leaving nitrogen, chemically inert and not readily removed, to accumulate as the dominant gas it remains. The decisive transformation was biological. For the first two billion years or so, life was anaerobic and the air held no appreciable oxygen. Then photosynthetic cyanobacteria evolved the ability to split water using sunlight and release oxygen as a waste product. For a long time this oxygen was consumed as fast as it was made, absorbed by dissolved iron and other reduced substances in the oceans, which precipitated as the vast banded iron formations found in ancient rocks. Once those sinks were saturated, oxygen began to accumulate in the air in an episode around 2.4 billion years ago known as the Great Oxidation Event, a change so profound that it has been called a catastrophe for the anaerobic organisms it poisoned even as it opened the way for oxygen-breathing life. Oxygen levels rose in fits and starts thereafter, climbing again in the later Proterozoic and reaching roughly modern values by the time complex animals appeared. A by-product of atmospheric oxygen was the formation of the ozone layer, which by screening out ultraviolet radiation eventually made it possible for life to colonise the land. Throughout the Phanerozoic, the past half-billion years, atmospheric composition continued to fluctuate; oxygen may have reached around thirty-five per cent during the Carboniferous period of great coal forests, and carbon dioxide has ranged widely, generally declining over the long term as it was buried in rocks and fossil fuels. The atmosphere, in short, is a product of its planet's whole history and, uniquely in the known solar system, of its life. Its oxygen-rich, low-carbon-dioxide state is not a given but a hard-won and dynamic condition maintained by ongoing geological and biological cycles.

sections.heading: Pressure, Density, and the Gas Laws
sections.body: The chemical make-up of the atmosphere is inseparable from its physical behaviour, and that behaviour is governed by the gas laws, which relate the pressure, volume, temperature, and amount of a gas. Air behaves very nearly as an ideal gas, described by the equation of state that pressure times volume equals the amount of gas times a constant times the absolute temperature, commonly written PV equals nRT. From this follow the classical relations: at fixed temperature, pressure and volume vary inversely, which is Boyle's law; at fixed pressure, volume increases in proportion to absolute temperature, which is Charles's law. A principle of special importance for composition is Dalton's law of partial pressures, which states that in a mixture of gases each constituent exerts the pressure it would exert if it alone occupied the volume, and the total pressure is the sum of these partial pressures. Because the major gases are well mixed, the partial pressure of oxygen is a nearly constant fraction, about twenty-one per cent, of the total pressure at every altitude within the homosphere. This is why breathing becomes difficult at high elevation: not because the percentage of oxygen falls, for it does not, but because the total pressure falls, so the partial pressure of oxygen, which drives its uptake into the blood, drops with it. Atmospheric pressure at any height equals the weight of all the air above that height, so pressure is greatest at the surface and decreases upward. Because air is compressible, this decrease is not linear but roughly exponential, described by the hydrostatic equation and, for an atmosphere of uniform temperature, by the barometric formula, in which pressure falls by a constant factor for each fixed increase in height. The height over which pressure falls to about thirty-seven per cent of its value, the scale height, is around eight kilometres for Earth's atmosphere, which is why pressure roughly halves for every five and a half kilometres of ascent. Density behaves similarly, decreasing rapidly with altitude, so that the air at the cruising height of a jet is only about a quarter as dense as at sea level. Temperature enters through the same relations: warm air is less dense than cold air at the same pressure, because its molecules move faster and spread further apart, and this density difference is the buoyancy that drives convection, lifts warm air, and organises much of the weather. Standardised reference profiles, such as the International Standard Atmosphere, tabulate how pressure, temperature, and density vary with height for engineering and aviation, taking a sea-level pressure of 1013.25 hectopascals, a temperature of fifteen degrees Celsius, and the standard lapse rate. These physical laws explain why the atmosphere thins as it does, why its constituents stay mixed in constant proportion within the homosphere, and how pressure, temperature, and density together set the stage on which weather and climate unfold.

sections.heading: Human Alteration of Atmospheric Composition
sections.body: For most of Earth's history the composition of the atmosphere changed only over geological or biological timescales measured in millions or thousands of years. Since the Industrial Revolution, human activity has begun to alter it measurably within decades, and understanding these changes is now among the most consequential tasks in science. The most far-reaching change is the rise in long-lived greenhouse gases. Atmospheric carbon dioxide has increased from about 280 parts per million before industrialisation to over 420 today, a rise of more than fifty per cent, driven mainly by the combustion of fossil fuels along with deforestation and cement production; methane and nitrous oxide have risen even more sharply in proportional terms. Because these gases absorb outgoing infrared radiation, their accumulation enhances the natural greenhouse effect and is warming the planet's surface and oceans, a conclusion supported by an overwhelming body of evidence including the instrumental temperature record, the retreat of glaciers and sea ice, the rise of sea level, and the isotopic fingerprint of fossil carbon in the added CO2. The scientific consensus, expressed by bodies such as the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, is that this warming is unequivocally caused chiefly by human emissions. A second, related change is ocean acidification, the drop in seawater pH as the oceans absorb roughly a quarter of emitted CO2, forming carbonic acid and threatening corals, shellfish, and the base of marine food webs; it is sometimes called the other carbon dioxide problem. A third change was the depletion of stratospheric ozone by chlorofluorocarbons, addressed by the Montreal Protocol and now slowly reversing, a rare success story showing that atmospheric harm can be halted by concerted action. A fourth is air pollution near the surface, the loading of the lower atmosphere with aerosols, ground-level ozone, oxides of nitrogen and sulphur, carbon monoxide, and particulate matter from vehicles, industry, and the burning of fuels; this pollution harms human health on a vast scale, produces smog and acid rain, and reduces visibility, though its reflective aerosols also exert a partial and temporary cooling that has masked some greenhouse warming. These changes are not independent. Cleaning up sulphate pollution improves health but can unmask warming; warming increases water vapour, which amplifies it; and the same combustion produces both CO2 and particulates. What distinguishes the human perturbation from natural variability is its speed and its cause. Natural changes in atmospheric composition, volcanic eruptions, orbital cycles, slow geological shifts, still occur, but the current rate of change in the long-lived greenhouse gases is faster than anything in the ice-core record spanning hundreds of thousands of years and, for CO2, faster than natural sinks can absorb. Because carbon dioxide persists for centuries, the composition changes now under way commit the planet to consequences that will unfold long after emissions themselves are curbed, which is why both reducing emissions and adapting to change have become central concerns of policy and science.

sections.heading: Measuring the Atmosphere and Connections Onward
sections.body: Everything known about atmospheric composition rests on measurement, and the instruments and networks that observe the air are as much a part of the science as the theories they test. Composition is measured across scales from the ground to space. Surface stations such as the Mauna Loa Observatory, which has recorded carbon dioxide continuously since 1958, provide long, precise records of the well-mixed gases far from local sources. Weather balloons, or radiosondes, launched twice daily from hundreds of sites worldwide, carry instruments aloft to measure temperature, pressure, humidity, and winds through the troposphere and lower stratosphere, building the vertical profiles on which forecasting depends. Aircraft sample the composition of the upper troposphere and stratosphere directly. Satellites observe the whole atmosphere from orbit, using instruments that measure how the air absorbs and emits radiation at particular wavelengths to map the global distribution of ozone, water vapour, carbon dioxide, methane, aerosols, and temperature. Ground-based remote sensing, including lidar and spectrometry, and networks such as those monitoring ozone in Dobson units, fill in the picture. The chemical make-up of ancient air is reconstructed from proxies, above all the bubbles of trapped gas in polar ice cores, which extend the record of carbon dioxide and methane back hundreds of thousands of years and provide the baseline against which modern change is judged. These observations feed into numerical models that encode the physics of the gas laws, the chemistry of ozone and pollutants, the radiative properties of greenhouse gases and aerosols, and the cycles of carbon and water, allowing scientists to test their understanding and to project how composition and climate may evolve. The study of atmospheric composition connects outward to nearly every branch of Earth and environmental science. It is the foundation of meteorology, since the water vapour, temperature, and pressure it describes are the raw materials of weather. It is the foundation of climatology and climate change science, since the greenhouse gases and aerosols it tracks control the planet's energy balance. It links to atmospheric chemistry, which studies the reactions that create and destroy ozone, smog, and other compounds; to the biogeochemical cycles of carbon, nitrogen, and sulphur that exchange elements between air, ocean, rock, and life; and to oceanography, ecology, and geology, since the atmosphere is coupled to all of them. It bears on air quality and public health, on aviation and space flight, and on the search for life beyond Earth, since the composition of an atmosphere, especially the presence of oxygen and other biosignature gases out of chemical equilibrium, is one of the few ways to judge whether a distant planet might be habitable or inhabited. To understand what the air is made of, then, is not a narrow or finished subject but an entry point into the workings of the whole planet, a mixture whose steady major gases, variable water, and potent traces together make the Earth uniquely alive and whose ongoing alteration by humanity is among the defining stories of the present age.

guides.title: The Troposphere and Where Weather Happens
guides.summary: A thorough tour of the lowest layer of the atmosphere: its structure, composition, temperature and pressure profiles, energy budget, and the physics of moisture, convection, wind, fronts, and clouds that make it the theatre of nearly all weather.

sections.heading: The Atmosphere in Layers: Locating the Troposphere
sections.body: The atmosphere is not a uniform blanket of air but a structured envelope divided into layers, and the layers are conventionally defined by how temperature changes with height. From the surface upward the layers are the troposphere, the stratosphere, the mesosphere, and the thermosphere, with a tenuous exosphere beyond, each separated from the next by a pause where the temperature trend reverses. The troposphere is the lowest and, for weather, by far the most important. Its name comes from the Greek tropos, meaning turning or mixing, and it is aptly chosen, because the defining feature of the troposphere is vigorous vertical overturning. It extends from the ground to an upper boundary called the tropopause, whose height is not fixed but varies with latitude and season. Over the equator the tropopause stands at roughly sixteen to eighteen kilometres; over the poles it lies as low as eight or nine kilometres; a global average is often quoted as about twelve kilometres, or roughly the cruising altitude of a long-haul jet. The layer is thicker where the surface is warmer, because warm air is more buoyant and convects higher, so the troposphere bulges over the tropics and thins toward the poles, and it is generally somewhat deeper in summer than in winter. Within the troposphere temperature falls with height at an average rate near six and a half degrees Celsius per kilometre, until it reaches a minimum at the tropopause, where values of around minus fifty-five degrees Celsius are typical and the coldest tropical tropopause can approach minus eighty. Above the tropopause, in the stratosphere, temperature stops falling and begins to rise with height, because the ozone layer there absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and warms the air from within. This temperature inversion at the tropopause acts as a lid: it suppresses vertical motion, so the mixing so characteristic of the troposphere largely stops, and the boundary marks the effective ceiling of weather. Only the most powerful thunderstorms punch briefly through it, their anvil tops spreading out against the stable stratospheric air. The troposphere is where humans live and breathe, where clouds form and rain falls, and where essentially all the phenomena we call weather occur, from a light breeze to a hurricane. It is a thin skin relative to the planet: if the Earth were the size of an apple, the whole weather-bearing troposphere would be thinner than the apple's skin. Understanding weather therefore means understanding this shallow, restless, overturning layer, how it is heated and cooled, how its air moves, and how the water it carries condenses and falls. The remainder of this guide builds that understanding from the ground up, beginning with what the troposphere is made of and how its temperature and pressure are arranged with height.

sections.heading: Composition and Mass: What the Troposphere Is Made Of
sections.body: Dry air in the troposphere is a remarkably uniform mixture, and because the troposphere is so well stirred, its major gases are found in nearly constant proportions everywhere up to the tropopause, a region sometimes called the homosphere for this reason. By volume, dry air is about seventy-eight percent nitrogen and twenty-one percent oxygen, with the remaining one percent made up chiefly of argon at just under one percent and carbon dioxide at roughly four hundred and twenty parts per million and rising. Trace amounts of neon, helium, methane, krypton, and other gases complete the mixture. These proportions are held constant by turbulent mixing, which acts far faster than the gravitational settling that would otherwise sort gases by molecular weight; such sorting only becomes important far higher up, above about a hundred kilometres. The one major constituent that is not uniform is water vapour, and it is the single most important variable for weather. Water vapour ranges from almost nothing in cold, dry polar or desert air to as much as four percent of the air by volume in warm, humid tropical air near the surface. Crucially, water is the only atmospheric substance that exists abundantly in all three phases, gas, liquid, and solid, at ordinary tropospheric temperatures, and the energy exchanged as it changes phase drives much of the weather. Because water vapour is concentrated in the lowest few kilometres where it evaporates from oceans and land, the troposphere holds about ninety-nine percent of the atmosphere's water. It also holds the great bulk of the atmosphere's total mass. Because air is compressible and pressure falls roughly exponentially with height, the lowest layers are the densest, and the troposphere, though only the bottom tenth or so of the atmosphere's vertical extent, contains between seventy-five and eighty percent of the entire mass of air and nearly all of the substances important to life and weather. In addition to gases the troposphere carries aerosols, tiny suspended particles of dust, sea salt, soot, pollen, volcanic ash, and pollution, in concentrations far higher than in the layers above. These particles are not incidental. Many of them serve as cloud condensation nuclei and ice nuclei, the microscopic seeds on which water vapour condenses into cloud droplets and ice crystals; without such nuclei, air could become greatly supersaturated before cloud would form. Aerosols also scatter and absorb sunlight, giving the sky its blue colour and sunsets their red, and they influence climate directly and through their effects on clouds. The troposphere, then, is a compressible, well-mixed reservoir of nitrogen and oxygen, carrying a small but decisive and highly variable cargo of water in all its phases together with a haze of particles, and it is this particular chemistry, above all the presence of water, that makes it the layer where weather lives.

sections.heading: The Vertical Temperature Profile and the Environmental Lapse Rate
sections.body: The most important single fact about the troposphere is that, on average, it gets colder as you go up. The rate at which the temperature of the still surrounding air decreases with height is called the environmental lapse rate, and its long-term global average is close to six and a half degrees Celsius per kilometre, equivalent to about three and a half degrees Fahrenheit per thousand feet. This average is only an average; the actual environmental lapse rate at any place and moment can be much steeper or much shallower, and it can even reverse. When temperature increases with height over some layer, the situation is called an inversion, and inversions are extremely important because they are exceptionally stable and trap air, pollution, and fog beneath them. The environmental lapse rate must be carefully distinguished from the adiabatic lapse rates discussed later, which describe how a moving parcel of air cools as it rises, not how the temperature of the stationary background air is arranged; confusing the two is the single most common error in learning atmospheric science. The environmental profile is what a weather balloon actually measures as it ascends, a snapshot of the real air, whereas the adiabatic rates are theoretical properties of a rising parcel. The reason temperature generally falls with height in the troposphere is bound up with how the layer is heated, which the following sections develop: the ground absorbs sunlight and warms the air in contact with it, so the air is warmest at the bottom and, because pressure falls with height, rising air expands and cools. The decline continues until the tropopause, where it halts. The tropopause is formally defined by the World Meteorological Organization as the lowest level at which the lapse rate falls to two degrees Celsius per kilometre or less, provided the average lapse rate above stays below that value for at least two kilometres. Above it, in the stratosphere, the presence of ozone absorbing solar ultraviolet reverses the trend and temperature climbs with height, creating a strong and persistent inversion that caps the troposphere and gives the tropopause its role as the ceiling of weather. The height and temperature of the tropopause vary systematically. Over the warm tropics it is high and very cold, near minus eighty degrees; over the cold poles it is low and, paradoxically, less cold at its own level. There are often two distinct tropopauses at mid-latitudes, a break between the high tropical one and the low polar one, and this break is associated with the jet streams. The vertical temperature structure is not a static curiosity; it governs whether the atmosphere is stable or unstable, whether air will rise or sink, and therefore whether clouds and storms can develop. Reading a plotted temperature profile, a skew-T diagram in a forecaster's hands, is the starting point for anticipating the day's weather.

sections.heading: Pressure, Density, and Hydrostatic Balance
sections.body: Air has weight, and the pressure at any level in the atmosphere is simply the weight of all the air lying above a unit area at that level. At sea level the average pressure is about one hundred and one thousand three hundred pascals, or 1013 hectopascals, also written as 1013 millibars, which corresponds to roughly ten tonnes of air pressing down on every square metre. Because pressure is cumulative weight from above, it must always decrease with height, and it does so rapidly. The governing relation is the hydrostatic equation, which states that the change in pressure with height equals minus the density of the air times the acceleration of gravity, written as dp divided by dz equals minus rho times g. This balance, between the downward pull of gravity and the upward decrease of pressure, is called hydrostatic equilibrium, and the atmosphere is very nearly in this state at all times on large scales because any imbalance is corrected almost instantly by vertical acceleration. Combining hydrostatic balance with the ideal gas law, which relates pressure, density, and temperature, shows that pressure falls off approximately exponentially with height, halving over a fixed vertical interval. This interval is characterised by the scale height, roughly eight kilometres in the lower atmosphere, over which pressure drops to about thirty-seven percent, one over the mathematical constant e, of its value. A useful rule of thumb that follows is that pressure roughly halves for every five and a half kilometres of ascent: about half the entire atmosphere by mass lies below that altitude, and about ninety percent lies below sixteen kilometres. Density, the mass of air per unit volume, behaves similarly, falling with height, though it also depends on temperature, since warm air is less dense than cold air at the same pressure. This is why the troposphere holds most of the atmosphere's mass despite being a thin layer, and why aircraft, which rely on air density for lift and engine performance, and human physiology, which depends on the partial pressure of oxygen, both feel the thinning of the air acutely with altitude. The rapid decline of pressure with height is also the engine of the adiabatic cooling of rising air. When a parcel of air ascends, it moves into surroundings of lower pressure, so it expands; in expanding it does work on the surrounding air and, if no heat is added, its internal energy and therefore its temperature must fall. Conversely, sinking air is compressed and warms. This intimate link between the vertical pressure structure and the temperature of moving air is the physical heart of convection, cloud formation, and the whole vertical dimension of weather, and it is why the pressure profile, though invisible, underlies everything the troposphere does. Horizontal differences in pressure, meanwhile, drive the winds, as later sections describe.

sections.heading: The Energy Budget: Why the Troposphere Is Heated From Below
sections.body: Weather is ultimately powered by the Sun, but the way solar energy reaches and warms the troposphere explains one of its most important features: the layer is heated mainly from below, at the ground, rather than directly from above by sunlight passing through it. Incoming solar radiation arrives chiefly as visible and near-infrared light, wavelengths to which the clear atmosphere is largely transparent. Much of this shortwave radiation therefore passes straight through the troposphere with little absorption and is taken up instead by the land and ocean surface, which warms. About thirty percent of incoming sunlight is reflected back to space, by clouds, by bright surfaces such as snow and desert, and by air molecules, a fraction called the albedo; roughly twenty percent is absorbed within the atmosphere itself, largely by water vapour, ozone, and clouds; and the remaining half or so is absorbed at the surface. The warmed surface then heats the air above it by three routes. It emits longwave infrared radiation, to which greenhouse gases, above all water vapour and carbon dioxide, are strongly opaque, so this radiation is absorbed by the lower air and re-emitted, a large part of it downward, in the process known as the greenhouse effect that keeps the surface far warmer than sunlight alone would. It transfers heat by conduction to the air molecules in direct contact with it, though air is a poor conductor and this acts only in a very thin layer. And most importantly for lifting heat through the depth of the troposphere, it drives convection and evaporation. Warm surface air, made buoyant, rises and carries heat upward as sensible heat, while water evaporated from the surface carries energy upward as latent heat that is released high in the atmosphere when the vapour later condenses into cloud. Because the heat source is at the bottom, the troposphere is warmest near the surface and cools with height, and because a fluid heated from below is unstable, it overturns; this is precisely why the troposphere convects and mixes, and why weather happens here and not in the stratosphere, which is heated from within by ozone and is stably stratified. The energy budget must balance over the long run: the Earth radiates to space as much energy as it receives from the Sun, otherwise it would steadily heat or cool, and the effective temperature at which it radiates corresponds to a level partway up the troposphere. But the balance is uneven across the globe. The tropics receive far more solar energy than they radiate, because the Sun is high and its rays concentrated, while the poles radiate more than they receive. This latitudinal imbalance in the energy budget is the fundamental driver of the general circulation of the atmosphere and ocean, the vast machinery that transports surplus heat from equator toward poles and, in doing so, generates the winds, storms, and climate zones examined in later sections.

sections.heading: Water Vapor, Humidity, and Latent Heat
sections.body: Water is the substance that transforms the troposphere from a simple heated fluid into the intricate machine of weather, and the key to its power is latent heat, the large quantity of energy absorbed or released when water changes phase without changing temperature. To evaporate one kilogram of water at ordinary temperatures takes about two and a half million joules, the latent heat of vaporisation; that same energy is released again when the vapour condenses back to liquid. Because evaporation happens at the warm surface and condensation happens higher up in rising air, water vapour acts as a conveyor that lifts enormous amounts of heat from the surface into the atmosphere and releases it aloft, fuelling clouds and storms. The amount of water vapour air can hold is not fixed but rises steeply with temperature, a relationship quantified by the Clausius-Clapeyron equation, which shows that the saturation vapour pressure roughly doubles for every ten-degree Celsius rise in temperature. Warm tropical air can therefore carry many times the moisture of cold polar air, which is why the heaviest rains and most violent convection occur in the warm, moist tropics and in summer. Meteorologists describe the moisture content of air in several ways. Absolute or specific humidity measures the actual mass of vapour present. Relative humidity, the figure usually quoted, expresses the vapour present as a percentage of the maximum the air could hold at its current temperature; it reaches one hundred percent at saturation. Because the capacity depends on temperature, relative humidity changes as air warms or cools even when the actual moisture is unchanged, rising as air cools and falling as it warms, which is why relative humidity is high on a cool morning and lower by midday though no water has been added or removed. The most physically meaningful measure is the dew point, the temperature to which air must be cooled at constant pressure for it to become saturated and dew or cloud to begin forming; a high dew point means genuinely moist air and, in warm weather, oppressive humidity. When air is cooled to its dew point, further cooling forces the excess vapour to condense onto aerosol particles, releasing latent heat and forming cloud, fog, or dew. This release of latent heat is not a side effect but a central driver: it warms the rising air, making it more buoyant and able to rise farther, which is why a moist atmosphere can convect so much more violently than a dry one and why hurricanes, which draw their energy directly from the latent heat of ocean evaporation, form only over warm seas. The whole apparatus of humidity, dew point, condensation, and latent heat release is the hinge on which cloud formation, precipitation, and the intensity of storms turn, and it is the reason the distribution of water vapour is watched as closely by forecasters as temperature and pressure.

sections.heading: Adiabatic Processes and the Dry and Moist Lapse Rates
sections.body: When a parcel of air rises through the troposphere it cools, and understanding exactly how fast it cools is the key to predicting clouds and storms. The cooling is adiabatic, meaning it occurs without any exchange of heat with the surroundings; the parcel cools purely because it expands as it moves into lower pressure aloft, doing work on the surrounding air at the expense of its own internal energy. As long as the rising air remains unsaturated, that is, its relative humidity stays below one hundred percent, it cools at a nearly constant rate called the dry adiabatic lapse rate, which is very close to nine point eight degrees Celsius per kilometre, often rounded to ten. This value is fixed by physics, being the acceleration of gravity divided by the specific heat of dry air at constant pressure, and it does not depend on the weather; any unsaturated parcel, rising anywhere, cools at this rate, and any sinking parcel warms at it. The behaviour changes decisively once the parcel cools to its dew point. At that level, called the lifting condensation level, the air becomes saturated and its vapour begins to condense into cloud, and this is the height of the cloud base you see as a flat-bottomed cumulus. Condensation releases latent heat into the parcel, partly offsetting the cooling from expansion, so above the condensation level a saturated parcel cools more slowly, at the moist or saturated adiabatic lapse rate. This rate is not constant; it depends on temperature and pressure because warmer air condenses more water and releases more latent heat, but a representative value in the lower troposphere is around five degrees Celsius per kilometre, ranging from about four in very warm moist air to nearly the dry value in cold air that holds little moisture. Comparing a parcel's adiabatic cooling with the environmental lapse rate of the surrounding air determines whether it keeps rising or sinks back, which is the subject of atmospheric stability treated next. A short worked example fixes the ideas. Suppose surface air at twenty-five degrees Celsius with a dew point of fifteen degrees is forced to rise. Being unsaturated, it cools at the dry rate of about ten degrees per kilometre while its dew point falls only slowly, at about two degrees per kilometre. The gap between temperature and dew point, ten degrees at the surface, closes at roughly eight degrees per kilometre, so saturation is reached after about one and a quarter kilometres. That altitude, near one thousand two hundred and fifty metres, is the lifting condensation level and marks the cloud base. Above it the parcel, now saturated, cools at the slower moist rate of about five to six degrees per kilometre, and if it remains warmer than its surroundings it will continue upward, building a cloud that may tower to the tropopause. This simple comparison of rates underlies the forecasting of showers, thunderstorms, and cloud heights.

sections.heading: Atmospheric Stability, Convection, and Cloud Formation
sections.body: Whether the troposphere is calm or stormy on a given day depends on its stability, which is decided by comparing how fast a displaced parcel of air cools adiabatically with how the temperature of the surrounding air actually falls with height, the environmental lapse rate. The principle is one of buoyancy. If a parcel nudged upward finds itself warmer, and therefore less dense, than its surroundings, it is buoyant and keeps rising on its own; the atmosphere is unstable. If the displaced parcel finds itself cooler and denser than its surroundings, it sinks back to where it started; the atmosphere is stable. Three regimes follow directly. When the environmental lapse rate is less than the moist adiabatic rate, the air is absolutely stable: a rising parcel always cools faster than its surroundings, becomes relatively cold and dense, and returns, so vertical motion is suppressed, skies tend to be clear or hold only flat, layered stratiform cloud, and any pollution is trapped, especially under an inversion. When the environmental lapse rate exceeds the dry adiabatic rate, the air is absolutely unstable: even unsaturated parcels remain warmer than their surroundings and accelerate upward, a condition that cannot persist for long because the vigorous overturning it triggers quickly mixes the air back toward stability, but which is common in a thin superadiabatic layer just above ground strongly heated by the summer Sun. The most interesting and common case lies between, when the environmental lapse rate falls between the moist and dry adiabatic rates. This is conditional instability, so named because the air is stable for unsaturated parcels but unstable for saturated ones: a parcel that can be lifted far enough to reach saturation, releasing latent heat and thereafter cooling only at the slower moist rate, may become buoyant and surge upward, whereas the same parcel not lifted that far would sink back. Conditional instability is the usual state of the warm-season atmosphere and the seedbed of showers and thunderstorms; it needs only a trigger to lift air to its lifting condensation level and its level of free convection. Several mechanisms provide that lift. Surface heating produces buoyant thermals that rise and form fair-weather cumulus by midday. Orographic lifting occurs when wind is forced up over hills and mountains. Frontal lifting occurs where a mass of cold, dense air undercuts and hoists warmer air along a front. And convergence, where surface winds flow together, forces air upward for lack of anywhere else to go. Once lifting carries moist air to saturation, cloud forms, and if the air is unstable the cloud grows vertically into the towering cumulus and cumulonimbus of thunderstorms; if the air is stable, cloud spreads horizontally into featureless sheets. The measured energy available to a rising parcel in an unstable atmosphere is quantified by forecasters as convective available potential energy, a direct index of a day's potential for deep convection and severe storms.

sections.heading: Winds, the Coriolis Effect, and the General Circulation
sections.body: Wind is air in motion, and air moves because pressure differs from place to place; the immediate cause of wind is always the pressure gradient force, which pushes air from higher toward lower pressure. If this were the only force, air would simply flow directly down the pressure gradient, but on a rotating planet two other influences reshape the flow. The first is the Coriolis effect, an apparent deflection of moving air arising from the Earth's rotation, which turns freely moving air to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern. The Coriolis deflection is zero at the equator and strongest at the poles, and it grows with the speed of the wind. Above the friction of the surface, the pressure gradient force and the Coriolis effect come into balance, and the resulting wind, called the geostrophic wind, blows not across the isobars but parallel to them, keeping low pressure on its left in the Northern Hemisphere. This is why winds circulate around, rather than straight into, areas of high and low pressure: air spirals clockwise and outward from a Northern Hemisphere high and counterclockwise and inward toward a low, the patterns reversing south of the equator. Near the ground, friction slows the wind, weakening the Coriolis effect relative to the pressure gradient, so surface winds cross the isobars at an angle, spiralling into lows and out of highs. On the largest scale these forces organise the whole atmosphere into the general circulation, the average global pattern of winds that redistributes the tropical surplus of heat toward the energy-starved poles. In each hemisphere the circulation breaks into three cells. The Hadley cell dominates the tropics: intense solar heating near the equator lifts air in a belt of low pressure and frequent thunderstorms called the Intertropical Convergence Zone, the risen air flows poleward aloft, cools, and sinks around thirty degrees latitude in the subtropical high-pressure belts, where the world's great deserts lie beneath the descending, drying air. The returning surface flow, deflected by the Coriolis effect, forms the reliable trade winds that blow from the northeast and southeast toward the equator. Poleward of the Hadley cell lies the Ferrel cell, a weaker, indirect circulation in the mid-latitudes where the prevailing surface winds are the westerlies, and the turbulent storms of the temperate zones do much of the heat transport. Nearest the poles the shallow polar cell has air sinking over the cold poles and flowing out as the polar easterlies. Where the cold polar air meets the warmer mid-latitude air, along the polar front, lies the battleground of much of the world's changeable weather. This three-cell scheme is an idealisation smoothed over land, sea, and season, but it captures the essential architecture of the winds and explains the global distribution of rain, desert, and storm tracks.

sections.heading: Jet Streams, Air Masses, and Fronts
sections.body: High in the troposphere, near the tropopause, run the jet streams, narrow ribbons of exceptionally fast wind that steer much of the world's weather. A jet stream is a concentrated current of air, thousands of kilometres long but only hundreds wide and a few kilometres deep, in which winds commonly blow at well over a hundred and sometimes over four hundred kilometres per hour, generally from west to east. Jet streams form where horizontal temperature contrasts are sharpest, because a strong temperature gradient, by the thermal wind relationship, produces strong vertical shear that concentrates fast winds aloft. The principal one at mid-latitudes is the polar-front jet, which snakes along the boundary between cold polar air and warm subtropical air at around nine to twelve kilometres altitude; a second, the subtropical jet, lies lower-latitude and higher, near the poleward edge of the Hadley cell. The polar jet does not run straight but meanders in great north-south waves called Rossby waves, and the troughs and ridges of these waves organise the development, track, and intensity of the surface storm systems below, which is why forecasters watch the upper-level flow so closely. The jet stream also acts as a conveyor along which storms travel and as a boundary that can lock cold or warm spells in place when its waves amplify and stall. At the surface, weather in the mid-latitudes is largely a story of air masses and the fronts between them. An air mass is a large body of air that has taken on fairly uniform temperature and humidity by sitting over a source region such as a warm ocean, a cold continental interior, or a tropical desert; meteorologists classify air masses as maritime or continental and as tropical, polar, or arctic. When air masses of different character meet, they do not readily mix, and the sloping boundary between them is a front, a concept developed by the Norwegian meteorologists Vilhelm Bjerknes and his colleagues after the First World War in what became the Norwegian cyclone model. Along a warm front, advancing warm air rides gently up over retreating cold air, producing a broad, slowly thickening deck of layered cloud and prolonged light rain ahead of the warmth. Along a cold front, advancing cold, dense air wedges beneath warm air and hoists it steeply, often triggering a narrow band of towering cumulonimbus, heavy showers, thunder, and gusty wind, followed by a clearing and a drop in temperature. A stationary front lies where neither air mass advances, and an occluded front forms in a mature storm when a faster cold front overtakes a warm front and lifts the warm air entirely off the ground. These fronts are the visible surface expression of the mid-latitude cyclones, the travelling low-pressure systems that, steered by the jet stream, bring the procession of changeable weather characteristic of the temperate zones.

sections.heading: Clouds, Precipitation, and the Water Cycle
sections.body: Clouds are visible aggregations of tiny water droplets or ice crystals suspended in the air, formed when rising, cooling air reaches saturation and its vapour condenses onto cloud condensation nuclei. Because a typical cloud droplet is only a few thousandths of a millimetre across, far too small and light to fall, the mere formation of cloud does not by itself produce rain; making precipitation requires that these minute droplets grow by a factor of about a million in volume until they are heavy enough to fall against the updraft. Two processes accomplish this growth. In clouds warmer than freezing, especially the deep, moisture-rich clouds of the tropics, growth occurs by collision and coalescence: larger droplets fall faster than smaller ones, sweep them up as they descend, and merge, snowballing into raindrops. In colder clouds that contain both supercooled liquid droplets and ice crystals together, a more efficient mechanism operates, the Bergeron or Wegener-Bergeron-Findeisen process. Because the saturation vapour pressure over ice is slightly lower than over liquid water at the same subfreezing temperature, water vapour migrates from the liquid droplets to the ice crystals, which grow rapidly at the droplets' expense until they are large enough to fall; melting on the way down, they reach the ground as rain, or if the air stays cold, as snow, sleet, or freezing rain depending on the temperature profile they pass through. The internationally recognised classification of clouds, descended from the scheme Luke Howard proposed in 1802, groups them by altitude and form. High clouds, above about six kilometres and composed of ice, are the wispy cirrus, cirrostratus, and cirrocumulus. Middle clouds, with the prefix alto, include the layered altostratus and altocumulus. Low clouds include the grey sheets of stratus and nimbostratus and the heaps of stratocumulus. Clouds of vertical development, the fair-weather cumulus and the towering cumulonimbus of the thunderstorm, span the whole troposphere and signal convection. Precipitation, whatever its form, is the return leg of the great hydrological cycle that circulates water endlessly through the troposphere and the Earth's surface. The Sun evaporates water from oceans, lakes, soil, and vegetation, the last by transpiration from plants, lifting it into the air as vapour; rising air cools this vapour to form clouds; the clouds precipitate rain and snow; and the water runs off in rivers, soaks into the ground, or is stored in ice and returns eventually to the sea, only to evaporate again. This cycle transports not only water but, through latent heat, vast quantities of energy, and it purifies water by distillation and shapes the distribution of life across the planet. The troposphere is the arena in which the atmospheric portion of this cycle plays out, and clouds and precipitation are the mechanism by which the water it carries is delivered back to the surface.

sections.heading: The Planetary Boundary Layer and Surface Weather
sections.body: The lowest portion of the troposphere, the part in direct contact with the ground and most affected by it, is called the planetary boundary layer, and it is where human beings actually experience weather. Its depth is variable, typically a few hundred metres to a couple of kilometres, and it is set apart from the free atmosphere above by the strong influence of the surface upon it through friction, heating, and the exchange of moisture. Friction with the rough ground slows the wind within the boundary layer and makes it gusty and turbulent, and because friction weakens the Coriolis balance, surface winds blow across the isobars toward low pressure rather than parallel to them, spiralling inward to lows and outward from highs. Above the boundary layer, in the smoother free atmosphere, the wind approaches the geostrophic value and turns to run along the isobars, so wind generally increases in speed and veers in direction with height through the boundary layer, an effect described idealised as the Ekman spiral. The boundary layer also breathes with the day. Over land, the daytime Sun heats the ground, which heats the air in contact with it, driving convective thermals that stir the layer deep and well-mixed, carrying heat, moisture, and pollutants upward and giving the bumpy ride familiar to light-aircraft pilots on a summer afternoon. After sunset the ground cools rapidly by radiating to space, chilling the air just above it and often producing a nocturnal temperature inversion, a shallow, stable layer in which cold air pools near the surface. This nighttime stability traps moisture and pollutants near the ground, and it is why radiation fog, dew, and frost form on calm, clear nights, and why the air can grow stagnant and smoggy under a persistent inversion. The daily cycle of a deep, turbulent, convective boundary layer by day and a shallow, stable one by night governs much of ordinary surface weather: the rise of cumulus in the late morning and their dissolution at dusk, the strengthening of surface wind after sunrise as momentum mixes down from aloft and its calming in the evening, the sea breezes and land breezes that reverse between day and night along coasts as land heats and cools faster than water, and the pooling of cold air in valleys. Local features complicate the picture further, producing microclimates: cities generate their own urban heat island, warmer than the surrounding countryside because concrete and asphalt store heat and release it slowly; mountains channel and block winds and force air to rise and rain on their windward slopes while a dry rain shadow lies to leeward; and the character of the surface, vegetated or bare, wet or dry, light or dark, shapes the temperature and humidity of the air above. The boundary layer is thus the crucial interface where the large-scale weather of the free troposphere is translated into the conditions actually felt at ground level.

sections.heading: Measuring, Forecasting, and the Troposphere in the Climate System
sections.body: Because weather lives in the troposphere, observing this layer in three dimensions is the foundation of forecasting, and the effort is enormous and global. At the surface, a worldwide network of stations measures temperature, pressure, humidity, wind, and precipitation, supplemented by ships, buoys, and automated aircraft reports. The vertical structure is probed chiefly by the radiosonde, a small instrument package carried aloft by a hydrogen or helium balloon released twice daily from hundreds of sites at synchronised times, transmitting temperature, humidity, pressure, and, by tracking its drift, wind as it rises through the whole troposphere and into the stratosphere before the balloon bursts. These soundings, plotted on thermodynamic diagrams such as the skew-T log-P chart, reveal the lapse rate, moisture, stability, and likely cloud and storm behaviour at a glance. Remote sensing has transformed observation. Weather satellites in geostationary and polar orbits image clouds, measure temperature and moisture profiles by infrared and microwave radiometry, and track winds by following cloud motion, giving continuous global coverage impossible from the ground. Weather radar detects precipitation and, using the Doppler shift, measures the motion of rain and hail within storms, revealing rotation and the early signatures of severe weather and tornadoes. From this flood of data, modern forecasting proceeds by numerical weather prediction: the governing equations of atmospheric motion, thermodynamics, and moisture, which have no exact solution, are approximated on a three-dimensional grid covering the globe and stepped forward in time by powerful computers. Because the atmosphere is a chaotic system, exquisitely sensitive to small differences in its initial state, a truth captured in Edward Lorenz's discovery of deterministic chaos and popularised as the butterfly effect, forecasts inevitably lose skill with time, and useful detailed prediction is limited to roughly a week or two ahead. Forecasters manage this uncertainty through ensemble prediction, running the model many times from slightly perturbed starting conditions to gauge the range of likely outcomes and express forecasts as probabilities. Finally, the troposphere is not only the seat of weather but a central component of the climate system, and the distinction matters: weather is the state of the atmosphere at a moment, climate is its statistics over decades. The troposphere exchanges heat, moisture, and momentum with the oceans, ice, land, and biosphere on every timescale, and its composition is changing. The rising concentration of carbon dioxide and other greenhouse gases is strengthening the greenhouse effect, warming the troposphere while, tellingly, cooling the stratosphere above, a fingerprint that distinguishes greenhouse warming from changes in the Sun. A warmer troposphere holds more water vapour, by the Clausius-Clapeyron relation about seven percent more per degree, intensifying the water cycle and loading the dice toward heavier downpours and more energetic storms. Understanding the thin, restless layer where weather happens is therefore inseparable from understanding the changing climate of the planet as a whole.

guides.title: The Structure and Layers of the Atmosphere
guides.summary: A full account of Earth's atmosphere: what it is made of, why it thins with height, and the temperature-defined layers from the troposphere to the exosphere, plus the ozone layer, the ionosphere, and how we measure it all.

sections.heading: What the Atmosphere Is
sections.body: The atmosphere is the envelope of gas held to the Earth by gravity, a thin shell of air that surrounds the planet and makes it habitable. Compared with the size of the Earth it is astonishingly thin. The solid Earth has a radius of about 6,370 kilometers, yet nearly all of the atmosphere lies within about 100 kilometers of the surface, and half of its entire mass is squeezed into the lowest 5.5 kilometers, below the height of many mountain peaks. If the Earth were shrunk to the size of an apple, the atmosphere would be no thicker than the apple's skin. This slender layer nonetheless does the indispensable work of sustaining life. It supplies the oxygen that animals breathe and the carbon dioxide that plants consume; it shields the surface from lethal ultraviolet radiation and from the constant rain of small meteoroids, most of which burn up before reaching the ground; it moderates temperature, trapping enough of the Sun's warmth through the greenhouse effect to keep the planet's average surface temperature near a comfortable fifteen degrees Celsius rather than the freezing conditions it would otherwise endure; and it is the medium in which all weather occurs, the churning of winds, the formation of clouds, and the fall of rain and snow. The atmosphere is held in place by the balance between two forces. Gravity pulls the gas molecules downward, tending to make the air settle toward the surface. Opposing gravity is the pressure of the gas itself, the outward push produced by the ceaseless motion of countless molecules colliding with one another and with everything around them. Because gravity is always pulling down while pressure pushes in all directions, the air packs most densely near the ground, where the weight of everything above compresses it, and grows steadily thinner with altitude. There is no sharp upper boundary where the atmosphere suddenly ends. Instead the air fades away gradually into the near-vacuum of space, becoming ever more tenuous until, at some conventional height, we simply agree to call it space. A commonly used marker is the Karman line at 100 kilometers, adopted for legal and record-keeping purposes to separate aeronautics from astronautics, but the choice is a convenience rather than a physical edge. Faint traces of atmosphere extend far higher. To make sense of this graded, layered shell, scientists divide it in several complementary ways, most importantly by how its temperature changes with height, but also by its chemical composition and by its electrical properties. The sections that follow build up the full picture: first the composition of the air, then the reasons pressure and density fall with altitude, then the temperature structure that defines the classic layers, and finally each layer in turn along with the special regions, such as the ozone layer and the ionosphere, that cut across the standard scheme.

sections.heading: The Composition of Air
sections.body: Dry air near the surface is a remarkably consistent mixture of gases, and its composition is worth knowing precisely because it explains so much of the atmosphere's behavior. By volume, nitrogen makes up about 78.08 percent of dry air, oxygen about 20.95 percent, and argon, an inert noble gas, about 0.93 percent. These three together account for 99.96 percent of every breath. The remainder is a collection of trace gases present in tiny but often crucial amounts. Carbon dioxide, though only about 0.04 percent, or roughly 420 parts per million as of the mid-2020s and rising, plays an outsized role because it is a powerful absorber of infrared radiation and so a central driver of the greenhouse effect and of climate change. Other trace gases include neon, helium, methane, krypton, hydrogen, nitrous oxide, and ozone, each present in minute concentrations yet in some cases, like methane and ozone, disproportionately important. Two features of this mixture deserve emphasis. First, up to about 80 kilometers the gases are kept thoroughly blended by turbulent stirring, so their proportions stay nearly constant regardless of altitude; this well-mixed region is called the homosphere. Above it the gases begin to separate by weight, an arrangement discussed later. Second, one component varies enormously and is deliberately excluded from the figures above: water vapor. The percentages given are for dry air, because the amount of water vapor is highly variable, ranging from almost nothing over deserts and polar regions to as much as four percent of the air by volume in warm, humid tropical settings. This variability is essential rather than incidental. Water vapor is the raw material of clouds and precipitation, it carries vast quantities of energy as latent heat that powers storms, and it is itself the most abundant greenhouse gas, so the changing distribution of water vapor is at the very heart of weather. The atmosphere also carries suspended solid and liquid particles collectively called aerosols: dust, sea salt, pollen, soot, volcanic ash, and droplets of sulfate and other compounds. Though they make up a negligible fraction of the mass, aerosols matter greatly because they scatter and absorb sunlight, influencing temperature, and because they serve as the tiny nuclei on which cloud droplets and ice crystals form. Without such condensation nuclei, clouds would struggle to develop at all. The present composition is not primordial. Earth's earliest atmosphere, rich in hydrogen and helium, was lost to space, and a second atmosphere of volcanic gases followed. The abundant oxygen that now sustains animal life is a biological product, generated over billions of years by photosynthesizing microbes and plants in the transformation known as the Great Oxidation Event. The air we breathe is thus partly the creation of life itself, a reminder that the atmosphere and the biosphere have evolved together and continue to shape each other.

sections.heading: Pressure, Density, and the Vertical Scale
sections.body: To understand why the atmosphere is layered, one must first understand how its pressure and density change with height, for these govern nearly everything else. Atmospheric pressure at any point is simply the weight of all the air above that point pressing down on a unit of area. At sea level this amounts to about 101,325 pascals, or roughly 1,013 millibars, in the customary units of meteorology, a value defined as one standard atmosphere. Expressed more vividly, the column of air above every square meter of ground weighs about ten tonnes, and every square centimeter bears the weight of about a kilogram of air. We do not feel this crushing load because the pressure of the fluids and gases inside our own bodies pushes outward to match it. Because pressure is the cumulative weight of the overlying air, it must fall as one climbs, since less air remains above. The fall is not linear but exponential, meaning that pressure drops by a roughly constant fraction for each equal step upward rather than by a constant amount. A convenient rule is that pressure and density each fall by about half for every 5.5 kilometers of ascent in the lower atmosphere. Thus at about 5.5 kilometers, near the summit of the tallest peaks, the pressure is about half that at sea level; at about 16 kilometers it is roughly a quarter; and the decline continues indefinitely, ever smaller but never quite reaching zero. This behavior follows from the hydrostatic equation of atmospheric physics, which states that the pressure change across a thin layer equals the weight of that layer, combined with the ideal gas law relating pressure, density, and temperature. Together they yield the barometric formula describing the exponential decline. The characteristic distance over which pressure falls by a factor of the mathematical constant e, about 2.718, is called the scale height, and for Earth's lower atmosphere it is roughly 7 to 8 kilometers. Density, the mass of air per unit volume, falls in a very similar exponential fashion and for the same reason, so the air grows rapidly thinner with height. This thinning has profound consequences. It is why mountaineers on the highest peaks need bottled oxygen, since although the proportion of oxygen stays constant, the number of molecules in each breath collapses. It is why aircraft cruise in the thin air of the upper troposphere and lower stratosphere, where reduced density means reduced drag. And it is the fundamental reason the atmosphere sorts itself into layers at all, because the sparse upper air responds to sunlight and to physical processes quite differently from the dense air below. Pressure and density decrease smoothly and monotonically with height throughout the atmosphere. Temperature, by contrast, does not. Temperature rises and falls in a complex profile as one ascends, and it is precisely these reversals of the temperature trend that scientists use to carve the continuous atmosphere into its named layers, as the next section explains.

sections.heading: Temperature and the Basis for Layering
sections.body: If pressure and density simply fall with height, why do we speak of distinct atmospheric layers at all? The answer is temperature. Unlike pressure, the temperature of the atmosphere does not change in one direction as one rises. Instead it decreases, then increases, then decreases, then increases again in a distinctive zigzag profile, and each reversal marks a boundary between layers. The four principal layers, from the ground upward, are the troposphere, the stratosphere, the mesosphere, and the thermosphere, with a fifth and outermost region, the exosphere, beyond. Their boundaries are named by adding the suffix pause, giving the tropopause, stratopause, and mesopause, each of which lies where the temperature trend turns around. Within the lowest layer, the troposphere, temperature falls with height at an average rate of about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometer, a figure known as the environmental lapse rate. This decline occurs because the troposphere is warmed mainly from below: sunlight passes largely through the air and heats the ground, which then warms the adjacent air by conduction, convection, and the emission of infrared radiation, so the air is warmest near its heat source and cools with distance from it. At the tropopause this cooling stops, and in the stratosphere above, temperature holds steady and then rises with height, a reversal called a temperature inversion. The stratosphere warms with altitude because it contains the ozone layer, where ozone molecules absorb ultraviolet sunlight and convert its energy into heat, so this layer is warmed from within its upper reaches. Above the stratopause the trend reverses once more: through the mesosphere temperature again falls with height, reaching the coldest natural temperatures anywhere in the Earth system near the mesopause, around minus 90 degrees Celsius, because this layer has little ozone to warm it and radiates heat away efficiently. Then, in the thermosphere, temperature soars dramatically with height, climbing to hundreds or even thousands of degrees, as the sparse gas absorbs the Sun's most energetic ultraviolet and X-ray radiation. This alternating pattern, cooling, warming, cooling, warming, is the master key to atmospheric structure, and it reflects a competition between the sources of heating at different altitudes and the physics of how each region loses energy. It is important to grasp that these temperature values describe the average kinetic energy of the gas molecules, not the warmth one would feel. In the thermosphere the temperature is enormous, yet an astronaut would not be scorched, because the air is so thin that the few fast-moving molecules carry very little total heat and transfer it slowly. Temperature in the ordinary sense of felt warmth depends on density as well as molecular speed, and in the near-vacuum of the upper atmosphere the two diverge. With this temperature framework in place, the following sections examine each layer in turn, from the dense, weather-filled troposphere at our feet up through the stratosphere, mesosphere, thermosphere, and finally the exosphere that merges with space.

sections.heading: The Troposphere
sections.body: The troposphere is the lowest layer of the atmosphere, the one in which we live and in which virtually all weather occurs. Its name comes from the Greek tropos, meaning turning or change, an apt description of its restless, mixing character. It extends from the surface up to the tropopause, whose height varies with latitude and season. Over the tropics the troposphere reaches as high as 16 to 18 kilometers, because the intense equatorial heating drives vigorous convection that pushes the layer upward, whereas over the cold poles it extends only about 8 to 9 kilometers, and the global average is often quoted as about 12 kilometers. Despite its modest depth the troposphere is by far the most massive layer, containing roughly 75 to 80 percent of the entire atmosphere's mass and nearly all of its water vapor, because the density of air is greatest near the ground. Within the troposphere temperature falls steadily with height at the environmental lapse rate of about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometer on average, so that the air at the tropopause is bitterly cold, typically around minus 55 to minus 60 degrees Celsius. This decrease of temperature with height is what makes the troposphere unstable and convective. Warm air near the heated surface is less dense than the cooler air above it, so it tends to rise, and as it rises it expands and cools, while cooler air sinks to take its place. This overturning, or convection, keeps the troposphere constantly stirred, lifts moisture to heights where it condenses into clouds, and generates the winds, storms, fronts, and precipitation that constitute weather. The presence of abundant water vapor makes the process still more energetic, because when vapor condenses it releases latent heat that fuels rising air and powers everything from ordinary thunderstorms to hurricanes. The lowest portion of the troposphere, typically the bottom one to two kilometers, is called the planetary boundary layer, and it is where the air is most directly affected by the surface through friction, heating, and the mixing of pollutants; above it lies the freer flow of the rest of the troposphere. The troposphere is also home to the jet streams, narrow ribbons of very fast wind that snake around the globe near the tropopause, where strong temperature contrasts between air masses drive winds that can exceed 200 kilometers per hour. These rivers of air steer weather systems and are exploited by long-distance aircraft. The tropopause that caps the troposphere acts as a kind of lid, because above it temperature stops falling and begins to hold steady or rise, creating a stable region that resists vertical motion. Rising air from below generally cannot punch through this inversion, so most weather, moisture, and pollution are trapped within the troposphere. The tallest thunderstorm clouds sometimes reach the tropopause and flatten out against it into the characteristic anvil shape, a visible sign of the boundary that separates the turbulent world of weather from the calm layer beyond.

sections.heading: The Stratosphere and the Ozone Layer
sections.body: Above the tropopause lies the stratosphere, extending from about 12 kilometers up to roughly 50 kilometers, where it ends at the stratopause. Its name comes from the Latin stratum, meaning a layer, because this region is stratified, or layered, and largely free of the vertical churning that characterizes the troposphere below. The defining feature of the stratosphere is that temperature increases with height rather than decreasing, rising from about minus 55 degrees Celsius at its base to near freezing, around zero degrees Celsius, at the stratopause. This inversion is caused by the ozone layer, a region of enhanced ozone concentration lying mostly between about 15 and 35 kilometers. Ozone, a molecule of three oxygen atoms with the chemical formula O3, is produced high in the stratosphere when ultraviolet sunlight splits ordinary oxygen molecules into single atoms that then recombine with other oxygen molecules. The Chapman cycle, described by the geophysicist Sydney Chapman in 1930, explains the continuous creation and destruction of ozone by ultraviolet light. In absorbing this ultraviolet radiation, ozone converts its energy into heat, warming the surrounding air, which is why the upper stratosphere is warmer than the lower. Because the warm air sits atop cooler air, the stratosphere is very stable: there is little convection, air moves mainly in horizontal layers, and vertical mixing is slow. This stability makes the lower stratosphere a smooth region prized by aircraft, and it means that material injected into the stratosphere, such as volcanic ash and sulfur from major eruptions, can linger for years, spreading around the globe and temporarily cooling the surface by reflecting sunlight. The ozone layer is of immense importance to life, for it absorbs the great majority of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet-B and ultraviolet-C radiation, which would otherwise reach the surface and cause severe damage to living cells, including skin cancers, cataracts, and harm to crops and marine ecosystems. The layer is not a distinct sheet of pure ozone; even where it is densest, ozone amounts to only a few molecules per million, and if all the ozone in a vertical column were brought to sea-level pressure it would form a layer only about three millimeters thick. In the late twentieth century scientists discovered that this vital shield was being depleted by human-made chemicals, chiefly the chlorofluorocarbons once used in refrigerants and aerosol sprays, which release chlorine that catalytically destroys ozone.
