During the Second World War the oceanographers Harald Sverdrup and Walter Munk formalised the same physics into a swell-forecasting method used to time surf conditions for Allied amphibious landings, including at Normandy in June 1944, where breaker height was as operationally critical as cloud cover.

A secondary and more local sign completes the picture. A confused, choppy sea running at an angle across the underlying swell usually means a fresh local wind is building ahead of an approaching front, while the older, longer swell beneath still points back toward the original system's birthplace. Reading the two layers separately tells you both where the distant storm sat and what the wind is about to do.

sections.heading: Getting the (Non-)Gear
sections.body:
The whole point of forecasting without instruments is that nothing manufactured is strictly required, and every method here works with empty hands. A few humble props nevertheless make the signs far easier to track consistently, and consistency is what converts scattered impressions into genuine skill. The reason is that human memory is unreliable in exactly the way that ruins forecasting. People remember the dramatic hit and forget the quiet miss, a bias so strong that most folk weather rules survive on it alone. A written record is the only cure, because it forces you to score every prediction, including the boring ones, and after two weeks it will tell you which signs genuinely earn their place in your local climate and which are decoration.

The hygrometric props deserve a note on how they actually work, since neither is alive. A pine cone's scales are built from two layers of tissue with different swelling rates, so absorbed moisture makes one layer expand more than the other and the scale curls closed; drying reverses it. This is pure bimetallic-strip mechanics using wood instead of metal, which is why a cone picked up years ago still responds accurately. Dried seaweed, traditionally bladderwrack or kelp, contains alginate salts that are strongly hygroscopic; it turns limp, cool and tacky as relative humidity climbs above roughly 75 percent and brittle when it falls below about 50. Neither gives you a number, and neither reacts instantly, so hang them in a shaded spot out of rain and direct sun and read them for trend across a day rather than for an absolute value.

A compass matters more than it first appears, because the whole of Buys Ballot's law and every backing-versus-veering judgement depends on knowing wind direction to within about twenty degrees, and estimating that by eye from memory of where the sun rose is where most beginners go wrong. A timer covers two jobs: counting cricket chirps in a fixed fourteen or sixty seconds, and timing successive swell crests to get a wave period. Above all, secure regular access to a spot with a genuinely open western horizon, because the single most valuable habit in this entire discipline is looking upwind at a sky nobody has built a wall across.
ingredients: A notebook and pencil for a daily log — a written record beats memory every time, especially when comparing a week of guesses to outcomes
A length of dried seaweed, or a closed pinecone, hung outside in a shaded spot — both are classic zero-cost hygrometers: seaweed turns tacky and damp as humidity rises, a pinecone's scales close up
A simple compass, for noting wind direction and its changes
A watch or phone timer, for timing sound-carry tests and estimating wave/swell periods
Binoculars, useful for judging cloud detail and reading distant surf or swell direction from shore
Access to a hilltop, open field, or shoreline with a clear view of sky and horizon in most directions

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: A Week of Naked-Eye Forecasts, Verified
sections.body:
Everything in this subject collapses into one habit, practised daily, and this routine is designed to build it. The reason the sequence insists on writing a prediction before consulting any real forecast is that it removes hindsight bias, which is the single largest obstacle to learning weather by eye. Once you have read that rain is expected, you will remember noticing the halo you actually walked straight past, and your self-assessment becomes worthless. Committing a specific, falsifiable statement to paper first, including a time window and not merely the word rain, is what makes the record honest enough to learn from. Never edit the original guess afterwards; the wrong ones teach more than the right ones.

A week is roughly the minimum useful sample because mid-latitude systems pass on a three to seven day rhythm, so a shorter run may contain only one weather change or none at all. Expect a hit rate around 50 to 60 percent in the first week, rising toward 70 or 75 as you learn which signs matter where you live, since their relative value genuinely varies with terrain, distance from the coast and season. Most people who keep the log discover the same two things: wind direction and its rate of change is by a clear margin the most reliable single input, and animal behaviour is the least.

The final instruction in the sequence is the one that matters most and is not really about forecasting at all. Naked-eye methods are a rewarding discipline and a genuine skill, but they are not a substitute for a warning service when the sky turns threatening. Treat any sign of severe conditions as an instruction to stop practising and start checking real information, and never let pride in a homemade forecast delay taking shelter.
steps: Each morning, before checking any forecast, go outside and read the wind (Buys Ballot's law), sky, and — if coastal — the swell; write a specific prediction for the next 12–24 hours.
Check a real forecast afterward for comparison, but don't edit your original written guess.
That evening or the next day, log the actual outcome beside your prediction and note which single sign was most responsible for getting it right or wrong.
On day one, hang a dried seaweed strand or pinecone in a shaded spot outside; check it at the same times each day and record whether its behaviour matched the day's real humidity trend.
On one calm evening, note whether a distant, familiar sound source (traffic, a train line, bells) seems unusually close or loud, and log it against the next day's weather.

After five to seven days, tally your forecasts against outcomes — most beginners find wind direction the single most reliable sign and animal/insect behaviour the least, since biological signs vary more between individuals and species.

Treat any sign pointing toward severe weather — a rapid, sustained pressure fall, a sickly greenish sky, or a sudden dead calm after gusty wind — as a cue to check an actual forecast or radar immediately, and to review this guide's severe-weather safety procedures rather than trusting the naked eye alone.

guides.title: Severe Weather: Storms, Tornadoes and Hurricanes
guides.summary: The physics, warning signs, measurement scales and survival procedures for thunderstorms, lightning, hail, tornadoes, tropical cyclones (hurricanes/typhoons), floods and winter storms — with specific numbers and step-by-step safety actions.

sections.heading: Thunderstorms: the engine of severe weather
sections.body:
A thunderstorm is a cumulonimbus cloud that produces lightning and thunder, and it requires exactly three ingredients. The first is moisture, meaning water vapour available to condense — condensation is what releases the latent heat that powers the whole system, roughly 2,260 kilojoules for every kilogram of water vapour that becomes liquid. The second is instability, meaning warm air near the surface sitting beneath cooler air aloft, so that a parcel nudged upward finds itself warmer and less dense than its surroundings and keeps rising on its own. The third is lift: a trigger to give that first nudge, supplied by a front, a mountain range forcing air upward, a sea-breeze boundary, or simply strong daytime heating of the ground. Remove any one and no storm forms, which is why forecasters check all three rather than one. Rising air is called an updraft; the cooled, rain-laden air sinking back down is a downdraft.

A single-cell storm follows a short life cycle of roughly twenty to sixty minutes. It grows while the updraft dominates, matures when rain begins falling and a downdraft develops alongside the updraft, and dissipates when that cold downdraft spreads out at the surface and cuts off the warm inflow feeding the storm — the storm strangles itself. A supercell escapes that fate. It is a long-lived storm, often lasting several hours, whose updraft rotates; that rotating updraft is called a mesocyclone, typically two to ten kilometres across. The tilt imposed by wind shear keeps the downdraft physically separated from the updraft so the inflow is never cut off, which is why supercells persist. They produce the most violent weather on the list: giant hail, destructive straight-line winds, and the large majority of strong tornadoes.

Meteorologists quantify instability with CAPE, Convective Available Potential Energy, measured in joules per kilogram. It represents the energy a rising parcel can gain over its ascent, and it can be read directly off a plotted atmospheric sounding as the area between the parcel's temperature curve and the environment's. Roughly 1,000 J/kg supports ordinary storms, 2,500 J/kg and above supports strong ones, and 4,000 J/kg or more is extreme. Wind shear — the change in wind speed or direction with height — is the second half of the equation, because it organises a storm and supplies the horizontal spin that an updraft tilts into rotation. High CAPE combined with strong deep-layer shear is the classic severe-weather setup; either alone rarely produces the worst outcomes.

Several visual signs indicate a storm is turning severe. Watch for rapidly towering cauliflower-textured tops, which indicate a strengthening updraft, and for a hard-edged anvil spreading toward you, which means the updraft has reached the tropopause. A darkening sky with a green cast often accompanies large hail. A shelf cloud or roll cloud on the leading edge marks the boundary of outflow air. A sudden cool gust — the gust front — and rapidly falling pressure both signal the storm's arrival within minutes.

sections.heading: Lightning and thunder: physics and the 30/30 rule
sections.body:
Lightning is an electrostatic discharge on a scale nothing in ordinary life approaches. The charge separation begins inside the storm when ice crystals and graupel — soft, rime-coated hail pellets — collide in the updraft. In the presence of supercooled water at temperatures roughly between minus ten and minus twenty degrees Celsius, these collisions transfer charge, leaving the lighter ice crystals positive and carried upward while the heavier graupel takes negative charge downward. The result is a cloud with a positive upper region and a negative lower region, with a strong electric field between them and between the cloud base and the ground.

When the field exceeds the insulating strength of air — about three million volts per metre in dry conditions, lower in moist or particle-laden air — the air ionises and a faint stepped leader propagates downward in roughly fifty-metre jumps. When it nears the ground, upward streamers rise from tall objects to meet it; the moment they connect, the return stroke surges up the established channel carrying on the order of 30,000 amperes and heating the channel to roughly 30,000 degrees Celsius, about five times the temperature of the sun's visible surface. That near-instantaneous heating expands the air explosively, and the resulting shock wave, decaying into a sound wave, is thunder. A flash often contains several return strokes down the same channel, which is why lightning appears to flicker.

Because light travels at about 300,000 kilometres per second — effectively instantaneous over these distances — while sound travels at only about 343 metres per second at 20 degrees Celsius, the delay between flash and bang measures distance. Distance in kilometres equals the count of seconds divided by three; in miles, divided by five. A nine-second gap therefore means about three kilometres, or two miles.

This underpins the 30/30 rule. When the flash-to-bang gap is thirty seconds or less, the strike was within roughly ten kilometres and you are within range of the next one — go indoors, meaning a substantial building with wiring and plumbing, or a hard-topped metal vehicle, not a shed, tent, dugout or picnic shelter. Then wait thirty minutes after the last audible thunder before resuming outdoor activity. That second half is where most people fail: the trailing anvil of a departing storm still produces bolts, and so-called bolts from the blue can strike more than ten kilometres from the parent cloud, under apparently clearing sky. The phrase worth memorising is that when thunder roars, go indoors.

Lightning kills chiefly through cardiac arrest and respiratory arrest caused by the current disrupting the heart's rhythm and the brainstem's breathing drive, and survivors frequently have lasting neurological injury. One point is critical and widely misunderstood: a person who has been struck carries no residual electrical charge and is entirely safe to touch. Begin CPR immediately and call emergency services. In a mass-casualty lightning strike the usual triage priority reverses — treat the apparently dead first, because respiratory arrest without cardiac damage is often reversible with prompt rescue breathing.

sections.heading: Hail, downbursts and flash floods
sections.body:
Hail forms when a strong updraft carries raindrops above the freezing level, where they freeze into embryos and are then recirculated through regions of supercooled liquid water, accreting layer after layer of ice. Cut a large hailstone open and the alternating clear and opaque bands record those passes: clear ice where accretion was slow and wet, allowing trapped air to escape, opaque white where it was fast and dry, freezing air bubbles in place. A stone falls when it grows too heavy for the updraft to hold, which means hail size is a direct readout of updraft strength — and supercell updrafts can exceed 150 kilometres per hour. The practical size ladder runs from pea at about 6 millimetres, through marble at 13 millimetres, golf ball at 44 millimetres where damage begins in earnest, baseball at 70 millimetres, to softball at over 100 millimetres, which is potentially lethal to anyone caught outside. Terminal velocity scales roughly with the square root of diameter: a golf-ball stone arrives near 100 kilometres per hour. Shelter under a solid roof and move away from windows, since hail driven by wind breaks glass inward.

Downbursts are the opposite phenomenon — air coming down hard rather than up. When rain falls into drier air below the cloud, evaporation cools that air, making it denser and accelerating its descent; the column hits the ground and spreads outward as straight-line winds that can exceed 160 kilometres per hour. A microburst is one under four kilometres across, and its compactness makes it especially violent and short-lived, often lasting under ten minutes. The damage is as severe as a weak-to-moderate tornado but the pattern is diagnostic: debris and trees fall outward in a diverging, fan-shaped or starburst pattern rather than the converging pattern a vortex leaves. Downbursts are a serious aviation hazard because an aircraft on approach first meets a headwind that lifts it, then loses that headwind and meets a downdraft and tailwind, losing airspeed and altitude at the worst possible moment.

Flash floods are, in many countries, the leading cause of thunderstorm deaths, and the numbers explain why people misjudge them so consistently. Just 15 centimetres — six inches — of fast-moving water can knock an adult off their feet, because the force of moving water rises with the square of its velocity. About 30 centimetres will float a small car, since a vehicle displaces its own weight in water long before the water reaches the doors; once buoyant, tyres lose traction entirely. Roughly 60 centimetres sweeps away most vehicles including many pickups and SUVs. The rule that saves lives is simply stated: turn around, don't drown. Never drive or walk into water of unknown depth across a road, and treat night as an absolute prohibition, since you cannot see that the roadbed beneath has been scoured away — undermined pavement is a common and invisible killer.

Move to higher ground and avoid canyons, dry washes and low bridges during heavy rain. The characteristic danger is that a wall of water can arrive where you stand in bright sunshine, generated by rain that fell kilometres upstream in a catchment you cannot see.

sections.heading: Tornadoes: formation, the EF scale, and detection
sections.body:
A tornado is a violently rotating column of air in contact with both the cloud base and the ground — both conditions are part of the definition. Most strong tornadoes descend from the mesocyclone of a supercell, and the process begins well before anything is visible. Horizontal spin already present in a sheared environment, imagine a rolling tube of air lying horizontally, is tilted into the vertical by the updraft and then stretched: as a rotating column is drawn out lengthwise it narrows and spins faster, the same conservation of angular momentum that speeds a skater pulling in their arms. The visible precursor is often a wall cloud, a lowered and sometimes visibly rotating block of cloud beneath the rain-free base, from which a funnel descends. Strictly it is a funnel cloud until circulation reaches the ground; the condensation funnel may never fully descend even while a damaging vortex is already at the surface, so a swirl of dust or debris beneath the cloud base is a tornado regardless of how the funnel looks.

Intensity is rated after the fact, from damage, on the Enhanced Fujita scale — an important point, because the wind speeds are inferred from what broke rather than measured directly, and a violent tornado crossing open farmland may be rated low simply for want of anything to destroy. EF0 corresponds to 105 to 137 kilometres per hour, 65 to 85 miles per hour, with branches broken and gutters damaged. EF1 spans 138 to 177, peeling roof surfaces and overturning mobile homes. EF2 spans 178 to 217, tearing roofs off framed houses and snapping large trees. EF3 spans 218 to 266, with well-built houses losing exterior walls. EF4 spans 267 to 322 and levels well-constructed houses. EF5 exceeds 322 kilometres per hour, 200 miles per hour, sweeping strong framed houses clean off their foundations.

The warning signs are worth committing to memory because you may have very little time. Look for a dark and often green-tinted sky, a rotating wall cloud, large hail — which frequently falls just ahead of the tornado — and listen for a loud continuous roar commonly compared to a freight train that does not pass. An eerie calm or an abrupt shift in wind direction often precedes arrival. At night, when the funnel is invisible, repeated blue-green flashes on the horizon are power flashes from lines being torn down.

One geometric cue can save your life. A tornado that is not moving left or right relative to you, but is steadily growing larger, is on a collision course with your position. Move at right angles to its path, never away from it along the same line.

Finally, understand the terminology. A watch means conditions are favourable across a broad region over the coming hours — the time to be alert and to plan. A warning means a tornado has been sighted or indicated by radar in your immediate area, and the only correct response is to take shelter now. Typical warning lead time is only about ten to fifteen minutes.

sections.heading: Tornado survival procedure
sections.body:
When a tornado warning is issued for your location, or you see one, act immediately; you may have only minutes, and every decision below is ordered by how much protection it actually buys. The single organising principle is to put as much sturdy structure as possible between yourself and the outside, and to get as low as possible, because wind speed increases with height above ground and the overwhelming majority of injuries come from flying debris rather than from the wind itself.

The best option is a purpose-built storm shelter or safe room, or failing that a basement or cellar. Underground, the wind cannot reach you at all and the only real hazard is the house collapsing into the space above you — so position yourself under a sturdy workbench, a staircase, or heavy furniture, and away from the area directly beneath heavy appliances on the floor above, since a refrigerator or piano can fall through.

With no basement, go to the lowest floor and find the smallest interior room without windows: a bathroom, a closet, or a central hallway. Small rooms have short wall spans and are structurally stiffer; interior rooms have more walls between them and the debris field. A bathtub offers useful protection because its plumbing is anchored into the structure, and covering yourself with a mattress, heavy blankets or cushions adds a layer against penetrating debris.

Protect the head and neck above all else. Head injury is the leading cause of tornado death. A cycling or sports helmet is genuinely recommended by emergency-management agencies for this purpose and costs nothing to keep in the shelter spot. Wear shoes, and put them on before the storm rather than after: the post-tornado environment is a field of broken glass, splintered wood and exposed nails, and foot injuries routinely prevent people from walking out to get help.

Mobile and manufactured homes are lethal in tornadoes, including those with tie-downs, and the statistics are stark — residents of manufactured housing account for a hugely disproportionate share of tornado deaths relative to their numbers. Leave immediately for a solid building, or as a genuine last resort a ditch. Do not wait to see the tornado first.

In a vehicle, do not attempt to outrun a tornado through traffic or on a rigid grid of roads where you may be forced to turn into its path. If the tornado is distant, traffic is light and your escape route is clear, drive at right angles to its track. If it is close, abandon the car — vehicles are readily lifted and rolled — and either enter a sturdy building or lie flat in a low ditch or depression well away from the vehicle, face down with hands over your head. Do not shelter under a highway overpass: the constriction accelerates the wind through the gap and channels debris directly at anyone sheltering there, and people have been killed in exactly that position.

Outdoors with no shelter, lie flat in the lowest ground you can reach, face down, hands over the back of your head and neck, away from trees and vehicles.

sections.heading: Hurricanes (tropical cyclones): formation and the Saffir–Simpson scale
sections.body:
A hurricane — called a typhoon in the northwest Pacific and simply a cyclone in the Indian Ocean and around Australia — is a large rotating storm system that forms over warm tropical oceans. Its formation requires a specific combination of conditions. Sea-surface temperature must be at least about 26.5 degrees Celsius, 80 degrees Fahrenheit, and crucially through a deep layer of perhaps fifty metres rather than just at the skin, because the storm's own winds churn cooler water up from below. The mid-atmosphere must be moist, or dry air entrained into the circulation kills the convection. Vertical wind shear must be low, the opposite of the tornado recipe, because shear tilts and ventilates the warm core and tears the storm apart. And the disturbance must be at least about five degrees of latitude from the equator, since the Coriolis effect vanishes at the equator and without it a low-pressure area cannot organise into rotation. The warm ocean is the fuel: evaporation lifts water vapour into the system, and the latent heat released when that vapour condenses is what powers the updrafts, which is why a hurricane weakens rapidly over land or cold water.

Structurally, a mature hurricane has a calm central eye, typically 20 to 60 kilometres across, where air subsides and skies can be clear and pressure is at its lowest. Around it stands the eyewall, a ring of towering convection containing the strongest winds and heaviest rain, and beyond that spiral rainbands. Intensity is rated by maximum sustained wind on the Saffir–Simpson scale. A tropical storm runs 63 to 118 kilometres per hour, 39 to 73 miles per hour. Category 1 is 119 to 153 kilometres per hour, 74 to 95 miles per hour, producing minor structural damage. Category 2 is 154 to 177 with extensive damage. Category 3, the threshold for a major hurricane, is 178 to 208 and devastating. Category 4 is 209 to 251 and catastrophic. Category 5 is 252 kilometres per hour, 157 miles per hour, or greater, leaving many areas uninhabitable for weeks or months.

The scale's critical limitation is that it rates wind and nothing else. The greatest killer is usually storm surge, the dome of seawater the storm pushes ashore, which can exceed six metres, along with inland freshwater flooding from rainfall that may occur hundreds of kilometres from the coast. A slow-moving Category 1 can kill far more people than a fast Category 4 through rain alone. Judging your risk by category is a common and dangerous error, and it is the reason surge warnings are now issued separately from the category itself.

One further hazard deserves explicit warning. When the eye passes overhead the wind drops to near calm for anywhere from ten to sixty minutes and the sky may brighten. This is not the end of the storm. The far eyewall follows, and the wind returns violently from the opposite direction — striking structures already weakened from the other side. Do not go outside during the eye.

sections.heading: Hurricane and winter-storm preparation, and general safety
sections.body:
Hurricane preparation is unusual among natural hazards in that you generally get days of notice, and the whole discipline is about converting that notice into action before conditions deteriorate. Start by knowing your evacuation zone, which coastal authorities publish in advance and which is defined by surge vulnerability rather than by distance from the water. If an evacuation is ordered, particularly for surge, leave early. Once surge begins there is nowhere to drive: roads flood from the lowest ground upward, and a coastal region's traffic capacity is far below the number who will try to use it at once. Evacuation usually means tens of kilometres inland, out of the surge zone, not hundreds.

If you are sheltering in place, stock one gallon — 3.8 litres — of water per person per day for at least seven days, covering drinking and basic sanitation, plus non-perishable food, a week of any prescription medication, a manual can opener, flashlights, spare batteries, a battery or hand-crank radio, and a first-aid kit. Board or shutter windows; tape does nothing useful and creates larger glass shards. Bring in or secure loose outdoor objects, since patio furniture and rubbish bins become missiles at 150 kilometres per hour. Fill the bathtub for washing and toilet-flushing water, charge every device and power bank, and fuel the car and any generator before the queues and outages start.

During the storm, stay in an interior room away from windows, on the lowest floor that is still above any expected flood or surge level — those two rules can conflict, and surge wins. Never run a generator, charcoal grill or vehicle engine indoors, in a garage, or near an open window. Carbon monoxide is colourless and odourless, incapacitates before most people realise anything is wrong, and post-storm generator poisoning kills people after every major landfall. Generators belong outdoors, well clear of doors and vents.

Winter storms demand a different discipline. Dress in loose layers: a wicking base layer, an insulating middle layer trapping air, and a windproof waterproof shell. Loose matters because compressed insulation stops insulating, and cotton next to the skin is actively dangerous when damp. The two principal injuries are hypothermia, meaning a core temperature below 35 degrees Celsius and presenting as shivering, clumsiness, confusion and slurred speech — with shivering paradoxically stopping as it worsens — and frostbite, presenting as numb, hard, white or waxy skin. Keep a vehicle winter kit with a blanket, food, water, a shovel and grit. If stranded, stay with the vehicle: it is shelter and far easier for rescuers to find than a person on foot. Run the engine roughly ten minutes per hour for heat, window cracked, and only after confirming the exhaust pipe is clear of snow — a blocked pipe pushes carbon monoxide into the cabin.

The general principle across all severe weather is that forecasts buy time. Prepare during the watch, not the warning. For suspected hypothermia, frostbite, lightning injury or carbon-monoxide poisoning, give basic first aid, perform CPR if trained and needed, and get professional medical help fast; this material is educational and is not a substitute for emergency services.

sections.heading: Derechos and Squall Lines: Wind Storms That Outrun the Storm That Made Them
sections.body:
Not every damaging wind event is a tornado, and the distinction matters both scientifically and for how you should react. A squall line is a linear band of thunderstorms, often riding along or just ahead of a cold front, that sustains itself through its own cold, dense outflow: the downdraft air spreading out ahead of the line undercuts the warm, moist inflow like a wedge, continuously triggering fresh updrafts along the leading edge rather than following the single rise-and-collapse life cycle of an isolated storm. This self-propagating arrangement is why a squall line can cross several countries and persist through the night, long after daytime heating has ended, when ordinary storms would have died.

When a segment of that line bulges forward into a curved, bow-like shape on radar, it is called a bow echo, and the apex of the bow marks the strongest surface winds along its length. The bowing itself is caused by a rear-inflow jet — a current of dry mid-level air drawn into the back of the system, which accelerates forward, is cooled further by evaporation, and descends to the surface at the apex. When a bow echo or a chain of them, collectively a mesoscale convective system, produces a long sustained corridor of damage, meteorologists call it a derecho, a Spanish word meaning straight ahead. The term was coined in 1888 by the University of Iowa physicist Gustavus Hinrichs, who wanted a word explicitly distinct from tornado — from the Spanish for turned — for the 1877 Iowa windstorm he studied.

The official criteria are specific: a damage swath at least 400 miles, about 650 kilometres, long; gusts of at least 58 miles per hour, 93 kilometres per hour, along most of that path; and several well-separated gusts of 75 miles per hour, 121 kilometres per hour, or greater. Individual derecho gusts have exceeded 160 kilometres per hour, comparable to a strong EF2 tornado, and the affected area is vastly larger — a single derecho can leave millions without power across several states or provinces.

Because the damaging wind is a straight-line downburst blast rather than a rotating vortex, storm-damage surveyors distinguish the two by debris pattern. A derecho lays trees and structures down in roughly parallel lines pointing consistently one direction, the direction the wind was travelling. A tornado leaves a converging or crossed pattern, with debris on opposite sides of the track pointing toward one another, because the wind on each side of the vortex blew the opposite way. This is the single most reliable field test.

The safety response carries the same urgency as a tornado warning, and it is worth stating plainly why people underestimate it. A fast-approaching dark, solid line of cloud with a shelf-cloud leading edge looks like an ordinary thunderstorm rather than the unmistakable silhouette of a funnel, so people watch it instead of sheltering. Derecho winds arrive with less visual warning than their destructive potential warrants, and they strike a whole region at once rather than along a narrow path. Move to an interior room away from windows as the line approaches, and expect a prolonged power outage afterwards.

sections.heading: Storm Surge: The Hurricane's Deadliest Hazard
sections.body:
The Saffir–Simpson scale ranks a hurricane by sustained wind speed alone, but storm surge — the abnormal rise of seawater driven ashore by the storm — has historically caused the majority of hurricane deaths, and it does not track cleanly with category. Understanding why requires separating two contributions that people habitually merge.

The dominant mechanism is wind stress. Sustained onshore winds drag on the sea surface and physically pile water against the coastline, and because a hurricane's strongest winds sit in its right-front quadrant relative to its direction of travel in the Northern Hemisphere — where the rotational wind and the storm's forward motion add together — that quadrant typically produces the highest surge. A community twenty kilometres to the right of the track can be devastated while one the same distance to the left sees comparatively little water. The storm's low central pressure contributes a much smaller share through the inverse barometer effect, in which the reduced atmospheric weight allows the sea to rise by roughly one centimetre for every one hectopascal of pressure deficit. Even an extraordinarily intense 900 hectopascal storm therefore gains only around a metre this way, while wind-driven piling adds many metres on top of it. The popular image of the sea being sucked up by low pressure is largely wrong.

Coastal geometry then amplifies or suppresses the result, sometimes by a factor of several. A shallow, gently sloping continental shelf gives the piled water nowhere to go downward, so it goes upward and inland; the northern Gulf of Mexico coast is the textbook high-vulnerability case for exactly this reason, while a coast that drops off steeply just offshore lets the water drain beneath and sees far less surge from an identical storm. Bays, estuaries and funnel-shaped inlets concentrate it further. A landfall coinciding with high tide — the combination is called the storm tide — can add another metre or two, which is why the timing of landfall relative to the tidal cycle matters as much as the storm's strength.

The historical record makes the case bluntly. Two of the deadliest weather disasters ever recorded were fundamentally surge events: the 1900 Galveston hurricane, which killed on the order of eight thousand people, and the 1970 Bhola cyclone in what is now Bangladesh, whose death toll reached into the hundreds of thousands across a low-lying delta. Hurricane Katrina in 2005 produced surge estimated as high as roughly eight to nine metres, about 28 feet, along the Mississippi coast.

Because a wide, slow-moving storm can push far more water ashore than a small, fast, more intense one — the water needs time and fetch to pile up — the United States National Hurricane Center now issues storm-surge watches and warnings and publishes inundation maps entirely separately from the wind category. It is surge risk, not category, that drives most coastal evacuation orders, and those orders are issued well ahead of landfall precisely because evacuation becomes impossible once low roads begin to flood.

sections.heading: Winter Storms: Blizzards, Ice Storms and the Physics of Wind Chill
sections.body:
Winter's severe weather works by different mechanisms than a summer thunderstorm, and the definitions are less intuitive than most people assume. A blizzard, under the United States National Weather Service definition, requires sustained winds or frequent gusts of 35 miles per hour, 56 kilometres per hour, or greater, combined with falling or blowing snow reducing visibility below a quarter of a mile, about 400 metres, for at least three hours. Note what is absent: there is no snowfall total in that definition at all. It is a criterion about wind and visibility, which is why a ground blizzard with no new snow whatsoever — merely existing snow lofted off the surface — fully qualifies, and why the principal danger is disorientation and being stranded rather than depth of accumulation.

An ice storm forms from a particular vertical temperature structure. A shallow layer of sub-freezing air sits trapped near the ground while warmer air overruns it aloft. Snow falling from that elevated warm layer melts completely into rain, then becomes supercooled as it re-enters the thin freezing layer near the surface, remaining liquid below zero because it lacks a nucleus to freeze around — until it touches a surface at or below zero degrees Celsius, when it freezes instantly on contact. That is freezing rain. Sleet is the same situation with a deeper cold layer near the ground, deep enough that the drop refreezes fully into an ice pellet while still airborne, which is why sleet bounces and rattles while freezing rain arrives silently and is far more dangerous.

Even a thin ice coating adds enormous and consistently underestimated weight. A quarter of an inch, about six millimetres, of accretion is widely cited by utilities as sufficient to snap branches and significantly stress conductors; half an inch can multiply a power line's load several times over, and wind acting on the thickened profile adds more. This is why ice storms, not blizzards, cause the most widespread and longest-lasting winter power outages, with restoration sometimes taking a week or more because thousands of individual spans fail at once.

Wind chill quantifies forced convective heat loss. Still air trapped against the skin forms an insulating boundary layer warmed by the body; moving air continuously strips that layer away and replaces it with cold air, so heat leaves the body far faster even though the actual air temperature is unchanged. The modern United States and Canadian wind chill index, revised in 2001 using human-subject facial cooling trials in a chilled wind tunnel, converts the combination into an equivalent still-air temperature. At sufficiently extreme values frostbite on exposed skin develops in well under thirty minutes, and at the most extreme readings in ten minutes or less.

One misconception is worth correcting explicitly, because it leads to real property damage. Wind chill applies only to exposed living tissue that is generating heat. It does not lower the temperature of an inanimate object below the true air temperature, so a car radiator or an outdoor water pipe freezes according to the actual air temperature alone — wind makes it reach that temperature faster, but never colder.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear for Severe-Weather Awareness
sections.body:
None of this concerns storm-chasing equipment. It concerns the small number of items that actually change outcomes during a warning, and each earns its place by covering a specific, documented failure mode rather than by being generally useful.

The first failure is not being woken. Most tornado deaths occur at night, when phones are silenced or charging in another room and people are asleep during the ten to fifteen minutes of lead time available. A dedicated weather radio with a tone-alert feature solves this because it stays silent until an official warning is transmitted for your area and then sounds loudly regardless of anything else — no network, no battery drain, no notification settings to have got wrong. Programming it to your specific county or zone code matters: without that step it alerts for a wide region and you will learn to ignore it, which is worse than not having one.

The second failure is losing the cellular network entirely. Towers lose commercial power and run on batteries measured in hours, and post-event congestion can block calls even where infrastructure survives. That is the argument for paper: printed contact numbers and a regional map do not depend on anything. Text messages, incidentally, get through congested networks far more reliably than voice calls, because they are tiny and will retry.

The third failure is darkness with no power. A hand-crank or battery flashlight plus a separate power bank covers both moving safely through a damaged building and keeping one phone alive for emergency contact. Keep them in the shelter room rather than distributed around the house, since you will not be collecting them at the time.

The helmet deserves particular emphasis because it looks faintly absurd and is nonetheless genuinely recommended by emergency-management agencies. Head injury dominates tornado fatalities, a bicycle or sports helmet is designed precisely against blunt impact, and it costs nothing to leave one in the closet you will shelter in. Sturdy closed-toe shoes belong beside it for the debris field afterwards.

Finally, distinguish an app that pushes official warnings from one that merely shows forecasts. Many weather apps default to notifying about rain rather than about warnings, and the difference is the entire point. Winter items — grit, a shovel, spare warmth in the vehicle — address the separate failure of being stranded rather than struck.
ingredients: A NOAA Weather Radio (or your country's equivalent) with battery backup and a tone-alert feature, from an electronics retailer
A battery- or hand-crank-powered flashlight and a backup battery bank
A basic first-aid kit, from a pharmacy or outdoor retailer
A helmet kept in your designated shelter room — a bicycle or sports helmet is genuinely recommended by emergency-management agencies for tornado sheltering — plus sturdy closed-toe shoes
A printed list of family emergency contacts and a paper regional map, in case phone networks go down
A weather app or service that pushes actual severe-weather warnings to your phone, not just routine forecasts
For winter storms: rock salt or sand, a snow shovel, and extra warm layers or a blanket kept in any vehicle you drive during the cold season

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Build and Practice Your Severe-Weather Action Plan This Week
sections.body:
A plan you have never rehearsed is a hope rather than a plan, and the reason is specific rather than motivational. Under imminent threat people lose the capacity for novel problem-solving; what remains is whatever has been made automatic. Disaster researchers have documented for decades that the common response to a warning is not panic but delay — people seek confirmation, telephone relatives, look out of the window, trying to reconcile the alert with a sky that still looks ordinary. That consumes most of a ten-to-fifteen-minute tornado lead time. Rehearsal replaces deliberation with reflex, the only thing fast enough.

Timing your own drill is what makes it honest. People consistently underestimate how long it takes to gather children, pets, shoes and a bag and get everyone into an interior room, and the gap between estimate and stopwatch is usually several minutes — precisely the margin available. Beat the clock comfortably when calm, because everything takes longer under stress and in the dark.

Doing the zone lookups before any storm is forecast matters for the same reason. Surge and flash-flood evacuation zones are published in advance, and the websites hosting them become unreachable under load exactly when a storm approaches. Knowing your zone turns an ambiguous broadcast into an unambiguous instruction.

The out-of-area contact addresses a known network behaviour: local circuits saturate inside a disaster footprint while long-distance routing often survives, so two separated household members can often both reach a distant relative when they cannot reach each other.

One caveat applies. A plan is not a guarantee, and no sheltering choice makes a violent tornado certainly survivable; what a plan removes is the avoidable loss — the delay, the wrong room, the journey begun too late — which is where most preventable casualties come from.
steps: Identify the safest sheltering spot in your home for tornadoes — a lowest-floor, windowless interior room, such as a bathroom or a closet under a stairwell — and do the same for wherever you spend most of your day.
Set up and test a NOAA weather radio, confirming it's programmed to your correct county or zone code so it only alerts for warnings that actually apply to you.
Walk your property and note anything that could become a projectile in high wind — patio furniture, a trampoline — and decide now where you'd secure or move it given a few hours' notice.
Assemble a small go-bag with your first-aid kit, flashlight, battery bank, copies of important documents, and any medications, stored in or near your shelter spot.
Physically practice moving to your shelter and time it — the average tornado warning gives only 8–13 minutes of lead time, so your drill should comfortably beat that.
If you live near a coast or river, look up your specific storm-surge or flash-flood evacuation zone now, before any storm is forecast, since most coastal counties publish these in advance.

Review the whole plan with everyone in your household, including a designated out-of-area contact to text if you're separated — since local phone lines can jam during a real event — and never treat severe weather as the moment to improvise a plan for the first time.

guides.title: Temperature, Humidity, Pressure and the Atmosphere
guides.summary: The measurable state of the air — its layered structure, temperature and heat, the water-vapour cycle and dew point, atmospheric pressure and the barometer, and how these three variables combine to drive all weather. With formulas, units and worked calculations.

sections.heading: The structure of the atmosphere
sections.body:
The atmosphere is the envelope of gas held to the Earth by gravity, and although it extends hundreds of kilometres upward, it is remarkably thin relative to the planet: if the Earth were a schoolroom globe, the whole of the weather-bearing layer would be about the thickness of a coat of varnish. Dry air is a strikingly consistent mixture almost everywhere on the planet, at 78.1 percent nitrogen and 20.9 percent oxygen by volume, with 0.93 percent argon, roughly 0.04 percent carbon dioxide, and traces of neon, helium, methane and others. That uniformity exists because turbulent mixing operates far faster than any process that would separate the gases by weight. Water vapour is the great exception, and it is deliberately excluded from the dry-air figures because it is wildly variable, ranging from almost nothing over a polar ice sheet or a high desert to about 4 percent by volume in saturated tropical air. Nearly all weather is the story of that one variable component condensing and evaporating.

The atmosphere is conventionally divided into layers not by composition but by the sign of its temperature change with height, because that sign determines whether a layer mixes vertically or resists doing so. The troposphere runs from the surface to about 8 kilometres over the poles and 18 over the equator, the difference arising because vigorous tropical convection pushes the boundary higher. Temperature falls with height here at an average of 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre, a figure called the environmental lapse rate. The troposphere holds 75 to 80 percent of the atmosphere's entire mass and almost all of its water vapour, and essentially all weather happens inside it. Its ceiling is the tropopause.

Above that, in the stratosphere from roughly 12 to 50 kilometres, temperature rises with height, because ozone concentrated between about 20 and 30 kilometres absorbs ultraviolet sunlight and heats the air directly. Warm air sitting on top of cold air is enormously stable and resists vertical motion, which is precisely why a thunderstorm's cloud tower cannot punch through the tropopause and instead spreads sideways into the familiar anvil, and why airliners cruise in the smooth lower stratosphere. The mesosphere, from about 50 to 85 kilometres, cools again to the coldest temperatures anywhere in the atmosphere, near minus 90 degrees Celsius, and is where most meteors burn up. The thermosphere, extending from 85 to perhaps 600 kilometres, has an extremely high kinetic temperature but so few molecules that it would not feel hot; the aurora glows here and the International Space Station orbits in it. Beyond lies the exosphere, fading imperceptibly into space. All of this is powered by about 1361 watts per square metre of solar energy, the solar constant, arriving at the top of the atmosphere and heating the tropics far more than the poles.

sections.heading: Temperature and heat: not the same thing
sections.body:
Temperature and heat are routinely used as synonyms in ordinary speech, and keeping them apart is the first genuine step into physical meteorology. Temperature measures the average kinetic energy of the molecules in a substance, which is to say how vigorously they are moving, and it is an intensive property that does not depend on how much material is present. Heat is the total quantity of thermal energy transferred from one body to another, and it very much does depend on quantity. A single spark from a grinder may be at 1000 degrees Celsius yet cannot burn you, because its total energy is minuscule, while a bathtub at 50 degrees carries enough energy to scald severely. This distinction is why the ocean moderates coastal climates: water has a specific heat capacity of about 4186 joules per kilogram per kelvin against roughly 1005 for air, so a given volume of sea stores vastly more energy than the same volume of atmosphere and changes temperature far more slowly.

Three scales are in common use. Celsius sets the freezing point of water at 0 degrees and its boiling point at 100 at sea-level pressure. Fahrenheit places those same points at 32 and 212, so a Fahrenheit degree is five-ninths the size of a Celsius degree. To convert, multiply Celsius by nine-fifths and add thirty-two; to reverse it, subtract thirty-two and multiply by five-ninths. A useful arithmetic check is that minus 40 reads identically on both scales, which is the single point where the two lines cross. Kelvin is the absolute scale used in all physics: its zero is absolute zero at minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, the point at which molecular motion reaches its quantum-mechanical minimum, and a kelvin is the same size as a Celsius degree, so kelvins equal Celsius plus 273.15. There are no negative kelvins, and the gas laws only work in kelvins, which is why meteorologists convert.

Heat moves in three ways, and all three matter to weather. Conduction is transfer by direct molecular contact, as when a metal spoon in hot soup burns your fingers; air is a poor conductor, which is why still air trapped in wool or a sleeping bag insulates so well. Convection is transfer by the bulk movement of a fluid carrying its energy with it, and it is the engine of thunderstorms, sea breezes and every rising thermal. Radiation is transfer by electromagnetic waves and needs no medium at all, which is how sunlight crosses the vacuum to warm the ground and how the ground sheds that heat back to space as infrared after dark. As worked conversions, a summer day of 30 degrees Celsius is 30 times nine-fifths plus thirty-two, or 86 degrees Fahrenheit, and 303.15 kelvin; normal human body temperature of 37 degrees Celsius is 98.6 degrees Fahrenheit.

sections.heading: Humidity, saturation and dew point
sections.body:
Humidity describes the water vapour present in air, and the single governing fact is that warm air can hold dramatically more of it than cold air. The relationship is exponential rather than proportional: as a rough working rule the maximum vapour the air can hold roughly doubles for every 10 degrees Celsius of warming, a consequence of the Clausius-Clapeyron equation describing how saturation vapour pressure varies with temperature. In concrete numbers, saturated air at 0 degrees Celsius holds about 4.8 grams of water per cubic metre, at 10 degrees about 9.4 grams, at 20 degrees about 17.3, and at 30 degrees about 30.4. That curve alone explains dew, fog, cloud formation and why a warming atmosphere produces heavier downpours.

Three different quantities are all loosely called humidity and they are not interchangeable. Absolute humidity is simply the mass of water vapour per unit volume of air, expressed in grams per cubic metre, and it is rarely quoted in forecasts because it changes when a parcel merely expands or compresses. Relative humidity is the ratio, expressed as a percentage, of the vapour actually present to the maximum the air could hold at its current temperature, formally the actual vapour pressure divided by the saturation vapour pressure, times one hundred. At 100 percent the air is saturated and condensation begins, producing dew, fog or cloud. Dew point is the temperature to which air would have to be cooled, at constant pressure and constant moisture content, for saturation to be reached. It is the honest measure of how much water the air is actually carrying, because unlike relative humidity it does not move when the temperature moves. As a comfort guide, a dew point of 10 degrees Celsius feels pleasant and dry, 16 to 20 feels noticeably humid, and anything above about 21 degrees, or 70 degrees Fahrenheit, feels oppressive and begins to impair the body's ability to cool itself by sweating.

The most important consequence of these definitions is that relative humidity rises as temperature falls even when not a single molecule of water has been added, because the denominator, the air's carrying capacity, has shrunk. This is why relative humidity is almost always highest just before dawn, when the air is coldest, and lowest in the middle of the afternoon, and why dew forms overnight without any moisture arriving from anywhere. A useful field approximation near saturation is that the dew point sits roughly 1 degree Celsius below the air temperature for every 5 percentage points that relative humidity falls short of 100. Applying it to air at 20 degrees with 70 percent relative humidity gives a dew point near 20 minus 30 divided by 5, or about 14 degrees. As a worked example of why dew point is the better measure, consider air at 25 degrees with a dew point of 25 degrees: it is fully saturated and fog is likely. Warm that identical air to 35 degrees during the afternoon and the dew point is still 25, the actual moisture is unchanged, but the relative humidity has dropped to about 55 percent and the air feels far less clammy.

sections.heading: Measuring humidity: the sling psychrometer
sections.body:
Humidity can be measured accurately with nothing more than two thermometers and a scrap of wet cloth, an instrument called a psychrometer that predates electronic sensors by two centuries and still serves as a calibration reference. One thermometer, the dry bulb, simply reads the true air temperature. The second, the wet bulb, has its bulb wrapped in a wick or muslin sleeve kept wet with clean water. Evaporation from that wick carries away latent heat at about 2.26 million joules per kilogram of water evaporated, cooling the bulb below air temperature. How much cooling occurs depends entirely on how readily the surrounding air will accept more vapour, so dry air drives fast evaporation and a large drop, while nearly saturated air permits almost none. The difference between the two readings is called the wet-bulb depression, and it maps directly onto relative humidity through standard psychrometric tables.

The procedure matters as much as the instrument. Wet the wick thoroughly with clean water at roughly air temperature, since ice-cold water will bias the first reading, then either whirl the sling psychrometer steadily on its handle or fan both thermometers vigorously for one to two minutes. Ventilation is not optional: without moving air of at least about three metres per second across the wick, a saturated microclimate builds around it and the reading is falsely high. Watch the wet bulb fall, and take the reading at its lowest stable point before it begins creeping back up as the wick dries. Read both thermometers quickly and in the shade. A large gap, for example a dry bulb at 25 degrees Celsius and a wet bulb at 15, a depression of ten degrees, indicates dry air near 40 percent relative humidity. A small gap, a dry bulb at 25 and a wet bulb at 24, indicates very humid air around 90 percent. If both read identically the air is saturated at 100 percent, and mist or fog is imminent.

The wet-bulb temperature is far more than a stepping stone to a humidity figure; it is one of the most important numbers in human physiology. Because it represents the lowest temperature any wet surface can reach through evaporation alone, it is also the lowest temperature a sweating human body can achieve. Metabolic heat production means a resting adult must continuously shed roughly 100 watts. A sustained wet-bulb temperature of 35 degrees Celsius is therefore the theoretical limit of human survivability, because at that point sweat cannot evaporate quickly enough to remove metabolic heat, core temperature climbs regardless of shade, hydration or fitness, and death follows within hours. Real-world thresholds are lower still, with recent physiological work suggesting dangerous limits nearer 30 to 31 degrees wet-bulb for many people. This is the precise reason that hot and humid conditions are vastly more lethal than hot and dry ones at the same air temperature.

sections.heading: Atmospheric pressure and the barometer
sections.body:
Pressure is force divided by area, and atmospheric pressure is simply the weight of the entire column of air standing above a given point, transmitted in all directions by molecular collisions. Standard sea-level pressure is defined as 1013.25 hectopascals, a unit numerically identical to the older millibar, which equals 101,325 pascals, 29.92 inches of mercury, 760 millimetres of mercury, or 14.7 pounds per square inch. Expressed physically, roughly one kilogram of air presses on every square centimetre of your body, which over an adult's surface area amounts to something like fifteen tonnes of total force. You feel none of it because it presses equally from every direction and the fluids and gases inside you push back at exactly the same pressure. The mercury units survive because Evangelista Torricelli's original 1643 barometer balanced the atmosphere against a column of mercury, and 760 millimetres was simply how high it stood.

Pressure falls with altitude because progressively less air remains above you, and near sea level the gradient is approximately 12 hectopascals per 100 metres of ascent, or about one inch of mercury per 300 metres. That relationship is what an aircraft altimeter exploits: it is a barometer whose dial has been relabelled in feet. Pressure also falls where air is warm and therefore less dense, and where air is rising and being removed from the column. Because the fall with height is exponential rather than linear, the rate itself slows aloft, so the simple 12-per-100 rule is only valid in the lowest kilometre or two.

The barometer remains the single most valuable weather instrument ever devised, and the reason is that its trend, not its absolute reading, carries the forecast. Falling pressure means a low-pressure system is approaching, with converging and rising air, so expect increasing cloud, strengthening wind and eventually precipitation. A fall exceeding 3 hectopascals in three hours is a formal warning of a rapidly deepening and potentially damaging storm; a fall of 1 to 2 hectopascals in three hours signals ordinary deterioration. Rising pressure means a high is building, with sinking, warming, drying air, so expect clearing and settling conditions. Pressure that is both high and steady predicts continued fair weather, with the winter caveat that a stagnant high traps fog and cold near the ground.

Typical sea-level readings range from about 950 hectopascals in a deep mid-latitude storm to about 1050 in a powerful continental winter anticyclone, and the eye of an intense tropical cyclone can fall below 920, with the world record standing near 870 hectopascals in Typhoon Tip in 1979. One practical trap catches nearly every beginner: household barometers and all published weather maps quote pressure corrected to sea level, so if you set an uncorrected instrument at 500 metres elevation you will read about 60 hectopascals low and conclude, permanently and wrongly, that a storm is imminent.

sections.heading: How the three variables combine to make weather
sections.body:
Temperature, humidity and pressure are not three separate subjects that happen to appear in the same forecast; they are three faces of one system, and weather is what happens when they adjust to one another. The chain begins with uneven heating. Sunlight falls on a planet of varied surfaces, and dark ploughed soil, pale sand, forest canopy, city asphalt and open water absorb and re-emit it at very different rates. Air over a strongly heated surface warms, expands, becomes less dense, and rises, and because some of the column's mass has moved away laterally aloft, surface pressure beneath it falls. Air over a cool surface is denser, sinks, and piles up, so surface pressure rises. Uneven heating therefore manufactures pressure differences continuously, everywhere, at every scale from a sunlit field to the equator-to-pole contrast.

Pressure differences then create wind, because a fluid cannot sustain an unbalanced force. Air accelerates from high toward low pressure down what is called the pressure-gradient force, and the steepness of that gradient sets the wind speed. On a weather map this is read directly from the spacing of the isobars, the lines joining points of equal pressure: isobars packed 2 hectopascals apart across a short distance mean a gale, while isobars spread lazily across half a continent mean calm. The flow does not go straight, however, because the Earth's rotation deflects any moving air, to the right in the Northern Hemisphere and to the left in the Southern, an apparent force named for Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis. Above the friction layer the deflection grows until the flow runs almost parallel to the isobars rather than across them, which is why cyclones and anticyclones spin instead of simply filling.

Humidity enters through the third link. Rising air expands into lower pressure and, exchanging essentially no heat with its surroundings over the short times involved, cools adiabatically at 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometre while unsaturated. Cooling drives it toward its dew point, and once reached, water vapour condenses onto microscopic aerosol particles to form cloud droplets, releasing latent heat that further fuels the ascent. Sinking air does the exact reverse, warming by compression, moving further from saturation and evaporating any cloud present.

The result is that a low-pressure system ties all three variables into one coherent object: converging surface air, forced ascent, adiabatic cooling, condensation, cloud, wind and rain. A high-pressure system inverts every term: subsidence, compressional warming, falling relative humidity, evaporating cloud, light winds and clear skies. Underneath sits the ideal gas law, written as pressure times volume equals the number of moles times the gas constant of 8.314 joules per mole per kelvin times absolute temperature in kelvin. For a parcel of air it states that temperature, volume and pressure cannot move independently, and that enforced seesaw between heating, expansion and pressure change is what powers every breeze on Earth and every hurricane.

sections.heading: Perceived temperature, common mistakes, and safety
sections.body:
A thermometer measures the air, not your experience of it, and two systematic corrections separate the reading from the sensation. The first is wind chill, which applies in the cold. A clothed or bare human body warms a thin boundary layer of still air against the skin, and that layer is a large part of your insulation. Wind strips it away and replaces it continuously with fresh cold air, raising the rate of convective heat loss steeply. At an air temperature of minus 10 degrees Celsius with a 30 kilometre per hour wind, the wind chill equivalent is roughly minus 20, and exposed skin can suffer frostbite in about thirty minutes. The essential caveat, widely misunderstood, is that wind chill describes a rate of heat loss from a body that is generating heat, so it applies only to living things. Wind cannot cool an inanimate object below the true air temperature, so a parked car's coolant will not freeze any sooner because the wind is blowing, though it will reach air temperature faster.

The second correction is the heat index, called humidex in some countries, and it applies in the heat. Sweating cools you only if the sweat actually evaporates, and high humidity slows evaporation toward zero. At 34 degrees Celsius with 70 percent relative humidity the heat index is approximately 49 degrees, squarely in the dangerous band. As a working rule, above a heat index of about 40 degrees you should curtail exertion, drink steadily, and move into shade or moving air. Heat stroke, defined by a core temperature above 40 degrees together with confusion, agitation or collapse, and classically though not reliably with hot dry skin, is a genuine medical emergency in which minutes matter.

Four mistakes recur constantly. The first is treating relative humidity as a quantity of water; it is a ratio whose value swings wildly with temperature alone, and dew point is the measure to watch instead. The second is reading a barometer's absolute number rather than its direction and rate of change, which is where nearly all the forecasting information actually lives. The third is forgetting altitude corrections, both to pressure readings and to the boiling point of water, which falls to about 93 degrees Celsius at 2000 metres and means food genuinely takes longer to cook because it is simmering cooler. The fourth is assuming a clear, calm, cold night is benign, when in fact those exact conditions maximise radiative heat loss from the ground and produce the hardest frost and the coldest dawn.

On safety, heat stroke, severe hypothermia and dehydration all kill. Learn to recognise the warning signs early, cool a heat-stroke casualty aggressively with water and moving air while summoning help, rewarm a hypothermia casualty gradually and handle them gently because rough movement can trigger cardiac arrhythmia, and seek professional medical care promptly. This material is educational and is not a substitute for a clinician's judgement.

sections.heading: The Gas Laws Behind It All: Why Pressure Falls With Altitude
sections.body:
Air obeys the ideal gas law to an excellent approximation, and meteorologists prefer to write it in density form as pressure equals density times the specific gas constant times absolute temperature, where the specific gas constant for dry air is about 287 joules per kilogram per kelvin. Combine that with the hydrostatic relation, which states that the pressure at any level equals the weight of the whole air column above it, and integrating the two together yields the barometric or hypsometric formula. Its central prediction is that pressure falls exponentially with height rather than linearly, roughly halving every 5.5 kilometres or about 18,000 feet through the lower atmosphere, governed by a characteristic scale height near 8 kilometres. Exponential decay is why there is no sharp edge to the atmosphere and why the density at 100 kilometres is about a millionth of that at the surface without ever reaching exactly zero.

That single relationship explains phenomena that otherwise look unrelated. The summit of Everest at 8,849 metres sits at only about a third of sea-level pressure, so each breath delivers roughly a third of the oxygen molecules it would at sea level, which is why unsupported human physiology fails so severely there and why the region above 8,000 metres is called the death zone. An airliner cruising near 35,000 feet, about 10,700 metres, moves through air at roughly a quarter of sea-level pressure, which is why cabins must be artificially pressurised, typically to an equivalent altitude of 6,000 to 8,000 feet. Should that pressurisation fail at cruise, the time of useful consciousness is only about 15 to 30 seconds, which is precisely why the safety briefing insists you fit your own oxygen mask before helping anyone else.

There is a second, subtler consequence hiding in the same equation. Rearranging pressure equals density times gas constant times temperature gives density as pressure divided by the product of gas constant and temperature, so at any fixed pressure warm air is less dense than cold air. Humid air is less dense still, counterintuitively, because a water molecule at 18 atomic mass units is lighter than the nitrogen and oxygen molecules it displaces at 28 and 32. A hot, humid, high-elevation airfield therefore behaves aerodynamically as though it sat thousands of feet higher than its surveyed elevation, a quantity pilots call density altitude. Wings generate lift in proportion to air density, propellers bite less, and normally aspirated engines make less power, so takeoff runs lengthen and climb rates collapse on hot afternoons. Density altitude must be computed for the actual conditions, never assumed, and mistakes here have killed a great many pilots at mountain strips.

The same thermodynamics governs mundane experience. A sealed bag of crisps carried to a mountain resort arrives visibly inflated because the trapped air retains its sea-level pressure while the outside pressure has dropped, and a bottle capped at altitude audibly crushes itself on the drive back down as the returning atmosphere squeezes it.

sections.heading: Lapse Rates, Stability, and Inversions
sections.body:
How fast temperature actually falls with height on a particular day, called the environmental lapse rate, determines whether the atmosphere encourages or suppresses vertical motion, and that single property decides whether the sky stays flat and quiet or erupts into thunderstorms. Its global average is about 6.5 degrees Celsius per kilometre, but the value measured by any individual weather balloon on any given morning may be nothing like that. To judge it you compare the observed profile against two reference rates that describe how a moving parcel of air behaves.

The dry adiabatic lapse rate, a fixed 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometre, is how fast an unsaturated parcel cools purely from expanding as it rises into lower pressure, exchanging no heat with its surroundings. The word adiabatic means exactly that, no heat exchanged. The moist or saturated adiabatic lapse rate is slower, ranging from about 4 degrees per kilometre in very warm, moisture-laden tropical air to nearly 7 in cold air, because once the parcel saturates, condensation releases latent heat inside it that partly offsets the cooling of expansion. The variability is not a rounding error but a direct measure of how much water was available to condense.

Comparing the environment against these two references yields the day's stability. If the environment cools faster than 9.8 degrees per kilometre, which is rare and usually confined to a shallow layer over strongly heated ground, the atmosphere is absolutely unstable and any parcel nudged upward finds itself warmer and lighter than its surroundings and accelerates away on its own. If the environmental rate lies between the moist and dry rates, which is the ordinary setup ahead of real thunderstorms, the air is conditionally unstable: it resists rising until some external agent, a front, a mountain slope or strong afternoon heating, lifts a parcel past the level of free convection where it saturates, after which it runs away upward and can build a 12-kilometre cumulonimbus in under an hour. If the environment cools more slowly than the moist rate, or warms with height, the atmosphere is stable and resists vertical motion at every level.

A layer in which temperature actually increases with height is a temperature inversion, the strongest form of stability. A radiational inversion forms on clear, calm nights when the ground radiates infrared to space and cools faster than the air above it, and it explains a cluster of familiar effects: valley towns collect the thickest fog, frost forms in low hollows even when the official forecast low stays above freezing, pollution accumulates near the surface, and sound and smell carry unusually far because the inversion refracts sound waves back toward the ground. A subsidence inversion is different in origin and far more consequential: air sinking beneath a stationary high-pressure system warms adiabatically as it descends, forming a warm lid perhaps a kilometre up that nothing can rise through. That lid is what turns an ordinary hot spell into a week-long heat wave and a city's exhaust into a multi-day smog episode.

sections.heading: Building a Simple Home Weather Station
sections.body:
You do not need professional equipment to start collecting real, useful data about your own local atmosphere, and a modest home station will quickly reveal that the official figure quoted for your town, measured perhaps at an airport twenty kilometres away, is often wrong for your garden by several degrees. What separates a station worth keeping from a decorative one is almost never the price of the sensors; it is siting and consistency. A cheap thermometer correctly placed beats an expensive one badly placed, every single time.

The single dominant source of error in amateur temperature measurement is solar radiation striking the sensor. A thermometer in direct sun does not measure air temperature at all; it measures its own equilibrium between absorbed sunlight and convective cooling, and can read 5 to 15 degrees Celsius too high. Mounting it against a south-facing wall, or over asphalt or gravel, reproduces the same error more subtly through re-radiated infrared and stored heat. This is exactly the problem the Scottish engineer Thomas Stevenson solved in the 1860s with the louvered white screen that still bears his name. The louvres block direct and reflected radiation while permitting free air exchange, and white paint reflects sunlight rather than absorbing it. The standard exposure is roughly 1.25 to 2 metres above short grass, well clear of buildings, with the door facing away from the equator so opening it never admits sun. A serviceable equivalent can be built from scrap timber or stacked plastic plant saucers, and it will improve your data more than any upgrade of the instrument inside.

A minimum-maximum thermometer earns its place because it records the extremes reached between your visits, which are the numbers climatology actually uses, and it frees you from having to be present at dawn to catch the daily minimum. On pressure, be aware that a smartphone barometer sensor is genuinely capable, typically resolving changes smaller than 0.1 hectopascals, which is ample for reading a trend, but many apps silently display a sea-level-corrected value derived from a nearby official station rather than the raw sensor reading, so establish which you are looking at before drawing conclusions. Whatever you use, record at fixed times rather than when you happen to remember, because an inconsistent log cannot show a trend and a consistent one made with humble instruments can.
ingredients: An outdoor thermometer, ideally a min/max recording type, mounted in a shaded, ventilated spot away from direct sun and pavement
A hygrometer (inexpensive digital ones are widely available from a hardware or electronics retailer), or your own sling psychrometer from earlier in this guide
A barometer, or simply a reliable barometric-pressure reading from a smartphone weather app — many phones have a built-in pressure sensor
A notebook, spreadsheet, or logging app for recording readings consistently
A basic radiation shield or louvered enclosure (a 'Stevenson screen' style box, buildable from scrap wood or PVC, or purchased from a garden retailer) so direct sun doesn't skew your thermometer
Optional: an anemometer and a rain gauge, both available from garden or hardware retailers, to round out a fuller station

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Log Your Own Pressure, Temperature and Humidity for a Week
sections.body:
This routine turns three abstractions into numbers you have personally watched move together, which is a different and far more durable kind of understanding than reading about them. The reason it insists on fixed observation times is that all three variables have strong daily cycles that will otherwise masquerade as weather. Temperature typically peaks two to three hours after solar noon, because the ground continues absorbing more energy than it sheds until mid-afternoon. Relative humidity runs almost exactly inversely, peaking at dawn. Pressure carries a small but real semidiurnal atmospheric tide, with maxima near 10 in the morning and 10 at night, amounting to about 1 to 3 hectopascals in the tropics and less at higher latitudes. Sampling at scattered hours mixes these rhythms into your data.

Writing a prediction beside each pressure reading, before the outcome is known, is the part that converts logging into learning. It forces you to commit to an interpretation while it can still be falsified, and it defeats the hindsight bias that otherwise convinces everyone that they saw the storm coming. Comparing air temperature against dew point at the evening reading is the most rewarding calculation here, because a gap of 2 degrees Celsius or less on a clear, calm evening strongly indicates overnight fog or low cloud, while a gap of 10 or more all but rules it out.

The two-height temperature comparison on a still, clear evening is worth doing carefully, since it is the one measurement here that lets you detect a piece of atmospheric structure directly rather than inferring it. Differences of 2 to 5 degrees Celsius between ankle height and chest height are common under strong radiational cooling, and in a hollow the difference can exceed 8. Note the honest limitation of the whole week: seven days may contain only one weather system, so treat any conclusion as provisional. The habit rewards months, not days.
steps: Set up your thermometer and hygrometer outdoors in a shaded, ventilated spot — never in direct sun or against a heat-radiating wall, the single most common cause of bad amateur readings.
Take readings of temperature, humidity, and pressure at the same two or three times every day (for example 7am, 1pm, 7pm) for seven days, logging each with its date and time.
At each pressure reading, note whether it's rising, falling, or steady compared with the last one, and write a one-line prediction for the following 12 hours based on that trend.

Calculate the dew point each session from your temperature and humidity readings (or a phone app), and compare it with the air temperature — a small gap predicts fog or low cloud overnight, a large gap predicts a clear, dry night.
