On one clear, calm evening, compare the temperature a few inches above the ground with the temperature at chest height — a noticeably colder ground-level reading means you've directly detected a radiational inversion forming.

At week's end, plot your logged pressure trends against what the weather actually did, and check whether the pressure-change categories described earlier in this guide correctly predicted the sky and precipitation you observed.

guides.title: Seasons, Microclimates and Local Weather
guides.summary: Why seasons exist (axial tilt, not distance), how latitude, altitude, oceans and terrain shape regional climate, and how to read and exploit microclimates — the small-scale weather of a hillside, valley, city or garden — with practical rules for siting, gardening and survival.

sections.heading: Weather versus climate, and why seasons happen
sections.body:
Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a particular place and moment, the rain falling outside this afternoon. Climate is the long-term statistical description of weather at a place, conventionally averaged over a thirty-year reference period and including not just the mean but the variability and the extremes. The distinction is captured in the old line that climate is what you expect and weather is what you get. It matters practically: a region's climate tells you what to build for and plant, while the weather tells you what to wear today, and confusing the two produces both bad gardening and bad arguments.

Seasons exist because the Earth's rotational axis is tilted 23.5 degrees from perpendicular to the plane of its orbit, and emphatically not because of any change in distance from the Sun. That misconception is easy to dismiss with a single fact: the Earth reaches perihelion, its closest approach to the Sun at about 147 million kilometres, in early January, during the depth of Northern-Hemisphere winter, and aphelion at about 152 million kilometres in early July. The three percent variation in distance produces roughly a seven percent variation in received energy, which is real but far smaller than the seasonal signal and acts in the wrong direction for half the planet.

The tilt works because it stays pointed in a fixed direction in space, currently toward the star Polaris, as the Earth travels around its orbit. Consequently each hemisphere leans toward the Sun for half the year and away for the other half. The hemisphere tilted toward the Sun receives sunlight arriving at a steeper angle, so a given beam of sunlight is concentrated onto a smaller patch of ground and delivers more energy per square metre, and it also receives longer days, so the heating continues for more hours. Both effects push the same way, and together they are summer. The hemisphere tilted away gets a low sun angle, sunlight smeared over a larger area, and short days, and that is winter.

Four dates anchor the cycle, given here for the Northern Hemisphere and reversed in the Southern. Around 21 June, the summer solstice, the Sun reaches its highest noon altitude and the day is longest, with the Sun directly overhead at the Tropic of Cancer at 23.5 degrees north. Around 21 December, the winter solstice, the Sun is lowest and the day shortest. Around 20 March and 22 September, the equinoxes, day and night are nearly equal everywhere and the Sun stands overhead at the equator. Crucially, the seasons lag the solstices by four to six weeks, which is why the hottest weather in most places falls in late July and August rather than late June, and the coldest in late January. This seasonal thermal lag exists because land and especially ocean take weeks to absorb and later release stored heat, so the surface keeps warming for as long as it gains more energy than it loses.

sections.heading: What controls a region's climate: LOWER factors
sections.body:
The major controls on any region's climate are conveniently remembered by the mnemonic LOWER, standing for Latitude, Ocean currents, Wind and air masses, Elevation, and Relief, with distance from water forming an essential sixth. No single one of these determines a climate; the character of a place is the product of all of them acting together, which is why two cities at identical latitude can be utterly unalike.

Latitude is the master control because it sets the angle at which sunlight strikes the surface and how much that angle varies through the year. Near the equator the Sun is high all year and day length barely changes, giving consistently hot conditions with only a small seasonal swing but often a pronounced wet and dry season instead. Toward the poles the noon Sun is low, its energy spread thin across the ground, and day length swings from continuous daylight to continuous darkness, producing cold conditions with violent seasonal contrast. This alone generates the familiar global bands of tropical, temperate and polar climate.

Ocean currents transport enormous quantities of heat and can override latitude entirely. The Gulf Stream and its extension, the North Atlantic Drift, carry warm tropical water northeastward and keep western Europe far milder than its latitude warrants; Bergen in Norway sits further north than most of Canada's inhabited land yet rarely freezes hard. Cold currents do the reverse, chilling and stabilising the air above them so it cannot rise and rain, which is how the Humboldt Current helps produce the Atacama Desert, where some weather stations have never recorded measurable rainfall.

Distance from water, formally called continentality, works through the enormous specific heat capacity of water, about 4186 joules per kilogram per kelvin, roughly four times that of dry soil or rock. Water also mixes heat through a deep surface layer and loses energy by evaporation, so it warms and cools slowly. Coastal climates are therefore mild and even, with cool summers, mild winters and higher humidity, while continental interiors swing to extremes with hot summers, bitter winters and low rainfall. The contrast is easy to quantify: a maritime city may show an annual temperature range of only 10 degrees Celsius between its warmest and coldest month, while an inland city at the same latitude shows 35 or more.

Prevailing winds and the air masses they carry import whatever conditions exist upstream. A wind arriving off a warm ocean brings mild, moist, cloudy air; the same latitude receiving wind off a frozen continent gets cold, dry, clear air. This is why the western coasts of mid-latitude continents, in the belt of prevailing westerlies, are systematically milder and wetter than their eastern coasts. Elevation and relief complete the list, and both act strongly enough at small scales to reorganise a regional climate entirely.

sections.heading: Elevation and the rain shadow
sections.body:
Elevation cools climate directly and predictably, because temperature in the troposphere falls with height at an average of about 6.5 degrees Celsius per 1000 metres, a figure called the environmental lapse rate. This is why snow-capped peaks stand above tropical jungle at the equator, and why a mountain summit can carry alpine tundra or permanent ice at a latitude where the lowland is rainforest. Kilimanjaro, three degrees south of the equator, carries glaciers on its summit precisely because of this. A worked example makes the magnitude concrete: if a valley floor sits at 25 degrees Celsius, a summit 2000 metres above it will average roughly 25 minus twice 6.5, or about 12 degrees, a drop of 13 degrees that is climatically equivalent to travelling something like 1400 kilometres toward the pole. Climbing a mountain is a compressed journey through the world's climate zones, which is why vegetation belts stack visibly up a hillside.

Relief, meaning the shape of the terrain itself, redistributes rainfall through orographic lift and the rain shadow, and the process runs in four stages. Moist air driven by the prevailing wind meets a mountain barrier and has nowhere to go but up, which is the windward side. Rising air expands and cools adiabatically, initially at 9.8 degrees Celsius per kilometre and then more slowly once condensation begins, and it dumps heavy rain or snow on the windward slopes, which become notably lush and wet. Having shed most of its water, the now-dry air descends the leeward side, warming by compression at the full dry rate because there is no longer moisture to evaporate and absorb heat. The leeward country therefore receives little precipitation and lies in a rain shadow, commonly a desert or dry steppe.

The contrast can be extraordinary. A windward slope may receive 3000 millimetres of rain a year while a valley only 50 kilometres to leeward receives 250. The wet western slopes of the Cascades and the Western Ghats sit against the arid Great Basin and the Deccan interior respectively for exactly this reason, and Mount Waialeale on Kauai receives over 9000 millimetres a year while the island's leeward coast is dry enough for cactus.

A dramatic secondary effect of descending leeward air is the warm, dry, gusty downslope wind known variously as the Föhn in the Alps, the Chinook east of the Rockies, the Santa Ana in southern California and the Zonda in Argentina. Because the descending air warms at the dry adiabatic rate of nearly 10 degrees per kilometre, it can arrive far warmer than the air it displaces, raising leeward temperatures by 10 to 20 degrees Celsius within hours and driving relative humidity below 10 percent. Chinooks have famously lifted temperatures more than 20 degrees in minutes on the Alberta plains. The consequences are practical and serious: snowpack can vanish in a day, causing sudden flooding, and the combination of heat, low humidity and strong wind is the classic recipe for catastrophic wildfire.

sections.heading: What a microclimate is
sections.body:
A microclimate is the distinctive climate of a small area that differs measurably from the surrounding regional climate. The scale can be a whole hillside, a valley bottom, one side of a building, the floor of a wood, a city block, or a single raised garden bed a few metres across. Differences are not trivial: two spots twenty metres apart can routinely differ by five degrees Celsius in overnight minimum temperature and by several weeks in the date of first and last frost, which is enough to determine whether a crop survives. Five local factors produce almost all of this variation.

Aspect is the compass direction a slope or wall faces, and in the Northern Hemisphere the south-facing aspect receives sunlight at a steeper angle for more hours and is therefore warmer, drier and earlier into spring, which is why classic European vineyards cling to south-facing valley sides. North-facing ground is cooler, shadier and moister and holds snow and ice much longer. Every one of these statements reverses in the Southern Hemisphere, where north-facing is the warm aspect, and forgetting that is among the most common errors in applying this subject.

Slope governs cold-air drainage. Air chilled against the ground on a clear night becomes denser than the air above it and flows downhill under gravity, gathering in valley bottoms and hollows to form frost pockets. Low ground can be several degrees colder than a slope only a short distance above it, and frost appears there first and lingers longest. This is why a hilltop is not the coldest place on a still night and a hollow often is.

Shelter modifies wind, which in turn modifies both heat loss and drying. A hedge, wall, fence or woodland edge creates a calmer, warmer pocket on its downwind side, reducing wind chill and evaporation. The rule of thumb is that a barrier shelters a downwind distance of roughly ten times its height, so a two-metre hedge protects about twenty metres. A permeable barrier such as a hedge or slatted fence, which lets perhaps forty to fifty percent of the wind through, actually shelters better than a solid wall, because a solid barrier generates damaging turbulence and a sharp downdraught immediately behind it.

Surface material determines how heat is stored and released. Dark rock, brick, asphalt and water have high thermal mass and absorb heat through the day, then re-radiate it slowly through the night, so the air beside a south-facing stone wall or a pond stays measurably warmer after dark. Finally, moisture and vegetation set the local humidity and moderate temperature: a pond, a shaded wood and bare sand each impose their own regime, with the wood cooler and damper by day and the sand swinging violently between extremes.

sections.heading: The urban heat island: a city-scale microclimate
sections.body:
Cities create the largest human-made microclimate on Earth. An urban heat island is a built-up area measurably warmer than the countryside around it, typically 1 to 3 degrees Celsius warmer during the day and, more significantly, up to 5 to 12 degrees warmer on calm, clear nights. The nocturnal peak is the crucial number, because it is the failure of a city to cool after dark that turns an ordinary hot spell into a lethal one. Five mechanisms combine to produce it.

First, urban surfaces have low albedo, meaning they reflect little of the sunlight that strikes them. Fresh asphalt reflects only about 5 to 10 percent of incoming solar radiation and dark roofing little more, against roughly 25 percent for grass and 30 or more for pale stone. The 90-plus percent that is absorbed becomes heat stored in the material. Second, concrete, brick and stone have high thermal mass and act as a heat battery, absorbing energy through the afternoon and releasing it slowly all night, so the city is still radiating warmth at three in the morning while the surrounding fields have long since chilled. Third, vegetation is scarce, and vegetation is the atmosphere's air-conditioning: a mature tree transpires hundreds of litres of water on a hot day, and each litre evaporated removes about 2.4 megajoules of heat. Pavement cannot do this at all. Fourth, waste heat is injected directly from vehicles, air-conditioning condensers, industry, and the metabolism of millions of people, amounting in dense districts to tens of watts per square metre. Fifth, tall buildings form street canyons that trap outgoing infrared radiation by bouncing it between facades rather than letting it escape to the sky, and simultaneously block the ventilating breezes that would carry heat away.

The consequences cut both ways. Cities enjoy longer frost-free and growing seasons and an earlier spring, and urban gardeners can often grow plants rated for a warmer zone than the surrounding region. Against that, the warm nights during a heatwave are genuinely dangerous, because the human body relies on a cool night to shed accumulated heat, and epidemiological studies of events such as the 2003 European heatwave consistently find nighttime minimum temperature a stronger predictor of excess mortality than the daytime maximum.

Countermeasures with demonstrated effect include cool roofs and pavements in light, reflective colours, which can cut roof surface temperature by 30 degrees Celsius, street trees and parks that provide both shade and transpirational cooling, green roofs, and deliberately preserving ventilation corridors along rivers and wide streets. At a personal level during a heatwave, the coolest refuge in a city is a shaded, vegetated, breezy spot, and the hottest place is sun-exposed paving, whose surface can measure 15 to 30 degrees Celsius hotter than nearby grass and is more than enough to burn a bare foot or a dog's paw.

sections.heading: Local wind circulations you can predict
sections.body:
Terrain and surface contrasts generate reliable daily wind cycles that reverse between day and night, and because they are driven by differential heating rather than by passing weather systems, they are among the very few winds you can genuinely predict without any instruments or forecast. All of them share one mechanism: two adjacent surfaces heat and cool at different rates, the air above them acquires different densities and therefore different pressures, and air flows from the higher pressure toward the lower.

The sea breeze operates by day. Land has a low heat capacity and heats a thin surface layer quickly, so by mid-morning the air over the shore is significantly warmer than the air over the water, which has distributed the same sunlight through many metres of depth. The warm air over land expands and rises, surface pressure there falls slightly, and cooler marine air flows inland to replace it. Expect a cooling onshore breeze on sunny afternoons that typically begins two to four hours after sunrise, strengthens through the day to perhaps 15 to 30 kilometres per hour, and can penetrate 20 to 50 kilometres inland, sometimes marked by a visible line of cumulus at its leading edge. Sailors and beachgoers plan around it.

The land breeze reverses the pattern at night. Land radiates its heat away far faster than water and by the small hours is colder than the sea, so the pressure gradient inverts and a gentle offshore flow develops. It is usually weaker than the daytime sea breeze, perhaps 5 to 15 kilometres per hour, because the nighttime land-sea temperature contrast is smaller than the daytime one.

The same physics operates on slopes at a smaller scale. The valley breeze, technically anabatic, blows by day: sunlit slopes warm the air in contact with them, and that buoyant air climbs the slope and up the valley, which is why paragliders and soaring birds work sunlit hillsides from late morning. The mountain breeze, technically katabatic, blows at night: once the sun sets, slopes radiate heat, the air against them chills and densifies, and it drains downhill and down-valley to pool in the lowest ground, which is the very mechanism that creates frost pockets. Over large ice sheets katabatic flow becomes genuinely dangerous, with sustained winds exceeding 100 kilometres per hour common at the coastal margins of Antarctica, where the whole continent acts as a vast cold-air reservoir draining seaward.

As a worked forecast on a clear summer coast, expect near calm at dawn, a light onshore breeze appearing mid-morning, a fresh onshore wind through the afternoon that peaks in mid-afternoon, calming toward dusk, and a light offshore breeze overnight. A picnic, a sail or a fishing trip can be planned around that cycle with real confidence, provided no large-scale weather system arrives to override it, which it always can.

sections.heading: Putting it to use: siting, gardening, survival, and mistakes
sections.body:
Knowledge of local weather pays for itself in three practical domains. In gardening and farming, tender heat-loving crops such as tomatoes, peppers, grapes and figs belong on a warm equator-facing slope or trained against a sun-warmed masonry wall, which absorbs solar energy through the day and re-radiates it after dark, holding the adjacent air two to four degrees Celsius warmer overnight and extending the usable season by two to four weeks at each end. Never plant frost-tender stock in a low hollow, however tempting the shelter looks; mid-slope is the correct position because cold air drains past rather than collecting. A hedge or permeable fence upwind creates a warmer, calmer growing pocket, and a pond or a mass of large stones nearby buffers the night minimum through sheer thermal inertia.

For campsite and shelter siting in the field, avoid valley bottoms and hollows, which collect the coldest air, pool surface water, hold fog and mosquitoes, and in the wrong terrain can flash-flood with no rain falling where you are standing. Equally avoid exposed ridgetops and isolated high ground, which take the full wind and carry the highest lightning risk. The correct compromise is almost always mid-slope, on the lee side of a sheltering feature such as a bank, boulder or treeline, ideally with an eastern exposure so the morning sun warms camp and dries gear early. Reverse the aspect logic according to the season and hemisphere: in heat seek a shaded pole-facing slope, in cold a sunny equator-facing one out of the wind.

In building and home design, orient the main living windows toward the winter sun, meaning south in the Northern Hemisphere and north in the Southern, for free passive solar heating, and shade those same windows in summer with an eave, awning or deciduous tree sized so that it blocks the high summer sun while admitting the low winter one. Site the building clear of cold-air drainage paths and known flood channels.

Four mistakes recur. The first is assuming the official regional forecast applies precisely to your own spot, when a frost pocket, a sea breeze or a city block can differ by many degrees and by hours in timing. The second is forgetting hemisphere reversal, so that south-facing is the warm aspect north of the equator and the cool aspect south of it. The third is ignoring seasonal thermal lag and dressing or planting by the calendar rather than the actual conditions, which is why late frosts kill so many optimistically planted seedlings. The fourth is underestimating radiative cooling on clear, calm nights, which produces the sharpest local frost even after a mild day.

On safety, local knowledge genuinely saves lives. Recognising that a dry desert wash can flash-flood from a storm you cannot see, that a leeward downslope wind raises wildfire danger within hours, or that a city's warm night can make a heatwave deadly lets you act ahead of an official warning rather than after it. Warnings are issued for regions; you live in a spot.

sections.heading: Frost Pockets and Cold-Air Drainage
sections.body:
On a clear, calm night the ground radiates infrared heat to space faster than it receives energy back, and because air is a poor absorber and a poor conductor, it is the thin layer of air in direct contact with the surface that chills fastest. Cold air is denser than warm air, roughly 0.4 percent denser for each degree Celsius of cooling, and that density difference is enough to make the chilled layer behave almost like a fluid poured onto the landscape. It drains downhill under gravity into the lowest ground available, following exactly the routes water would take, and meteorologists call this terrain-driven cold-air drainage. Flow speeds are modest, often only 0.5 to 2 metres per second, but they are persistent and they run all night.

The result is a genuinely counterintuitive pattern. On a still, clear night the coldest spot in a landscape is frequently not the highest ground but a low hollow, which can measure five to ten degrees Celsius colder than a slope only a hundred metres upslope at the same moment. Anything that dams the flow, a hedge, an embankment, a road on a causeway or a wall across the valley, deepens the pool behind it and makes the frost worse, which is why removing a single obstructing hedge has been known to cure a chronic frost problem in an orchard.

These frost pockets experience damaging frost weeks earlier in autumn and weeks later in spring than surrounding higher ground, which is precisely why orchardists and vineyard planners have for centuries sited frost-sensitive fruit trees and vines on a mid-slope thermal belt rather than in the valley bottom, which is too cold, or on the exposed hilltop, which loses too much heat to wind and gains no shelter. The thermal belt is often a remarkably narrow band, and in traditional wine regions its boundaries are visible in the planting from a distance.

The same physics, applied inversely, explains why a bridge deck ices before the road on either side of it. A road surface is thermally coupled to the enormous heat reservoir of the ground beneath, which supplies warmth upward all night. A bridge is exposed to the atmosphere on top and underneath, has no such reservoir, and therefore cools to air temperature far faster, freezing while the approaches remain merely wet.

One practical qualification matters more than any other. Even a light wind, perhaps 2 metres per second, is sufficient to break up a frost pocket by mixing the chilled surface layer back into the warmer air above, and cloud cover blocks the radiative loss that creates the cold layer in the first place by re-emitting infrared back down to the ground. Frost pockets therefore form almost exclusively on the same still, clear, radiational-cooling nights that favour fog and heavy dew, and scarcely at all on cloudy or breezy ones. This is why commercial orchards fight frost with wind machines and helicopters that deliberately stir the warmer air down.

sections.heading: Lake-Effect Snow and the Moderating Reach of Large Water Bodies
sections.body:
Large, deep bodies of water reshape the climate around them for two connected reasons. Water has a specific heat capacity of about 4186 joules per kilogram per kelvin, roughly four times that of dry soil, so a given quantity of energy raises its temperature far less. More importantly, water mixes: waves and convection distribute absorbed heat through tens of metres of depth, whereas sunlight heats only the top few centimetres of soil, which then conducts downward very slowly. The combination means a lake or sea warms and cools through the seasons with a lag of weeks to months, so a lakeside or coastal location typically shows cooler summers, milder winters, a smaller daily range and a smaller annual range than an inland site at the same latitude.

The most dramatic and locally violent expression of this thermal inertia is lake-effect snow. In late autumn and early winter a large lake is still holding a great deal of summer's stored heat while the first genuinely cold continental air masses begin sweeping across the continent. As that cold, dry air crosses the comparatively warm water it absorbs both heat and moisture from below, which destabilises it precisely the way heating a pan destabilises the water in it. The warmed, moistened lower layer becomes buoyant, rises, and organises into long parallel cloud streets or, when the wind aligns with the lake's long axis, a single intense convective band. That band unloads extraordinarily heavy snow the moment it reaches the downwind shore and is lifted further by surface friction or rising terrain.

The geometry of the result is what makes lake-effect snow so distinctive and so hazardous. A band is often only a few kilometres wide but can be a hundred long, so one town may be buried under a metre or more while another fifteen kilometres away sits under clear blue sky. Snowfall rates within a strong band can reach 5 to 15 centimetres per hour, and single events on the lee shores of Lake Ontario and Lake Erie have exceeded 150 centimetres in under three days. Driving into a band is like driving into a wall, with visibility collapsing from kilometres to a few metres within seconds, which is why these events produce hundred-vehicle pileups.

Two conditions govern whether it happens at all. The temperature contrast between the water surface and the air about 1500 metres above it must be large, and the working meteorological rule of thumb is a difference of roughly 13 degrees Celsius, or 23 degrees Fahrenheit, or more. Second, the air needs sufficient fetch, meaning uninterrupted travel distance over open water, usually at least 100 kilometres, to load itself with moisture. Both conditions explain the seasonality precisely: lake-effect snow is strongest in early and mid winter while the water is still relatively warm, and it fades or ceases entirely once a lake substantially freezes over, because ice cover severs the supply of both heat and moisture. The deepest lakes, which rarely freeze, keep producing it longest.

sections.heading: Getting the Gear to Map Your Own Microclimates
sections.body:
Mapping the small-scale climate variation around your own property requires almost no special equipment, only a willingness to move between a handful of sites within a short window of time. That last constraint is the entire methodology and deserves explanation. Temperature at any single site changes continuously through the evening as the ground cools, often falling one to three degrees Celsius per hour in the first hours after sunset. If you measure one site at eight o'clock and another at nine, most of the difference you record is simply the passage of an hour, not a property of the places. Visiting every site inside a thirty to sixty minute window, and noting the exact clock time of each reading so you can mentally correct for drift, is what makes the comparison meaningful.

A minimum-maximum thermometer is worth carrying because it can be reset and then read to capture the extreme reached at a site while you were elsewhere, though for the moving survey described here you mostly want its instantaneous reading. Whatever instrument you use, give it two to three minutes to equilibrate at each stop before reading, hold it at a consistent height, shade it from any direct light including a torch beam, and keep it away from your own body, which radiates roughly a hundred watts and will bias a sensitive sensor held too close.

A soil thermometer measures something genuinely different from air temperature and matters for gardening decisions, because seed germination is governed by soil temperature rather than air. Many common vegetables will not germinate reliably below 10 degrees Celsius in the soil, and warm-season crops such as beans and maize want 15 or more, regardless of what the air is doing on a bright afternoon.

A compass earns its place because aspect, the direction a slope or wall faces, is the single largest predictor of how much solar energy a site receives, and estimating it by impression is unreliable once you are among buildings and trees. A smartphone altimeter is useful with an important caveat: barometric altimeters drift as the weather changes and can wander by ten metres or more across a day, so use one to compare sites within a single outing rather than to establish absolute heights. Finally, the sketch map matters more than any instrument. A record of readings without a record of where they were taken is unusable a year later, and a year later is exactly when you will want it.
ingredients: A portable min/max thermometer, from a hardware or garden retailer, that you can carry between locations
A soil thermometer, useful for gardening and siting decisions, from a garden retailer
A notebook or simple notes app, plus a hand-drawn sketch map of your yard or neighbourhood
A compass, to note each site's slope aspect — which direction it faces relative to the sun
A GPS unit or smartphone with altimeter capability, to confirm small elevation differences between sites
Comfortable walking shoes or a bicycle, since you'll be visiting several nearby sites within the same short time window to compare them fairly

sections.heading: Step-by-Step: Map Your Own Yard or Neighbourhood's Microclimates in One Week
sections.body:
This exercise turns the abstract idea of a microclimate into a concrete, personally-measured map you can actually act on, and the sequence is designed around one insight: microclimate differences are largest precisely when the weather is quietest. On a windy or overcast night the atmosphere is well mixed and clouds return infrared radiation to the ground, so every site converges toward the same temperature and you will conclude, wrongly, that your land is uniform. On a clear, calm night the differences can exceed eight degrees Celsius across two hundred metres. If the forecast turns breezy, postpone.

Three rounds are specified rather than one because a single reading cannot distinguish between the two quite different causes of a cold site. Simple shade, such as the north face of a building, is cold whenever the sun is up but behaves ordinarily at night. Cold-air drainage into a hollow is the opposite: unremarkable at midday, and progressively colder through the night as the pool deepens, reaching its extreme just before dawn. Sampling at dusk, in the middle of the night and near dawn traces that deepening directly, and the midday round is the control that separates the two mechanisms.

Choosing sites that differ in only one obvious variable is what makes the result interpretable. Comparing a shaded low spot against a sunlit high spot confounds two variables at once and tells you nothing about which produced the difference. Compare a low spot against a slope of the same aspect, or two walls of opposite aspect at the same elevation, and each measurement isolates a single cause. Finish by converting the data into one real decision, then repeat the route in a different season, because one clear night is a sample of one.
steps: Pick four to six nearby sites that each differ in one obvious way — a low spot versus a slope, a south-facing wall versus a north-facing one, open field versus tree cover, paved surface versus grass.

On a clear, calm evening (the conditions that make microclimate differences most visible), visit all sites within the same 30–60 minute window around sunset and record the temperature at each, noting the exact time at every stop.
Repeat the same route a few hours after dark, and again near dawn — the coldest point of the night, and when a frost pocket or thermal-belt difference will show up most clearly.
Log each reading on your sketch map, marking which site or sites were consistently the coldest and warmest across the three rounds.

Repeat the whole exercise at midday on a sunny, calm day and compare: a spot that was coldest at dawn (a drainage hollow) is often unremarkable or even warm at midday, which is the tell-tale signature of cold-air drainage rather than simple shade or exposure.

Use the week's data to make one concrete decision — where to plant something frost-sensitive, where ice will linger longest on your property, or which side of a building makes the warmest spot for winter — and keep the log for reference next year.
